lectures.name: Abortion in Canada
lectures.title: Abortion in Canada
lectures.framing: Gestational age chooses the method, and the method chooses the risks. Everything below 12 weeks can go medical or surgical; above it the options narrow and the complication profile changes. 98% of abortions are uncomplicated.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ the 70-day / 10-week / 14-week / 25-week ladder is the spine of this lecture. Cervical shock is vasovagal at the paracervical block, not haemorrhage. Asherman syndrome risk is 8% after one curettage and up to 30% after a third within 24 hours — trauma, not infection, is the major cause. Dilation & evacuation is the safest 2nd-trimester method, and the limiting factor in Canada is the shrinking number of trained practitioners. Ovulation returns 2 weeks after a 1st-trimester abortion, so contraception starts the same day. Legal termination carries a lower maternal death rate (0.567 per 100,000) than live birth (7.06).

blocks.html: 1. Before the procedure

• No referral needed — most clinics self-refer
  • Pre-abortion evaluation
    • gestational age by ultrasound · medical and surgical history · Rh status · consent · counselling
2. Choosing a method by gestational age
• The 70-day / 10-week / 14-week / 25-week ladder:

rows: mifepristone 200 buccal or oral (the slide prints mcg; the approved dose is 200 mg, so treat "mcg" as a slide typo and check with the lecturer) → misoprostol 800 mcg 24-48 h later
Rigid or flexible cannula + manual vacuum, in the office
Vacuum aspiration with a rigid cannula on an electric suction machine
Cervical ripening, then decompression + removal under general anaesthetic
misoprostol induction of labour, after intracardiac digoxin or potassium chloride
Cervical block with or without sedation, or general anaesthetic
Chemical misoprostol 1-12 h · osmotic laminaria/Dilapan in the os 24 h before
Gastrointestinal effects · 10% delayed evacuation · heavy bleeding · up to 5% fail
Contraindications to local · non-compliant or nulliparous patient
Cervical shock (vasovagal at the block) · uterine perforation · hemorrhage · hematometra
<mark class="lo">↑ perforation vs D&C · hemorrhage · infection · incomplete</mark>
Non-invasive · private · can be done at home

blocks.html: 3. Medical abortion

• Mechanism
    • mifepristone blocks the progesterone receptor → decidual necrosis + cervical ripening → rhythmic contractions → detachment → expulsion · contractions peak at 36-48 h
    • misoprostol (prostaglandin E1) works down two arms: ↓ collagen → ↑ matrix metalloproteinases → cervical ripening · inhibits adenyl cyclase → ↓ cyclic adenosine monophosphate → ↑ calcium → ↑ uterine tone
    • methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, acting on cytotrophoblast, not the embryo · teratogenic

blocks.cap: Mifepristone: progesterone blockade leads to decidual necrosis, contractions and cervical ripening, then detachment and expulsion

blocks.alt: misoprostol mechanism - cervical ripening and uterine tone.png
blocks.cap: Misoprostol: the collagen arm ripens the cervix, the adenyl cyclase arm raises uterine tone

blocks.html:
• Follow-up: appointment within 11 days · beta human chorionic gonadotropin after medical abortion
    • ↓ 50% by day 3 or ↓ 80% by days 7-14 = success · a plateau = failure
  • Treatment of failure: > 50% abort with a second 800 mcg misoprostol · < 5% need surgical evacuation
4. Surgical abortion

• Dilatation required = the number of weeks of gestation · Hegar dilators
  • Skipping mechanical dilation ↓ discomfort and ↓ infection when cervical prep is adequate
  • Cervical shock is vasovagal at the paracervical block, not haemorrhage
  • Dilation & evacuation is the safest 2nd-trimester method · the limiting factor in Canada is the shrinking number of trained practitioners
5. Risk of abortion vs pregnancy
• Maternal deaths per 100,000 (United States 1991-1999, Grimes 2006)
6. Contraceptive counselling

• ovulation returns 2 weeks after a 1st-trimester abortion, so contraception starts immediately
    • if one method already failed, offer a different one
    • same-day intrauterine device (IUD; expulsion slightly higher post-procedure, 3.8%) or DepoProvera
    • tubal ligation the same day if done under general anaesthetic and childbearing is complete
7. Post-abortion fertility: Asherman syndrome

• Asherman syndrome = adhesions inside the uterine cavity
  • Asherman syndrome risk is 8% after one curettage and up to 30% after a third within 24 hours — and trauma, not infection, is the major cause.

blocks.cap: Asherman syndrome on hysterosalpingogram: adhesions show as filling defects in the uterine cavity

lectures.name: Fertilization & Infertility
lectures.title: Fertilization and Infertility
lectures.framing: Infertility is 50% female and 50% male, so both partners are investigated. The lecture runs from how fertilization happens, through who to work up and why couples are infertile, to a six-step work-up timed to the cycle, and ends on recurrent pregnancy loss.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ primary infertility means she has never been PREGNANT — not that she has no children, and a partner's children from another relationship do not change it. AMH measures reserve and does NOT predict natural fertility. Male aging ↓ volume, motility and morphology but leaves sperm concentration stable, and is NOT associated with aneuploidy — that is the maternal-age effect. Recurrent pregnancy loss is ≥ 2 losses, consecutive or not, including biochemical, and ~50% stay unexplained; the treatable one is antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (5-20%), treated with heparin + aspirin at the first positive test.

blocks.html: 1. Fertilization and timing intercourse

• Sperm meet the egg in the Fallopian ampulla
  • Fertilizable lifespan: oocyte 12-24 hours after ovulation · sperm survive up to 5 days but fertilize for only 2-3 days
  • Best chance of pregnancy is about two days before ovulation — have sperm already waiting
    • urine luteinizing hormone (LH) — a true surge is both lines equally dark, and ovulation follows in ~36 h
2. Infertility: definition and when to work up

• Primary infertility = she has never been pregnant — not that she has no children; a partner's children from another relationship do not change it
  • When to start: under 35 → after 12 months · 35 and over → after 6 months · a known cause (irregular cycles) → immediately
  • How common: 10-15% of reproductive-age couples · 85% conceive by 1 year, 93% by 2 years
  • Age: infertility 7% at 20-24 → 15% at 30-34 · miscarriage 10-15% under 35 · ~1 in 4 at 35-39 · ~60% over 40 (mostly aneuploid embryos)

blocks.html: 3. Causes of infertility

• Male factors, in order
    • idiopathic (commonest) · varicocele (2nd)
    • exogenous steroids · erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction · infections · genetic (Klinefelter syndrome, Y microdeletions) · radiation or chemotherapy · lifestyle — marijuana, smoking, hot tubs
  • Male aging ↓ volume, motility and morphology but leaves sperm concentration stable, and is NOT associated with aneuploidy — that is the maternal-age effect
  • Abnormal semen analysis also means ↑ lifetime cancer risk and earlier mortality — counsel him
  • Female factors the lecture works
    • polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) — the most common ovulatory disorder; ovulation induction (a pill, sometimes an Ovidrel trigger) · 5-10% weight loss can restart ovulation
    • endometriosis — in 30-50% of infertile women (closer to 80% in the lecturer's clinic); harms fertility four ways: embryotoxic peritoneal fluid · lower implantation · impaired follicle development (↓ reserve) · inflamed tubes impair transport
      • stage I-II → laparoscopic ablation or excision helps for up to 9 months · stage III-IV → in vitro fertilization (IVF) · avoid endometrioma surgery if she wants future fertility
4. The standard work-up: six steps timed to the cycle

blocks.lead: Each step answers one question: is the brain signalling? is the cavity and are the tubes open? did she ovulate? are the sperm adequate?
rows: follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), LH, estradiol, prolactin, thyroid stimulating hormone
Is the brain signalling the ovary? Rule out prolactin and thyroid disease
Cavity (polyps, fibroids) and tubal patency and antral follicle count
Required by law in Ontario before assisted reproductive technology

blocks.html:
• Ordering estradiol, LH and FSH together is the point
    • an FSH of 30 alone reads as diminished reserve — but if estradiol is also 500 she is not on day 2, and that FSH may be normal
    • LH is checked early because it should be low

blocks.cap: Uterine cycle: follicle-stimulating hormone, estradiol, luteinizing hormone and progesterone across a 28-day cycle

blocks.html: 5. Investigating the cavity and tubes

• Sonohysterogram with ExEm foam (days 6-12) shows the cavity, tubal patency and the antral follicle count in one test
  • Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) — dye and X-ray in hospital — if the sonohysterogram is inconclusive or tubal patency is in doubt

blocks.alt: hysterosalpingogram - tubal patency hydrosalpinx and unilateral block.png
blocks.cap: Hysterosalpingogram: both tubes open, a hydrosalpinx, and one tube blocked

blocks.html: 6. Ovarian reserve and confirming ovulation

• AMH: > 28 suggests PCOS · 15-28 normal · < 15 diminished reserve
    • AMH measures reserve and does NOT predict natural fertility. — it guides in vitro fertilization dosing
  • Confirming ovulation, five ways
    • mid-luteal progesterone (day 21)
    • urine LH strips (a true surge = both lines equally dark)
    • ultrasound (needs daily scans)
    • cervical mucus: 2 consecutive clear, stretchy days
    • basal body temperature
7. What counts as an irregular cycle

• By time since menarche
    • first year — normal
    • after 1 year — > 90 days is abnormal
    • 3 years to perimenopause — < 21 days, > 35 days, or < 8 cycles a year
  • Primary amenorrhea: no menarche by 15, or > 3 years after breast development (thelarche)
  • In PCOS baseline LH can be 18, which is why ovulation strips fail in PCOS

blocks.alt: normal vs polycystic ovary - transvaginal ultrasound.png
blocks.cap: Transvaginal ultrasound: normal ovary vs polycystic ovary with a string of pearls of follicles

blocks.html: 8. Recurrent pregnancy loss

• ≥ 2 losses, consecutive or not, including biochemical pregnancies
  • ~50% stay unexplained
  • The treatable one: antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (5-20%) → heparin + aspirin at the first positive pregnancy test
  • Other causes: uterine anomalies 10-15% · endocrine (thyroid, prolactin, poorly controlled diabetes) · chronic endometritis → 2 weeks of antibiotics · balanced reciprocal translocation ~5% → karyotype both partners

lectures.name: Contraception
lectures.title: Contraception and drugs used in gynecology
lectures.framing: Two questions, in this order. First, which axis is this drug on — estrogen, progestin, or androgen — because the indication and the adverse effects both follow from it. Then, for contraception specifically, counsel from the TYPICAL-use column, never the perfect-use one. The lecture ranks the methods, walks natural, barrier, permanent, hormonal and intrauterine methods, then emergency contraception and the CHOICE project.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The progestin-only contraceptive's primary mechanism is LOCAL, not central — cervical mucus, tubal peristalsis and endometrium, with ovulation suppressed in only ~50% of cycles (the injection excepted), which is exactly why the mini-pill fails at 3 hours late while a combined pill forgives. Estrogen and progestin oppose each other on the endometrium but are synergic on the breast — the one risk adding a progestin does not fix. Combined methods are contraindicated over age 35 at more than 15 cigarettes per day, and a past deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism contraindicates them only when she is off anticoagulation AND at higher risk of recurrence. tamoxifen is the selective estrogen receptor modulator that raises endometrial cancer risk; raloxifene is not — both raise VTE. clomiphene raises gonadotropins by blocking central negative feedback, which is why an estrogen receptor antagonist induces ovulation.

blocks.html: 2. Natural, barrier and permanent methods

• Natural family planning: lactational amenorrhea needs all three — under 6 months postpartum · fully breastfeeding · no return of menses
  • Condoms
    • nonoxynol-9-coated condoms ↑ human immunodeficiency virus transmission and are NOT recommended
    • lambskin gives no HIV protection · polyurethane ↑ slippage and breakage
  • Vasectomy
    • needs a follow-up semen analysis showing azoospermia or fewer than 100,000 non-motile sperm
    • requires monogamy of the female partner to protect her
  • Tubal interruption: regret is the commonest complication, and young age is the risk factor
  • Hysteroscopic tubal occlusion: less invasive, but needs imaging at 3 months and effective contraception for at least 3 months after
3. Hormonal methods: who can take them

• Contraindications are graded on the Medical Eligibility Criteria — the vocabulary the question stem will use
    • ① no restriction
    • ② advantages generally outweigh the risks
    • ③ risks usually outweigh the advantages — avoid unless other methods have failed or are unacceptable
    • ④ unacceptable health risk — the true absolute contraindication
  • Read the table this way: almost every entry in the left column is there because of the estrogen, which is exactly why the same patient can still have a progestin-only or intrauterine method.

cols: Intrauterine (copper intrauterine device / levonorgestrel intrauterine system, LNG-IUS)
rows: acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT) / pulmonary embolism · known thrombophilia incl. antiphospholipid syndrome · major surgery with prolonged immobilization · past DVT/pulmonary embolism only if she is OFF anticoagulation and at high recurrence risk (estrogen-, pregnancy-associated or idiopathic · thrombophilia/antiphospholipid syndrome · active cancer except non-melanoma skin · recurrent)

blocks.html: • The two lectures grade hypertension differently — the drugs lecture calls it relative, the contraception lecture makes it category ④ at ≥ 160/≥ 100. Both are right: below that threshold it is relative, at or above it, absolute.
4. Progestin-only vs combined

blocks.lead: The contrast almost every question turns on.
rows: ~50% of cycles (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection excepted)

blocks.html:
• Benefits of hormonal contraception
    • ↓ ovarian cysts · ↓ ovarian and endometrial cancer · ↓ PID · ↓ dysmenorrhea · ↓ endometriosis · lighter, predictable periods · improved acne and premenstrual syndrome
    • weigh these against the risks of pregnancy itself, not against zero
5. Combined hormonal methods: pill, patch, ring

• The three routes share a drug pair and a failure rate, so effectiveness does not choose between them — the route does, and first-pass metabolism is the whole story
    • the pill has it, and loses potency to CYP inducers and gut-flora disruption
    • the patch and ring bypass it, and carry the higher venous thromboembolism risk for exactly that reason
  • Progestin potency, relative to 1 mg norethindrone (progestational / androgenic)
    • levonorgestrel 5.3 / 8.3 — the most androgenic · desogestrel 9.0 — the most progestational / 3.4
    • norgestimate 1.3 / 1.9 · norethindrone acetate 1.2 / 1.6 · ethynodiol diacetate 1.4 / 0.6
    • drospirenone 1.5 / 0.0 · cyproterone acetate not applicable / 0.0
    • that androgenic column is why Yaz and Diane-35 are reached for in acne and hirsutism, and Alesse is the one to avoid
  • Choosing a pill by complaint: breakthrough bleeding → higher estrogen · acne → avoid Alesse and androgenic pills · premenstrual dysphoric disorder → Yaz · mood symptoms or sensitivity to fluctuation → avoid triphasics, lower progestin · headaches → low estrogen · breast tenderness → low estrogen and progestin
6. Intrauterine contraception

• Absolute contraindications — the list is very short, which is the point
    • pregnancy · current pelvic inflammatory disease or cervicitis · immediately after septic abortion · known distorted uterine cavity
    • abnormal vaginal bleeding not yet evaluated · malignant trophoblastic disease with persistently raised beta human chorionic gonadotropin · pelvic tuberculosis
    • current progestin-receptor-positive breast cancer — hormonal device only, the copper device is still fine
  • Not on the list, and each one is a distractor: smoking · age · nulliparity · HIV · a PAST PID
7. Emergency contraception
The decision is made on the calendar, not on preference.

lectures.name: Drugs Used in Gynecology
lectures.title: Drugs Used in Gynecology
lectures.framing: Every agent here does one of three things: disrupt the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, block the overgrowth of a sex-hormone-dependent tissue, or replace a hormone that is absent. Work out which, and the indications and adverse effects follow from it. The lecture walks the hormonal contraceptives first, then estrogen modulators, progesterone modulators, androgens, the non-hormonal drugs, and the gonadotropin-releasing hormone modulators.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The progestin-only contraceptive's primary mechanism is local, not central — that is the single most-tested fact here, and it is what makes adherence matter so much more for the mini-pill. Every contraindication in the combined column is an ESTROGEN contraindication — which is why the answer to “what can she have instead?” is almost always a progestin-only or intrauterine method. migraine with aura and an acute thromboembolic event are category ④ for combined methods only; hypertension crosses from relative to absolute at ≥ 160 systolic or ≥ 100 diastolic. The patch and the ring bypass first-pass metabolism, and that — not the dose — is why they carry more VTE risk than the pill. Drospirenone is the anti-androgenic progestin (spironolactone-derived) — the one to reach for in hormonal acne, and the one that risks hyperkalemia; estranes and gonanes are androgenic instead. Ulipristal beats levonorgestrel at every interval, including inside 72 hours — an Elentra module question keys this the other way, and the lecture's own meta-analysis slide is the one to trust. GnRH agonists flare before they suppress; antagonists never flare. Finasteride lowers dihydrotestosterone, it does not block the androgen receptor — which is why it shrinks a prostate and thins body hair without touching muscle mass. No emergency contraceptive works once implantation has happened — only mifepristone acts on an established pregnancy.

blocks.html: 1. Hormonal contraceptives: how they work

• Combined hormonal contraceptives — estrogen + progestin
    • Examples: estrogen component ethinyl estradiol or mestranol, 10-50 mcg · pill · patch (weekly) · ring (monthly)
    • Mechanism: Primarily central: suppress gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) → ↓ luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone → no ovulation · plus the same local actions as progestin-only
    • Indications: contraception · dysmenorrhea · acne · cycle control
    • Adverse effects: ↑ venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk (estrogen ↑ factors VII, VIII, IX, X, ↓ anticoagulant factors) — still substantially less than pregnancy · VTE risk factors: age, obesity, smoking, past VTE or hypertension · common to all: nausea, bloating, breast tenderness, headache · estrogen also peripheral edema · hepatic metabolism → cytochrome P450 interactions (antiepileptics, antibiotics, aprepitant)
    • Metabolic, overall: slight ↑ triglycerides · no significant change in total cholesterol · fluid retention (↑ aldosterone) · ↑ gallbladder disease
  • Progestin-only contraceptives — progestin alone
    • Examples: Norethindrone mini-pill · levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) · depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (every 3 months) · etonogestrel implant
    • Mechanism: Primarily LOCAL, not central — thickened cervical mucus, altered tubal peristalsis, non-receptive endometrium · ovulation is suppressed in only ~50% of cycles; the DMPA injection is the exception and suppresses it consistently
    • Indications: contraception where estrogen is contraindicated · heavy bleeding (the intrauterine system)
    • Adverse effects: no ↑ VTE risk except the injection, and except drospirenone/cyproterone preparations (the type of progestin matters) · injection and implant share weight gain, may contribute to bone loss, irregular bleeding, painful, acne · mini-pill missed by >3 h = backup needed
    • Progestin side effects follow the receptor: breast tenderness · axis changes → libido change, depression, bone · androgenic → weight gain, hirsutism, acne, oily skin · mineralocorticoid → weight gain, ↑ potassium
    • Progestin families: pregnanes (from progesterone; medroxyprogesterone) — progestational · estranes (norethindrone) — androgenic · gonanes (levonorgestrel, desogestrel, norgestimate) — some androgenic · 4th generation (drospirenone, from spironolactone) — anti-androgenic

blocks.html: 2. Combined methods: pill, patch, ring

blocks.lead: All three are the same drug pair at the same typical-use failure rate (90 per 1000). What separates them is the route, and the route is what changes the risk.

blocks.html: 3. Adverse effects, benefits and contraindications

• The whole hormone story in one line: estrogen and progestin are opposing on the endometrium — estrogen proliferates (↑ endometrial cancer), progestin opposes it (protective), which is the only reason a progestin is added to an estrogen — but they are synergic on the breast, both driving proliferation, which is why adding a progestin does not fix the breast-cancer risk

• Benefits of hormonal contraception
    • ↓ ovarian cysts · ↓ ovarian and endometrial cancer · ↓ pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) · ↓ dysmenorrhea · ↓ endometriosis · lighter, predictable periods · improved acne and premenstrual syndrome
    • weigh these against the risks of pregnancy itself, not against zero
  • Contraindications are graded on the Medical Eligibility Criteria — the vocabulary the question stem will use
    • ① no restriction · ② advantages generally outweigh the risks
    • ③ risks usually outweigh the advantages — avoid unless other methods have failed or are unacceptable
    • ④ unacceptable health risk — the true absolute contraindication
    • read the table as: almost every entry in the left column is there because of the estrogen, which is exactly why the same patient can still have a progestin-only or intrauterine method

vascular disease · current or past ischemic heart disease · history of stroke · complicated valvular heart disease (pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation risk, prior endocarditis) · peripartum cardiomyopathy (moderate-severe, or normal-mild < 6 months) · hypertension at systolic ≥ 160 or diastolic ≥ 100 mmHg

• This lecture's own contraindication list: breast or other reproductive-tract cancer · past stroke, thromboembolic disease, myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease · severe cirrhosis or liver tumour · hypertension (relative) · undiagnosed abnormal bleeding · caution: smoker over 35
  • Not on the intrauterine list, and each one is a distractor: smoking · age · nulliparity · HIV · a past PID
  • The two lectures grade hypertension differently — the drugs lecture calls it relative, the contraception lecture makes it category ④ at ≥ 160/≥ 100. Both are right: below that threshold it is relative, at or above it, absolute
4. Selective estrogen receptor modulators and clomiphene

• Selective estrogen receptor modulators — tamoxifen, raloxifene
    • Mechanism: agonist in some tissues, antagonist in others — set by ligand selectivity, receptor conformation, and local co-activators/co-repressors
      • Tamoxifen: breast –, endometrium +, bone +
      • Raloxifene: breast –, endometrium –, bone ++
    • Indications: tamoxifen for estrogen-dependent tumours · raloxifene for prevention and treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women
    • Adverse effects: both ↑ VTE · Tamoxifen alone ↑ endometrial cancer (endometrial agonist); raloxifene does not · tamoxifen efficacy ↓ by paroxetine
  • Clomiphene
    • Mechanism: estrogen receptor antagonist at hypothalamus + anterior pituitary, partial agonist at the ovary → removes negative feedback → ↑ GnRH and gonadotropins
    • Indication: ovulation induction in infertility

blocks.html: 5. Estrogen antagonists

• Pure estrogen receptor antagonist — fulvestrant: full antagonism, no partial agonism → advanced breast cancer
  • Aromatase inhibitors — exemestane, formestane, anastrozole, letrozole: block conversion of androgens → estrogens → breast cancer and other estrogen receptor-positive tumours
6. Selective progesterone receptor modulators and emergency contraception

• Selective progesterone receptor modulators — ulipristal (partial) · mifepristone (antagonist)
    • Mechanism: a spectrum from agonist to antagonist, at three sites
      • fibroids: ↓ size by inhibiting proliferation + inducing apoptosis
      • endometrium: stops bleeding · progesterone receptor modulator associated endometrial changes
      • pituitary: amenorrhea
    • Indications: Ulipristal: emergency contraception, endometriosis, uterine fibroids · Mifepristone: termination of pregnancy, Cushing syndrome (anti-glucocorticoid)
  • Emergency contraception acts before implantation, by delaying ovulation and inhibiting follicular rupture

blocks.html: 8. Non-hormonal: anti-inflammatories and tranexamic acid

• Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs — diclofenac, ibuprofen, naproxen (non-selective)
    • Mechanism: ↓ prostaglandin synthesis via non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibition → ↓ uterine cramping
    • Indications: dysmenorrhea, and ↓ heavy bleeding
    • Adverse effects: gastrointestinal disturbance, renal damage · contraindicated in severe kidney disease, gastritis/peptic ulcer, coagulopathies
  • Tranexamic acid
    • Mechanism: Antifibrinolytic — blocks the plasminogen lysine-binding site → no plasmin → clot not degraded · symptomatic only
    • Indication: menorrhagia

9. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) modulators

lectures.name: Vaginal Discharge
lectures.title: Vaginal Discharge
lectures.framing: pH is the first discriminator and it splits the four diagnoses in half. The lecture teaches how to assess discharge, then the four causes in order of frequency: bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, and atrophic vaginitis. Know the ranking, the symptoms and the diagnostic test; for treatment know the route, not the dose.
lectures.keypoints: Know the ranking, the symptoms and the diagnostic test; for treatment know the route, not the dose. ⭐ BV is the #1 infectious vaginitis and is NOT an STI — but it potentiates acquiring one, which is half the reason to treat it. A symptomatic swab reporting "altered vaginal flora" is treated as BV. The classic trichomonas findings are the rare ones — frothy discharge in < 10%, strawberry cervix in only 2%, and the exam may be entirely normal. Trichomonas coexists with BV in 60%; 20% of women culture positive for Candida while asymptomatic, which is why it is treated only when symptomatic. Physiologic discharge is stretchy like raw egg white at ovulation — ↑ estrogen, not disease.

blocks.html: 1. Normal discharge and how to assess it

• Normal: estrogen drives discharge containing glycogen, which feeds lactobacilli and holds the pH acidic — so a pH above 4.5 means the flora has already changed
    • physiologic discharge is stretchy like raw egg white at ovulation — ↑ estrogen, not disease
    • Across the cycle: dry (days 1-3 after the period) → sticky, white or cloudy globs (days 4-6) → creamy, abundant and thick (days 7-9) → clear, stretchy and slippery like raw egg white (days 10-14, most fertile)
    • high-estrogen states such as pregnancy make lots of physiologic discharge
    • colour charts are only a guideline — assess the patient
  • History: amount, colour, odour vs odourless, onset, better or worse, past treatments, itch or rash, full gynecologic and sexual history
  • Physical exam
    • look at the vulva and vagina, not just the cervix — they have their own pathology
    • hair pattern and removal (folliculitis) · architecture · speculum
  • Investigations
    • swab the lateral walls, away from the cervix
    • pH strips read 3.5-7 and are read while still WET (blood has a pH of 7)
    • whiff test: 10% potassium hydroxide alkalizes the amines anaerobes make
    • wet mount, saline or potassium hydroxide, read on low and high power
2. The four causes side by side

Symptoms only — 20% carry Candida asymptomatically and are not treated

blocks.html: 3. Bacterial vaginosis

• Amsel criteria (any 3 of 4)
    • pH > 4.5 · > 20% clue cells per high-power field (epithelial cells with adherent bacteria) · positive amine ("whiff") test · homogeneous milky discharge adherent to the walls
  • Nugent score: 0-3 normal · 4-6 intermediate · 7-10 = BV
  • A symptomatic swab reporting "altered vaginal flora" is treated as BV
  • Post-operative cuff infection after hysterectomy follows both BV and trichomoniasis — the anaerobic environment is what the two have in common
  • No alcohol on metronidazole

blocks.html: 4. Candidiasis

• 20% of women culture positive for Candida while asymptomatic, which is why it is treated only when symptomatic
  • Treatment cautions
    • boric acid is toxic if swallowed and contraindicated in pregnancy
    • long-term antifungals cause hepatotoxicity and cross-react with calcium channel blockers, warfarin, oral hypoglycemics and phenytoin

blocks.cap: Wet mount: Candida pseudohyphae and budding yeast, with an artifact for comparison

blocks.html: 5. Trichomoniasis

• The classic findings are the rare ones — frothy discharge in < 10%, strawberry cervix in only 2%, and the exam may be entirely normal
  • Coexists with BV in 60%
  • Do not use vaginal metronidazole gel for trichomonas — it is not as effective

lectures.name: Cervical Cancer Screening
lectures.title: Cervical Cancer Screening
lectures.framing: Screening works because the precursor lasts years. Most human papillomavirus (HPV) infections clear; some produce a squamous intraepithelial lesion; a few progress to carcinoma, usually after 10+ years. Treat the lesion and the cancer never happens — which is why cervical cancer is 16th in Canada and 4th worldwide. The lecture runs HPV → vaccines → the Pap test → primary HPV screening → self-sampling.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ eligibility is any ASYMPTOMATIC person with a cervix who has EVER been sexually active, from about age 25 — screening is not for symptomatic people, and a never-sexually-active patient may defer. Vaccination does not replace screening. At least 75% of people are exposed to HPV in a lifetime and condoms are only partially protective, because transmission is skin-to-skin beyond what a condom covers. Ontario switched to primary HPV screening in March 2025: HPV negative returns to screening in 5 years, HPV 16/18 goes straight to colposcopy, and cytology is only the triage for other high-risk types. An LSIL alone does not tell you which strain caused it — which is why the strain matters more than the grade.

blocks.html: 1. HPV and how cervical cancer develops

• At least 75% of people are exposed to HPV in a lifetime
    • condoms are only partially protective, because transmission is skin-to-skin beyond what a condom covers
    • risk factors: multiple sexual partners · early onset of sexual activity · high-risk partner · cigarette smoking

rows: Does NOT produce HSIL and does NOT cause cervical cancer
HSIL can progress to cervical cancer if untreated

blocks.html: • An LSIL alone does not tell you which strain caused it — which is why the strain matters more than the grade

blocks.cap: HPV infection through squamous intraepithelial lesion to invasive carcinoma

blocks.html: 2. Vaccines

• Dosed by age, not by a single schedule
    • 9-20 → 1 dose · 21-26 → 2 · 27+ → 2 · immunocompromised → 3
  • Vaccines: Cervarix (16, 18) · Gardasil (16, 18, 6, 11) · Gardasil-9 (those plus 31, 33, 45, 52, 58)
  • Best given at 11-12 years — Ontario's school programme offers it in grade 7
  • Does it work: England has almost eliminated cervical cancer in women born since 1 September 1995, most in those vaccinated at 12-13
  • Vaccination does not replace screening.
3. The Pap test

• Who is screened: eligibility is any ASYMPTOMATIC person with a cervix who has EVER been sexually active, from about age 25
    • screening is not for symptomatic people · a never-sexually-active patient may defer
  • Sample collection — what gets a specimen rejected
    • know the system: ThinPrep: do NOT leave the device in the vial; SurePath: it may be left
    • lukewarm water for the speculum · gel only if water-based and sparing
    • full legal name, date of birth, collection date · check the vial expiry
    • the sample must include the transformation zone

blocks.cap: The cervical transformation zone between the original and current squamocolumnar junction

rows: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy — 95% of results
Repeat the HPV test in 1 year
LSIL · atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance
Repeat the HPV test in 1 year
HSIL · atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL · squamous cell carcinoma
Adenocarcinoma in situ · atypical glandular cells · atypical endocervical cells · atypical endometrial cells

blocks.html: 4. Primary HPV screening

• Implemented: Prince Edward Island May 2023 · British Columbia January 2024 · Ontario March 2025
  • The Canadian algorithm (Zigras 2023)
    • HPV negative → back to screening in 5 years
    • HPV 16/18 positive → colposcopy
    • other high-risk HPV positive → reflex cytology: ASC-H, HSIL, atypical glandular cells or AIS → colposcopy · normal, ASC-US or LSIL → repeat HPV in 1 year; still positive after a second year → colposcopy
    • inadequate test → repeat it

rows: The causative agent itself — high-risk HPV DNA
Cytology becomes the TRIAGE, used only if high-risk HPV is present
Higher — detects more high-grade lesions, and earlier
LOWER — more false positives; HPV+ ≠ high-grade lesion
High, which is what buys longer screening intervals
Degrades it — lower disease prevalence ↓ the positive predictive value

blocks.cap: Positive predictive value of a positive test falls as disease prevalence falls

blocks.html: 5. Self-sampling

• She collects her own vaginal sample
    • it holds mostly vaginal cells and only rare cervical cells · HPV testing still works purely because the test is that sensitive
  • Purpose: to reach the under- and never-screened
  • Where: Australia offers it to all screen-eligible people since 2022 · British Columbia to specific populations
  • A positive self-sample for an HPV type other than 16/18 needs a provider-collected cytology (Pap) sample; 16/18 → colposcopy
  • Equivalence to provider sampling is cautious optimism, not settled

lectures.name: Public Health and STIs
lectures.title: Public Health and STIs
lectures.framing: This lecture is about the population, not the patient. The clinical question is who has an infection; the public-health question is what makes a disease reportable, and what does reporting buy.
lectures.keypoints: the list of risk factors is broad enough that most sexually active people meet at least one — which is the argument for offering testing rather than selecting for it. ⭐ Reportability is what makes contact tracing possible, so it is not an administrative detail but the mechanism by which a diagnosed infection stops spreading. Youth under 25 carry the most chlamydia and gonorrhea.

blocks.html: 1. Sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections (STBBIs)

• STBBI = an infection spread by sexual contact and/or by blood
    • grouped together because the risk factors are shared
    • includes: HIV · hepatitis B · hepatitis C · chlamydia · gonorrhea · syphilis · human papillomavirus
2. Global burden

• Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) acquired daily, worldwide: more than 1 million
  • New infections yearly with one of four STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, trichomoniasis): 376 million
3. Local epidemiology (London)

• chlamydia is the commonest STI in London
  • gonorrhea and syphilis are rising
  • HIV rates have been stable

blocks.alt: sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections reported by year - middlesex-london 2005-2018.png
blocks.cap: Sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections reported each year in Middlesex-London, 2005 to 2018

blocks.html: 4. Gonorrhea and antibiotic resistance

• Gonococcal resistance has forced three changes of drug class
    • penicillins and tetracyclines until resistance emerged in the 1980s → fluoroquinolones in the 1990s → 3rd generation cephalosporins since the mid-2000s
5. Risk factors

• Partner
    • sexual contact with a known STI · a new partner, or more than two in the past year
    • a serially monogamous pattern, since these individuals are less likely to be tested
    • anonymous partnering (internet, bathhouse, rave)
  • Age
    • sexually active youth under 25, in whom chlamydia and gonorrhea are especially concentrated
  • Contraception
    • none, or sole use of a non-barrier method: oral contraceptives, Depo Provera and the intrauterine device all count, because none is a barrier
  • Substances
    • injection drug use · alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy, crystal meth, especially when associated with sex
  • Practices
    • unprotected oral, genital or anal sex · sex with blood exchange, including sadomasochism · sharing sex toys
  • Circumstance
    • sex workers and clients · "survival sex", exchanging sex for money, drugs, shelter or food · street involvement and homelessness · victims of sexual assault or abuse
  • History
    • a previous STI
6. Reportable diseases

• Reportable disease = a disease that specified individuals are required by legislation to report to public health
    • places obligations on clinicians, laboratories, institutions, public health authorities and governments
  • Reportable STBBIs: chlamydia · gonorrhea · HIV · syphilis · hepatitis B · hepatitis C
  • Benefits of reportability
    • Surveillance: incidence and risk in the community, and risk-factor information
    • Public health action: individual-level information enabling contact tracing, and it triggers the legislative authority of the Medical Officer of Health
    • International obligation: fulfils Canada's duties under the International Health Regulations
7. Population-level interventions

• Canadian Guidelines on Sexually Transmitted Infections — the national guide for prevention, diagnosis, treatment and management of STIs
  • Pan-Canadian STBBI Framework for Action
    • desired outcome: reduce the health impact of STBBIs in Canada by 2030
    • strategic goals: reduce incidence · improve access to testing, treatment and ongoing care · reduce stigma and discrimination
    • four core pillars: prevention · testing · initiation of care and treatment · ongoing care and support, on an enabling environment

lectures.name: Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections
lectures.title: Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections
lectures.framing: Treat the syndrome, then trace the contacts. Chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis are reportable, and every one of them is mostly asymptomatic, which is why screening rather than symptoms drives detection.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Test of cure, when it is needed, waits 4 weeks — non-viable organisms persist that long and give a false positive. (Slide 9 says > 3 weeks, slide 10 says 4 weeks — check with the lecturer.) The azithromycin added to gonorrhea treatment is there for chlamydia co-infection. Condyloma lata (syphilis, flat) is not condylomata acuminata (human papillomavirus, cauliflower). Trichomonas' classic signs are rare — frothy discharge < 10%, strawberry cervix 2%, and the exam may be normal. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatic adhesions after PID.

blocks.html: 1. Bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs): chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis

• After the diagnosis

blocks.html: 2. Hepatitis B serology

• hepatitis B serology
    • hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) = acute or chronic
    • IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (IgM anti-HBc) = acute
    • antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs) alone = vaccinated
    • ⚠ total anti-HBc alone is uninterpretable
3. Viral STIs with lesions: genital herpes and warts

rows: Double-stranded DNA virus, herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2
Painful blisters in 24-72 h · may present with urinary retention · resolves 2-6 weeks
Unroof the lesion, fluid for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) · culture less sensitive · bloodwork non-specific
acyclovir, famciclovir, valacyclovir — inhibit replication, do not clear it
Topical podophyllin, imiquimod, liquid nitrogen, trichloroacetic acid; laser, excision, cautery
cervical cancer, oral and anal cancer

blocks.html: 4. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)

PID — the mechanism is a barrier failure. The endocervical canal normally separates the sterile upper tract from the polymicrobial lower tract; a sexually transmitted infection breaches it, and symptoms can appear anywhere along the ascending route.

• How common: 100,000 cases a year in Canada · 10-15% of reproductive-age women have at least one
  • Organisms
    • Polymicrobial — chlamydia and gonorrhea are commonest, but < 50% culture positive for either
    • also anaerobes · G. vaginalis · H. influenzae · enteric gram-negative rods · Streptococcus agalactiae
    • → broad-spectrum cover is required
  • Presents as
    • pelvic pain · dyspareunia · discharge · fever · cervical motion tenderness — the "chandelier sign" · pelvic mass
  • Admit if
    • cannot exclude a surgical emergency · failed oral therapy · severe illness · tubo-ovarian abscess · immunodeficient · pregnant · youth or adolescent
  • Treatment
    • outpatient regimen A: ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscular once + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days with or without metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 14 days
    • inpatient regimen A: cefoxitin 2 g intravenous every 6 hours + doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours, stepping down at 24 hours of improvement
    • surgery only for medical failure or tubo-ovarian abscess — ⚠ PID is NOT easily treated surgically while preserving fertility
  • Complications
    • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome = perihepatic adhesions after PID
