blocks.cap: Pelvic inflammatory disease: infection ascends from the cervix through the uterus and tube to the ovary and pelvis

blocks.html: 5. Other STIs: trichomonas

• Trichomonas' classic signs are rare
    • frothy discharge < 10% · strawberry cervix 2% · the exam may be normal
  • Trichomonas treatment: metronidazole 2 g once, or 500 mg twice daily for 7 days — and treat the partner
    • complications: preterm prelabour rupture of membranes · preterm labour · post-hysterectomy and post-caesarean infection

lectures.name: Early Pregnancy Complications - Spontaneous Abortion and Ectopic
lectures.title: Early Pregnancy Complications
lectures.framing: Two questions run this lecture: is the pregnancy inside the uterus, and is it viable? A positive beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) with pain or bleeding is an ectopic pregnancy until the ultrasound says otherwise, and the ultrasound is only interpretable against the β-hCG level.
lectures.keypoints: IUD + positive β-hCG = ectopic until proven otherwise. ⭐ Rh-negative + positive β-hCG + vaginal bleeding = Rh immunoglobulin, whether the pregnancy is a miscarriage or an ectopic. β-hCG is the most important predictor of methotrexate failure — 92% success below 5000, and 4x the failure rate above it. Half of miscarriages have a normal karyotype; of the abnormal half, trisomy 16 is commonest and always lethal, and XO is the commonest isolated aneuploidy. Cerclage is elective at 12-16 weeks and rescue below 23 weeks.

blocks.html: 1. Types of spontaneous abortion (miscarriage)
• Told apart by the cervix (open or closed), what is still in the uterus, and whether there is a fetal heartbeat

rows: Expectant — no progesterone; treat bacterial vaginosis if found. 20-25% of all pregnancies; ~43% go on to miscarry
Partly passed — before 10 weeks fetus and placenta come together, separately after
Remove tissue at the os; expectant succeeds in 91%
Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics + dilation and curettage (D&C) — 1-2% of incomplete or threatened

blocks.html: • ⚠ Threatened abortion: no progesterone

blocks.alt: spontaneous abortion types.png
blocks.cap: Types of spontaneous abortion side by side: threatened and missed have a closed cervical os, inevitable and incomplete an open one; only threatened (and sometimes inevitable) still has fetal cardiac activity

blocks.html: 2. Ultrasound criteria for a non-viable pregnancy

rows: > 7 mm with no fetal heartbeat
After a sac WITHOUT a yolk sac
After a sac WITH a yolk sac
No embryo ≥ 6 weeks after the last menstrual period · yolk sac > 7 mm · sac small for the embryo (< 5 mm between mean sac diameter and crown-rump length)

blocks.html: 3. Causes of miscarriage

• Half of miscarriages have a normal karyotype
  • Abnormal karyotype (the other half)
    • trisomy 16 is commonest and always lethal
    • XO is the commonest isolated aneuploidy
  • Cervical cerclage: elective at 12-16 weeks · rescue below 23 weeks
4. Management of a spontaneous abortion

rows: 4 weeks is safe and effective; most complete within 2 weeks
200 mg by mouth then 800 mcg vaginally. Expulsion 84-93%, and only 8.8% go on to D&C. Approved in Canada for therapeutic abortion only; $$$
800 mcg vaginally, up to 3 doses at least 3 hours apart. Expulsion 67-76%, and 23.5% go on to D&C. This is the one indicated for spontaneous abortion in Canada; $
95-100% successful, serious morbidity 1%; consider doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 2 doses

blocks.html: • ⚠ Mifepristone is approved in Canada for therapeutic abortion only
5. Ectopic pregnancy: where it implants and who gets it

• How common: 2% of all pregnancies (in-class deck: 7-20 per 1000, up to 2%) · the leading cause of early pregnancy-related death
  • Sites
    • tube 80% on the handout — ampulla 70% · isthmus 12% · fimbria 6% (the in-class deck says 96% in the tube, its diagram > 95%, with fimbrial 11%)
    • interstitial 2% · ovarian 0.5-3% · cervical < 0.1% · abdominal and cesarean section scar 1 in 2000
    • heterotopic 1 in 30,000 but 1% with assisted reproductive technology
  • ⚠ The decks disagree on the tubal share: the handout says 80%, the in-class deck 96%, and the acute pelvic pain deck 98% (and an incidence of 6-16%) — check with the lecturer.

blocks.alt: ectopic pregnancy sites.png
blocks.cap: Sites of ectopic implantation

blocks.html:
• Risk factors (handout)
    • high: previous ectopic · previous tubal surgery · tubal pathology · sterilization (tubal ligation or salpingectomy) · intrauterine device (IUD), past or current, including levonorgestrel · in vitro fertilization in this pregnancy
    • moderate: previous STI · previous pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) · in utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure · smoking · previous pelvic or abdominal surgery
    • low: infertility · age > 40 · first intercourse < 18 · previous appendectomy
  • IUDs (in-class deck): an IUD prevents intrauterine, not ectopic, pregnancy → IUD + positive β-hCG = ectopic until proven otherwise, but an IUD in general does not increase the risk of ectopic
6. Ectopic pregnancy: diagnosis

• History and physical exam
    • the handout's triad is pain, amenorrhea and vaginal bleeding; the in-class deck's rule: abdominal pain + bleeding + positive β-hCG is an ectopic until proven otherwise
    • then: displaced or enlarged uterus · orthostatic hypotension · pelvic mass · bulging fornix · cervical motion tenderness · shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation · lightheadedness · rectal pain · nausea and breast tenderness
  • Investigations: β-hCG · complete blood count · group and screen · transvaginal ultrasound
    • β-hCG doubles every 1.4-2.1 days, and 85% of viable intrauterine pregnancies (IUPs) rise by 66% in 48 hours
    • β-hCG timeline: serum negative < 5 mU/mL · ~100 at the missed period · ~1000 at 6 weeks · peaks ~100,000 at 10 weeks
    • transvaginal ultrasound should see an IUP above a β-hCG of 1500, and 99% by 3150 (transabdominal needs 6500)
    • "ring of fire" · free fluid
    • pregnancy of unknown location = positive test, no IUP or ectopic on transvaginal ultrasound → serial β-hCG and serial ultrasound; β-hCG above the threshold with an empty uterus and no history of heavy bleeding with tissue → high suspicion of ectopic

blocks.alt: ectopic pregnancy on ultrasound - right adnexal sac with possible yolk sac.png
blocks.cap: Ectopic pregnancy on ultrasound: a small gestational sac with a possible yolk sac in the right adnexa, outside the uterus

blocks.html: 7. Ectopic pregnancy: treatment

• Expectant if β-hCG declining and < 200, mass < 3.5 cm, no rupture, asymptomatic, no fetal heart — resolves in 50-70%, more likely if β-hCG < 1000; patient must be reliable
  • Medical — methotrexate (folic acid antagonist): suspected ectopic · hemodynamically stable · unruptured (no free fluid) · compliant with follow-up
    • pre-treatment: complete blood count · AST/ALT · creatinine · group and screen · quantitative β-hCG · transvaginal ultrasound
    • single dose (most common): 50 mg/m² intramuscular on day 1, looking for a 15% β-hCG drop from day 4 to day 7; plateau or rise → repeat
    • multidose: 1 mg/kg intramuscular on days 1, 3, 5, 7, until β-hCG falls 15% from the previous level
    • contraindications — absolute: breastfeeding · immunodeficiency · liver disease or alcoholism · blood dyscrasias · methotrexate hypersensitivity · active pulmonary disease (e.g. tuberculosis) · peptic ulcer disease · hepatic, renal or hematologic dysfunction · β-hCG > 5000 · intrauterine pregnancy; relative: gestational sac > 3.5 cm (in-class deck: mass > 4 cm) · embryonic cardiac activity
    • β-hCG is the most important predictor of methotrexate failure — 92% success below 5000, and 4x the failure rate above it · 15-20% need a second dose · washout 3-6 months of contraception (with folic acid)
    • side effects: GI upset and stomatitis · raised liver enzymes · alopecia · pneumonitis · bone marrow suppression → neutropenia
  • Surgery — salpingectomy or salpingostomy: hemodynamic instability · rupture · previous ectopic in the same tube · unable to follow up or patient request · methotrexate contraindicated · known tubal disease (in-class deck adds β-hCG > 5000 · fetal cardiac activity · significant pain)
8. Rh immunoglobulin
• Any Rh-negative patient with a positive β-hCG and vaginal bleeding needs Rh immunoglobulin — WinRho or Rhogam — to protect her future pregnancies

lectures.name: Endometriosis
lectures.title: Endometriosis
lectures.framing: The disease does not behave the way its extent predicts. The lecture defines it, explains why the pain and the findings mislead, then treats it two ways depending on whether she is trying to conceive.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ most women with endometriosis do NOT experience infertility, despite it being the headline complication. Disease severity does not predict pain, and a normal examination does not rule it out. Pain begins about 2 days BEFORE menses — which is what separates it from primary dysmenorrhea, where pain comes with the bleeding. Many patients have had YEARS without a diagnosis, told repeatedly that painful periods are normal in the teenage years.

blocks.html: 1. What endometriosis is

• Endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity
  • Prevalence
    • 1-7% of the population · 7% of first-degree relatives · 5-33% of infertile women
  • Etiology — unknown
    • retrograde menstruation (most cited — but most women have some degree of it)
    • coelomic metaplasia · haematogenous / lymphatic spread
  • Sites, in order
    • ovaries → uterine ligaments → rectovaginal septum → pelvic peritoneum · can be anywhere in the body

blocks.alt: endometriosis common sites - ovaries ligaments rectovaginal septum peritoneum.png
blocks.cap: Endometriosis sites in order of frequency: ovaries (where an endometrioma forms), uterine ligaments, rectovaginal septum and cul-de-sac, then pelvic peritoneum; it can occur anywhere in the body

blocks.html: 2. Pain, and why the diagnosis is late

• Pain mechanism: inflammation, incompletely understood
  • The severity of disease does not correlate with the degree of pain
  • Pain begins about 2 days BEFORE menses — primary dysmenorrhea hurts with the bleeding
  • Many patients have had YEARS without a diagnosis, told repeatedly that painful periods are normal in the teenage years
3. Asking about dyspareunia

• Ask, because she will not raise it
    • "Have you ever had penetrative sexual activity? If yes, do you experience pain with it?"
    • maintain a non-judgmental, normalizing approach
  • Where the pain is tells you the cause
    • superficial pain on penetration → vulvodynia · atrophy · vulvar skin conditions · vaginismus
    • deep pain points to endometriosis, masses, adhesions or musculoskeletal causes
4. Physical examination

rows: Nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments / cul-de-sac
A normal examination does not rule it out

blocks.html: • ⚠ A normal examination does not rule it out — which is why it takes years to diagnose
5. Diagnosis and staging

• Gold standard: laparoscopy with biopsy
    • the pathologist needs any 2 of 3: endometrial glands or epithelium, endometrial stroma, and hemosiderin
    • early lesions are "blueberry" · late ones are "powder burns" with adhesions
    • ⚠ late disease burns out — no endometrial tissue remains, so a negative late biopsy does not exclude it
  • Because not everyone can be scoped, most diagnoses rest on symptoms and response to medical therapy
  • Staging: the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine classification
    • I-II minimal/mild: superficial plaques without significant adhesions
    • III-IV moderate/severe: ovarian involvement · deep disease · dense adhesions · kissing ovaries · a frozen pelvis
6. Treatment

rows: Suppress ovulation + pain control (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) — the disease is estrogen sensitive
combined oral contraceptive · progestin-only pill · Visanne · progestin intrauterine device · implant · Depo-Provera
Stage I-II: laparoscopic ablation or excision — improves spontaneous pregnancy for up to 9 months post-surgery
Orilissa or Lupron — a chemical menopause
Stage III-IV: in-vitro fertilization, which bypasses the toxic pelvic environment, though implantation stays reduced
Excision or ablation at laparoscopy — reserved for diagnosis, infertility optimization, or refractory disease when fertility is wanted; do NOT repeat it — surgical risk
Endometrioma surgery is avoided where fertility is wanted — it costs ovarian reserve
hysterectomy with or without oophorectomy — not first line

blocks.html:
• Two ways to suppress ovulation, and the split is the discriminator
    • Pseudopregnancy — flood it with progestin: oral contraceptive pill · NuvaRing · Evra patch · Depo Provera · hormonal intrauterine system · Visanne
    • Pseudomenopause — withdraw the estrogen: danazol, a testosterone derivative · Lupron or Zoladex, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists
  • ⚠ Endometrioma surgery costs ovarian reserve — avoid it where fertility is wanted
7. Complications: infertility, chronic pain, dyspareunia

• Complications on the deck: infertility (via tubal occlusion) · chronic pain · dyspareunia
  • Other mechanisms of infertility:
    • embryotoxic factors in the peritoneal fluid · lower implantation rates · impaired follicle development with diminished reserve · impaired tubal transport from a chronically pro-inflammatory pelvis
  • Most women with endometriosis do NOT experience infertility

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
lectures.title: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
lectures.framing: One test sorts the differential, and it is the beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG). Everything that can kill her quickly is either pregnant or bleeding, and the β-hCG tells you which branch you are on before the ultrasound arrives.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ an intrauterine device does NOT increase the incidence of ectopic pregnancy — it increases the likelihood that a pregnancy IS ectopic, if one occurs. That is a denominator effect, not a risk. A ruptured cyst mimics a ruptured ectopic exactly, and only the β-hCG separates them. Significant haemorrhage from a ruptured cyst is uncommon — most bleed minimally, which is why instability is notable.

blocks.html: 1. The pathway: vitals, then the β-hCG
• ⚠ Identify the life- and limb-threatening causes first — that is what the β-hCG and the haemoglobin are for
2. Differential diagnosis by system

• Differential by system:
    • gynecologic — pregnancy and its complications · dysmenorrhea · endometritis · neoplasm · salpingitis
    • gastrointestinal — appendicitis · obstruction · diverticulitis · intussusception · Crohn's disease
    • urologic — cystitis · pyelonephritis · nephrolithiasis
    • musculoskeletal — hernia · trauma · muscle strain
    • vascular — ischaemic bowel · sickle crisis
    • neurologic — herpes zoster · abdominal migraine
    • respiratory — pneumonia
3. History, examination and investigations

• History
    • onset · duration · quality · location · radiation · aggravating and relieving factors
    • associated gastrointestinal, genitourinary, fever, discharge, bleeding
    • past medical, surgical, medication, gynecologic and family history
    • the social history matters enormously in pelvic pain
  • Physical exam
    • vitals · general appearance · abdomen (inspection, auscultation, palpation) · pelvic (inspection, palpation)
  • Investigations
    • complete blood count · quantitative beta hCG · urinalysis and culture · vaginal and cervical cultures · ultrasound · group and screen
4. The four emergencies side by side

rows: Sudden, during vigorous activity — golf, intercourse, exercise
2-3 weeks from the last menstrual period — at ovulation
Stable — she hurts, she is not bleeding
cervical motion tenderness — chandelier sign, discharge
Visceral — stretching of the hollow tube; shoulder pain is from blood on the diaphragm, so it is a RUPTURE sign
Ascending infection through a breached endocervical barrier
Infundibulopelvic ligament compressed → venous outflow blocked while arterial inflow continues → oedema → further compression → ischaemia
Salpingectomy or salpingostomy, or methotrexate if stable, < 3-4 cm, no fetal heartbeat, β-hCG < 5000, normal liver and renal function, reliable with access to emergency care
Antibiotics; admit if pregnant, adolescent, severe or failing oral antibiotics
Surgical emergency — untwist and judge viability, then investigate the mass
Usually self-limited; surgery or interventional radiology if bleeding continues; prevent recurrence with ovulatory suppression

blocks.alt: ectopic pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound - adnexal mass beside uterus and ovary.png
blocks.cap: Ectopic pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound: a gestational sac outside the uterus, between the uterus and the left ovary

blocks.html: 5. Ectopic pregnancy and the intrauterine device

• Presents as pelvic pain, amenorrhea and vaginal bleeding; confirmed with a positive β-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound
  • Risk factors on this deck: pelvic infection · previous ectopic · smoking · adhesions · multiple sexual partners · intrauterine device in situ

• An intrauterine device does NOT increase the incidence of ectopic pregnancy
    • it increases the likelihood that a pregnancy IS ectopic, if one occurs — a denominator effect, not a risk
6. Ovarian torsion: which ovaries tort

• A normal ovary can, but rarely
  • Enlarged ovaries behave like a weighted pendulum — so torsion is usually a symptom of an underlying mass, benign or malignant

blocks.alt: ovarian torsion.png
blocks.cap: Ovarian and adnexal torsion: the ovary, often with the tube, twists on its ligaments and cuts off its own blood supply; the tube rarely twists alone

blocks.html: 7. Ruptured ovarian cyst

• Mimics a ruptured ectopic — only the β-hCG separates them
  • Significant haemorrhage is uncommon — most bleed minimally, which is why instability is notable

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectures.title: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectures.framing: Chronic pain serves no purpose, and it rarely matches the damage. The lecture defines it, maps where it can come from, then walks five causes that are told apart by when the pain comes and what the uterus feels like.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ up to 50% of women with chronic pelvic pain have experienced some kind of abuse or trauma — take the history. Boggy distinguishes adenomyosis from the firm irregular uterus of fibroids. Pain with no cyclic pattern and a normal structural examination is myofascial, and the honest goal there is pain reduction and improved function, not cure.

blocks.html: 1. What chronic pelvic pain is

• Pain below the umbilicus for at least 6 months, severe enough to cause functional disability or require treatment.
  • Acute pain is protective; chronic pain serves no physiologic purpose
    • the intensity is often not proportional to the tissue damage — which is why the examination so often finds less than the story predicts
  • How common: 10% of outpatient gynecology referrals · 40% of laparoscopies · 20% of hysterectomies for benign disease
  • History: up to 50% have experienced abuse or trauma — take the history
2. Where the pain can come from

• Where the pain can come from:
    • pelvic viscera (uterus, ovaries, bladder, urethra, rectum, sigmoid)
    • somatic structures (skin, vulva, clitoris, vagina)
    • musculoskeletal and ligamentous structures
    • gastrointestinal and urologic referred pain
3. The five causes side by side

rows: ~50% of women over 40 on imaging; 25% clinically apparent
Any age; often years of pain
NOT related to the cycle at all
Normal — no lab or physical findings
Uterosacral nodularity · fixed uterus · endometrioma · often NOTHING
Globally tender pelvis, normal uterus, no masses
Endometrial glands and stroma DEEP IN the myometrium — a histological definition; 15-30% of resected uteri (pathology deck)
High resting tone in levator ani and piriformis
Laparoscopy + biopsy (2 of 3: glands, stroma, hemosiderin)
Mostly a clinical diagnosis — history and examination; ultrasound and MRI sometimes help; NOT by biopsy — the glands are too deep, often incidental at hysterectomy
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and ovulatory suppression
Suppression · danazol · gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists · uterine artery embolization (UAE) · hysterectomy is the gold standard
Suppression; submucosal → hysteroscopic resection; large or pedunculated → myomectomy or hysterectomy
Multidisciplinary; manual soft tissue release is essential; trigger-point local anaesthetic; amitriptyline, gabapentin

blocks.html: • ⚠ Adenomyosis is NOT diagnosed by biopsy — the glands are too deep — so although it is defined histologically, it is mostly a clinical diagnosis
4. Primary dysmenorrhea: why NSAIDs are first line

• Menses is a generalized inflammatory state
    • prostaglandins from endometrial sloughing induce contractions → uterine pressure exceeds arterial pressure → uterine ischaemia → anaerobic metabolites accumulate → stimulate type C pain neurons
  • Any hormonal method that reduces menstrual flow improves it, because there is less endometrium to slough
5. Adenomyosis
• Boggy distinguishes adenomyosis from the firm irregular uterus of fibroids

blocks.alt: adenomyosis on mri - thickened myometrium.png
blocks.cap: Adenomyosis on MRI: the arrows mark the thickened myometrium dotted with bright foci, with the endometrium (E) and bladder (Bl) labelled

blocks.html: 6. Uterine fibroids: location decides everything

• Risk factors
    • more common in African American, obese, early menarche and hereditary cases
    • smoking is associated with LESS risk
  • Location → treatment
    • submucosal → bleeding and hysteroscopic resection
    • intramural, subserosal and submucosal → may respond to uterine artery embolization
    • pedunculated → risk of torsion, and myomectomy or hysterectomy
  • Reproductive dysfunction only occurs with fibroids that distort the cavity
  • ⚠ Pregnancy after uterine artery embolization is NOT advised — case reports only, which is what separates UAE from myomectomy for a patient who still wants to conceive

blocks.alt: leiomyoma sites in the uterus - submucosal intramural subserosal cervical.png
blocks.cap: Fibroid locations, which decide both the symptoms and the operation: submucosal fibroids bulge into the cavity and bleed, intramural sit in the wall, subserosal and pedunculated push outward and cause mass effect; cervical and broad ligament fibroids are less common

blocks.alt: uterine artery embolization - catheter route and angiography.png
blocks.cap: Uterine artery embolization: a catheter passed from the femoral artery into the uterine artery releases particles that cut off the fibroid's blood supply, with angiography images of the procedure

blocks.html: 7. Myofascial pelvic pain

• Pain with no cyclic pattern and a normal structural examination is myofascial
  • Goal: pain reduction and improved function, not cure

lectures.name: Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain
lectures.title: Approach to the Pathology of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding and Pelvic Pain
lectures.framing: Exclude the structural causes first, then use age, common reasons and clues to narrow what is left. The differential is ABCDEHIN (Anatomic, Baby, Coagulopathy, dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB), Endocrine, Hormones, Infectious, Neoplasia), and one visible finding can delete five of the eight letters.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ of the four lesions here, endometriosis, polyps and leiomyomas cause infertility — adenomyosis does NOT. Fibroids are not pre-malignant and are not a precursor to malignancy. A mass at the os narrows the differential to the structural letters and away from the functional ones, which is the entire method of this lecture.

blocks.html: 1. The pathway: structural causes first

• A mass at the os narrows the differential to the structural letters and away from the functional ones
    • a mass at the os points to Anatomic · Baby · Neoplasia
    • structural = Anatomic / Neoplasia / Infectious (benign PALE + malignancy) and Baby · functional = Coagulopathy · DUB · Endocrine · Hormones

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Abnormal uterine bleeding"] --> B["Is she stable? Check vitals FIRST"] B --> C["History: general + full gynecologic and obstetric
Physical exam: general, abdominal and pelvic
Investigations: complete blood count, beta human chorionic gonadotropin, Pap if indicated"] C --> D{"Is there a visible lesion?"} D -->|"YES — e.g. a mass at the cervical os"| E["STRUCTURAL
Anatomic · Baby · Neoplasia"] D -->|"NO"| F["Ultrasound in selected patients"] E --> G["Remove the lesion
Send the ENTIRE specimen to pathology"] F --> H{"Functional causes"} H --> I["Coagulopathy · DUB
Endocrine · Hormones"] I --> J["DUB is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION"]

blocks.html: 2. Endometrial polyp

• A benign overgrowth of the lining, in the uterine cavity
  • Two microscopic types
    • those resembling the background endometrium
    • hyperplastic ones, which carry an association with endometrial hyperplasia
  • Rarely a polyp harbours malignancy, so always send the ENTIRE polyp
  • What to tell the patient: not a tumour, a benign growth of the lining, sent to pathology to confirm

blocks.alt: endometrial polyps.png
blocks.cap: Endometrial polyps grow from the lining into the uterine cavity, either broad-based (sessile) or on a stalk (pedunculated), and a pedunculated one can protrude through the cervical os

blocks.html: 3. Leiomyoma (fibroid)

• A benign smooth muscle neoplasm — not pre-malignant, and not a precursor to malignancy
  • ⚠ Rapid growth + a SINGLE mass + an older patient = consider leiomyosarcoma, not a fibroid
  • What to tell the patient: a benign tumour of uterine muscle

blocks.alt: leiomyoma sites in the uterus - submucosal intramural subserosal cervical.png
blocks.cap: Where leiomyomas sit - submucosal, intramural, subserosal, pedunculated, cervical, broad ligament

blocks.html: 4. Adenomyosis

• Why it bleeds: more endometrial tissue, plus entrapped blood in cystic areas that rupture
  • Why it hurts: the myometrium contracting because blood irritates it, plus the same rupture
  • ⚠ NOT diagnosed by biopsy — the tissue is too deep
  • What to tell the patient: not a tumour, not pre-malignant, the lining sitting deeper in the wall than usual

blocks.alt: adenomyosis gross specimen - thick trabeculated myometrium with entrapped blood - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Adenomyosis on a cut uterus: the myometrium is thick and trabeculated, and a dark cystic pocket of entrapped blood sits deep in the wall, well below the endometrium

blocks.html: 5. Endometriosis

• Endometrial tissue outside the uterus
  • What to tell the patient: the lining occurring outside the uterus, going through the cycle just as it does inside
6. The four benign lesions side by side

rows: Uterine cavity, can protrude through the os
Yes — rapid growth in pregnancy, regresses at menopause or after ovary removal
Commonest neoplasm in females; 25% clinically apparent in reproductive age
15-30% of resected uteri; uncommon in nulligravids
Yes — the #1 cause of abnormal uterine bleeding
Cystic from entrapped blood; thick trabeculated myometrium; a DIFFUSE process
Blueberry lesions early, powder burns and adhesions late
Well circumscribed nodule of smooth muscle bundles
Endometrial tissue deep in myometrium with smooth muscle hypertrophy

blocks.html: 7. Dysmenorrhoea: primary versus secondary

• Sorts by age, in the same direction as the bleeding
    • Primary (functional) — late teens and 20s, then declines
    • Secondary (structural, acquired) — more common with aging: PALE (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, endometritis) plus endometriosis
  • ⚠ The E in PALE is endometritis, not endometriosis.

lectures.name: Vulvar Lesions and Vulvar Cancer
lectures.title: Vulvar Lesions and Vulvar Cancer
lectures.framing: The vulva is skin, and three questions separate the three lichens: does it scar, does it involve the vagina, and how much does it itch? Get those right and most of the rest is pattern recognition against a biopsy threshold that is deliberately low.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ 50% of women with vulvar cancer are ASYMPTOMATIC, and where there are symptoms pruritus is the commonest complaint — the same symptom as every benign condition above it. Lichen sclerosus is the commonest cause of chronic vulvar disease and is premalignant, which is why treatment is lifelong. LP is the only lichen in the vagina and mouth — so a normal vulva does not end the examination.

blocks.html: 1. The three lichens

blocks.alt: vulva anatomy - labia vestibule bartholin and skene ducts.png
blocks.cap: Vulvar anatomy - labia majora and minora, vestibule, urethral orifice, Skene and Bartholin ducts

rows: In the vagina AND the mouth
White or waxy papules and plaques · cellophane-like sheen, crinkled, atrophic · figure-of-eight pattern, perianal in 30%
Classic: white lacy or fern-like papules · Hypertrophic: thick, white, looks like LS · Erosive: red plaques with lacy edges, erosions, ulcers
Multifactorial — autoimmune, familial, environmental, hormonal; associated with hypothyroidism
The end stage of itch → scratch → itch
~4% → squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), after > 7 years and in poorly controlled disease
None — but vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) is on its list of causes
clobetasol or halobetasol 0.05% once to twice daily until controlled, then 1-3x weekly — TREAT FOREVER; intralesional triamcinolone if thick
Clobetasol once to twice daily · vaginal hydrocortisone 25 mg suppositories · DILATORS
Superpotent steroid taper: twice daily for 2 weeks → once daily for 2 weeks → Monday, Wednesday, Friday for 2 weeks; night sedation — doxepin or hydroxyzine; patch testing

blocks.html:
• Lichen sclerosus is the commonest cause of chronic vulvar disease and is premalignant, which is why treatment is lifelong
  • Lichen planus is the only lichen in the vagina and mouth — so a normal vulva does not end the examination
    • ⚠ its treatment includes DILATORS
2. Melanosis

• Dark, flat, smooth, 5-25 mm, asymmetric, on non-keratinizing tissue, unchanging
  • Biopsy to exclude dysplasia, because the differential for any dark vulvar lesion is melanoma
3. Aphthae

• After a viral syndrome, in girls 9-20
  • Treatment: prednisone
4. Other vulvar lesions

• Vitiligo — screen for autoimmune disease (thyroid-stimulating hormone, anti-thyroid peroxidase, anti-thyroglobulin, fasting glucose)
  • Molluscum contagiosum — a poxvirus · umbilicated papules · never on palms and soles · self-limiting
  • Yeast vulvitis — splash dysuria · satellite lesions · fissures
5. Vulvar masses

• Bartholin's gland cyst and abscess
    • Bartholin's gland cysts and abscesses are the commonest disorder of the gland; carcinoma is rare.
    • Presents as: cysts usually asymptomatic · abscesses tender, warm, soft or fluctuant, with difficulty walking or sitting
    • ⚠ location is key — do not confuse it with a labial abscess
    • Treatment: incision and drainage, a Word catheter, or marsupialization
  • Vulvar lipoma
    • soft and painless · 1 cm to > 10 cm · the patient often has lipomas elsewhere

blocks.alt: bartholin gland cyst location - lecture diagram.png
blocks.cap: Bartholin gland cyst - where it sits beside the vaginal opening, next to a healthy gland

blocks.html: 6. Vulvar cancer: presentation and workup

• Presents as
    • 50% of women with vulvar cancer are ASYMPTOMATIC
    • where there are symptoms, pruritus is the commonest complaint — the same symptom as every benign condition above
  • History and physical exam
    • LOOK and FEEL: cancers feel firm and can be tender
    • the inguinal node chain must be palpated
  • Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN)
    • most VIN is multifocal and sits on the NON-hairy vulva
    • lesions are often raised, verrucous and white, but may be red, pink, gray or brown
    • ⚠ LS, LP, condylomata acuminata and condyloma lata all mimic VIN — if one is suspected and the lesion does not fully resolve or is refractory to therapy, biopsy it
  • Investigations
    • when in doubt = BIOPSY · multiple biopsies if areas differ · at minimum a 4 mm punch
7. The vulvar malignancies

rows: Younger women; MULTIPLE lesions; vestibule, labia majora, perivulvar, perianal
Flat-topped red, brown or skin-coloured papules and plaques; biopsy shows VIN, invasion occasional
Older women; a SOLITARY lesion; vestibule and labia minora
Pink, red or white papule, nodule or ulcer; frequent association with LS or LP; biopsy often shows INVASION
Basically black, with colour variegation; consider amelanotic if pink or red; friable or ulcerated
Solitary pink or skin-coloured plaque; occurs ONLY on keratinizing (non-mucosal) skin — labia majora, perianal
Eczematoid, well demarcated, raised edges, red background dotted with pale islands; invasive adenocarcinoma beneath in 4-17%

blocks.html: • ⚠ Basal cell carcinoma occurs ONLY on keratinizing (non-mucosal) skin — labia majora, perianal

lectures.name: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
lectures.title: Approach to Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
lectures.framing: Develop an approach rather than memorizing definitions, and divide by age first. Anovulation is the major underlying cause of abnormal uterine bleeding, so the workup walks down the axis asking two questions at each level: is the feedback working, and did the structure form and is it functioning.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anovulation is the major cause of abnormal uterine bleeding - and the ventricular fibrillation arrest with a hemoglobin of 38 was diagnosed only because someone finally asked about her cycles. Nobody had asked. Dysfunctional uterine bleeding cannot be reached while a structural cause is unexplained, because it is a diagnosis of exclusion. The pituitary makes TSH and PRL too, so either can stop ovulation. Every patient over 40 with abnormal uterine bleeding gets an endometrial biopsy.

blocks.html: 1. What abnormal uterine bleeding is

• Abnormal uterine bleeding = any change in frequency, duration or amount of flow, or bleeding between cycles
  • Divide by age first: pre-pubertal · adolescence · reproductive age · perimenopausal · postmenopausal (Week 5)
    • adolescence and perimenopause have the higher rates of anovulation · perimenopause also has higher rates of malignancy
2. The causes: PALM-COEIN and the ABCs
• PALM-COEIN splits the causes into a structural half (PALM) and a functional half (COEIN)

blocks.alt: PALM-COEIN.png
blocks.cap: PALM-COEIN: the structural half and the functional half

blocks.html: • The ABCs say the same thing with other letters:

rows: von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia, liver, leukemia
polycystic ovarian syndrome, thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin, Cushing syndrome

blocks.html: 3. Anovulation: walk down the axis

• Anything that interferes with the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis can stop ovulation
  • At each level ask: is the feedback working? · did the structure form, and is it working?

blocks.alt: hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis - positive and negative feedback.png
blocks.cap: The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis - positive feedback mid-cycle, negative feedback over most of the cycle

rows: Stress · body mass (exercise, anorexia, malnutrition) · chronic disease
The same gland makes these, so an abnormality in either interferes
Follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone → estrogen and progesterone
Did the ovary form (Turner syndrome)? Was it hurt (radiation, surgery)?

blocks.html: 4. Physical exam

• The functional causes show themselves here
  • Inspection: vulva, vagina, cervix
    • skin and colour change (atrophy, fissures) · abnormal discharge · lesions · irregular vascularity
  • General appearance
    • body habitus and BMI · bruising and petechiae (coagulopathy) · cushingoid appearance · signs of thyroid disease · galactorrhea · hirsutism and acne (polycystic ovarian syndrome)
  • Bimanual exam
    • enlargement (fibroids, adenomyosis, pregnancy) · fixation (cancer, endometriosis) · abnormal descent (prolapse)
5. Investigations

• Imaging: ultrasound
  • At the pelvic exam: Pap test with or without swabs (gonorrhea and chlamydia) · biopsy (vulva, cervix, endometrium)
  • Blood tests
    • complete blood count · international normalized ratio · partial thromboplastin time
    • follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, estradiol · TSH, PRL · 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androgen profile
    • beta human chorionic gonadotropin

blocks.alt: endometrial biopsy.png
blocks.cap: Endometrial biopsy in three steps: the thin sampler is passed through the cervix to the fundus, the piston is withdrawn to create suction, then the sheath is twirled and moved in and out to fill it with endometrium

blocks.html: 6. Treatment
• Start conservatively with medicines, then move up the tiers

rows: OCP · Depo · Mirena · Visanne · gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist
vaginal hysterectomy · laparoscopically assisted vaginal hysterectomy · total abdominal hysterectomy

blocks.html: • Choosing a hormonal or non-hormonal agent comes down to the trade-off:

rows: Oral route often preferred, but needs daily remembering

Covered by ODSB (the slide prints "ODSB" - probably the Ontario Drug Benefit (ODB) program or the Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP); check with the lecturer), sustained therapy window — but an "injection" or a "foreign body"
Immediate and effective, but a high side-effect profile and very costly
Non-hormonal and as needed only — but costly, and ⚠ it reduces INTENSITY only, not duration or regularity

blocks.html: 7. Adolescence

• Why it happens
    • the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis takes 2 years to mature · eating disorders and heavy exercise
    • menarche can unmask an undiagnosed coagulopathy, commonest von Willebrand disease
    • always a beta human chorionic gonadotropin, asked in private
  • Treatment by severity
    • Mild = iron and reassurance · moderate = low-dose OCP, the best first line · severe = serial hemoglobin, coagulation studies, intravenous (IV) estrogen.
8. Perimenopause

• Usually anovulation, but rates of malignancy are higher — biopsy
  • Management
    • ⚠ Unstable: IV fluids + airway, breathing, circulation + packed red blood cells · a Foley catheter into the uterus to tamponade · IV Premarin or high-dose oral estrogen, switching to oral at 24 hours · operating room if she cannot be stabilized
    • Stable: estrogen plus progesterone or progesterone alone · TXA · imaging · referral
  • The case: a ventricular fibrillation arrest with a hemoglobin of 38
    • previously 28-day cycles with a pad every 4 hours · now 14-45 day cycles with a pad more than hourly, flooding and clots
    • nobody had asked about her cycles

lectures.name: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
lectures.title: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
lectures.framing: Primary prevention happens before conception; secondary prevention happens after it. Every couple has a 2-3% chance of a baby with some congenital anomaly regardless of screening — that baseline never reaches zero, and every result is interpreted against it.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ In Ontario NIPT is NOT a first-line screen for low-risk women, despite being the best performer - it is kept for the funded indications. A screen gives a risk; only CVS or amniocentesis gives an answer, and only for the assay ordered on it. Noonan has a normal karyotype; Turner does not. Maternal serum screening does not cover trisomy 13. Carrier screening starts with the mother.

blocks.html: 1. Primary prevention: the family history

• Before conception: counselling, a personal and family history, and referral in time to test before pregnancy
    • folic acid from 3 months before pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects
  • Take 3 generations · ask about ethnic background on both sides and any past carrier screening
  • Red flags in the family history — the referral triggers
    • Consanguinity and neonatal deaths · developmental delay or autism · birth defects and congenital anomalies
    • 3 miscarriages, recurrent loss and infertility
    • male infertility — congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, associated with mutations in the cystic fibrosis gene (CFTR)
    • an existing genetic diagnosis anywhere in the family · early-onset heart disease or sudden death · ethnic backgrounds on either side
2. Example: fragile X

• Three triggers to refer
    • a personal or family history
    • ovarian insufficiency with elevated follicle-stimulating hormone before 40, of unknown cause
    • male relatives with isolated cerebellar ataxia and tremor
  • Genetics: an X-linked CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 — over 200 = the syndrome · 50-200 = premutation
    • the premutation causes fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (often misdiagnosed as Parkinsonism) or primary ovarian insufficiency — see FMR1 disorders
3. Carrier screening by ancestry
• Offer screening by the ancestry of both partners:

rows: cystic fibrosis — recurrent mutation analysis
thalassemias and haemoglobinopathies — trigger on mean corpuscular volume < 80 fL or an abnormal electrophoresis. Always start with the mother
Tay-Sachs disease · Canavan disease · familial dysautonomia
1/30 · 1/37 · 1/32 (the SickKids panel on the next slide prints 1/29 · 1/57 · 1/30; check with the lecturer)
French Canadian — Bas-St-Laurent, Gaspésie, New Brunswick

blocks.html: 4. Secondary prevention: screen or diagnose?

• After conception, every test is either a screen (gives a risk) or a diagnostic test (gives an answer)
  • A positive screen always needs a diagnostic test.
5. Non-invasive screening
• Every one of these returns a RISK, never an answer:

cols: What it is actually looking for
rows: a risk marker, not a condition — aneuploidy (21, 18, 13, 45X), congenital heart disease, skeletal dysplasia, Noonan syndrome
Enhanced first trimester screen (eFTS) — NT plus 1st trimester markers
Maternal serum screen (MSS) — serum only, triple or quad; needs no NT
Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) — cell-free placental DNA
trisomy 21, 18, 13 and sex-chromosome aneuploidy — a screen, not a diagnosis
structure — major anomalies, plus soft markers for 21 and 18

blocks.html:
• Every screen answers one short question — is this a common aneuploidy? — and nothing else
    • eFTS, MSS and NIPT were never built to look for a single-gene condition · a condition with no fetal structural phenotype is invisible to the anatomy scan as well
  • In Ontario NIPT is NOT recommended as a first-line screen for low-risk women, despite being the best performer in the table
    • funded indications: previous trisomy · maternal age 40+ · NT > 3.5 mm · positive eFTS
  • NT > 3.5 mm raises the risk of aneuploidy (21, 13, 18, 45X) · congenital heart defect · skeletal dysplasia · Noonan syndrome
    • ⚠ Turner is 45,X with streak ovaries and a webbed neck; Noonan overlaps physically but has a NORMAL karyotype, affects BOTH sexes, is autosomal dominant, and risks cardiomyopathy — so the karyotype that settles Turner is the test that misses Noonan
6. Invasive diagnosis
• These return an ANSWER, because they put fetal DNA in your hands:

rows: 1/400, ~1% (as printed; 1/400 is 0.25%, so the two figures disagree - check with the lecturer)
1/800, ~0.5% (as printed; 1/800 is about 0.13% - check with the lecturer)

blocks.alt: chorionic villus sampling - transcervical procedure diagram.png
blocks.cap: Chorionic villus sampling - a suction tube guided by ultrasound takes chorionic villi for chromosome analysis

blocks.alt: amniocentesis - transabdominal procedure diagram.png
blocks.cap: Amniocentesis - an ultrasound-guided needle through the abdomen draws amniotic fluid

blocks.html:
• Both are only as good as the assay ordered on them: karyotype · microarray · targeted single-gene testing when the family's mutation is already known
    • a karyotype or microarray on that same sample would still miss a 1 base pair variant
    • a mutation already known in the family is answered only by fetal DNA — CVS or amniocentesis — with the mutation-specific test ordered on it

blocks.alt: genetic test resolution - karyotype microarray single gene by size of abnormality.png
blocks.cap: Which test sees which size of abnormality - karyotype, microarray, single-gene testing

blocks.html:
• Timelines are the real constraint, against a 24-week limit on termination
    • NIPT ~10 days · CVS microarray ~2 weeks · single gene test ~3 weeks minimum
    • ⚠ "Lethal" does not necessarily mean the baby dies immediately after birth — technology can sustain life for indefinite periods
7. What each test can and cannot find
• Condition by condition — the route in, and the test that will not find it:

rows: NIPT 99% or eFTS/MSS → confirm on CVS or amniocentesis karyotype
NIPT; midline defects on the anatomy scan → karyotype
maternal serum screening — it does not cover 13
autosomal dominant, several genes; karyotype is NORMAL, affects both sexes
NT > 3.5 mm raises it → CVS/amniocentesis with a single-gene panel
karyotype, microarray and NIPT — all come back normal
amniocentesis (or CVS) with targeted testing for the family's known mutation
eFTS · NIPT · the anatomy scan — neurofibromatosis type 1 has no fetal ultrasound findings
X-linked CGG expansion in FMR1 — > 200 = syndrome, 50-200 = premutation
carrier-test the mother first, then CVS/amniocentesis repeat sizing
carrier screening — mother first, then the partner; both carriers → CVS/amniocentesis targeted CFTR
NIPT; the anatomy scan (echogenic bowel is a soft hint only)
ancestry-triggered carrier screening → CVS/amniocentesis if both are carriers
mean corpuscular volume < 80 fL or abnormal electrophoresis → carrier screen, mother first
an unbalanced fetal karyotype → karyotype the parents

blocks.html: • When a fetal aneuploidy proves translocation-derived, karyotype the parents — a daughter has a 50% chance of carrying it, and the carrier's siblings need counselling too
8. Preimplantation genetic testing

• Preimplantation genetic testing requires in vitro fertilization with or without intracytoplasmic sperm injection, embryo biopsy and selected transfer
  • DNA from: polar bodies · one blastomere from a cleavage-stage embryo · 5-10 trophectoderm cells from a blastocyst
  • Tested by: polymerase chain reaction for single genes · fluorescence in situ hybridization for translocations and de novo aneuploidy
  • Not covered by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan

lectures.name: Early Pregnancy Counselling
lectures.title: Early pregnancy counselling
lectures.framing: Most of what a pregnant patient asks about is safer than she fears. The counselling job is to say what is actually safe, name the few things that do carry risk, and in each case explain why.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Toxoplasmosis risk comes from undercooked meat far more than from cats, and it presents as chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications. The lecture sets two numbers: 18-23 weeks' gestational age for travel and 300 mg of caffeine a day. Zero alcohol is the advice, but low-level exposure is not likely to harm the baby, so a patient who drank before she knew she was pregnant can be reassured. ⚠ The one drug caveat the lecture names is that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may slightly increase postpartum hemorrhage. They do not cause birth defects.

blocks.html: 1. Prenatal care providers
• Midwives, family physicians and obstetricians (see 08 - OB Care Providers)
2. Alcohol

• Zero alcohol is safest (the general consensus)
  • But low levels are not likely to be harmful · use is common worldwide and usually does not lead to fetal alcohol syndrome
    • so a patient who drank before she knew she was pregnant can be reassured
3. Weight gain and exercise

• Weight gain: lower BMI → gain more · higher BMI → gain less
    • many factors drive it, and it may be a sensitive topic, so discuss it respectfully
  • Exercise (uncomplicated pregnancy): aerobic + strength conditioning, regularly, whatever her previous activity level
    • screening tool: the Physical Activity Readiness Medical Examination for Pregnancy (PARmed-X for Pregnancy)
4. Travel

• 18-23 weeks' gestational age is the safest window
  • Some vaccines and antimalarials are safe
  • Most travel insurance does not cover the baby · refer most questions to travel medicine
5. Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

• Very common · onset as early as 4 weeks, peaks at 9 weeks, resolves around the end of the 1st trimester
  • Treatment
    • non-drug: ginger · acupressure
    • drugs: doxylamine-pyridoxine · dimenhydrinate
6. Tobacco, cannabis and drugs

• Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada: ask all pregnant women periodically about alcohol, tobacco, prescription and illicit drugs
  • Tobacco and cannabis smoking are linked to adverse pregnancy and childhood outcomes → offer cessation counselling
7. Medications

• Likely safe: antihistamines · antiemetics · puffers · antidepressants · many common antibiotics
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
    • no link to birth defects, preterm birth, preeclampsia or stillbirth
    • ⚠ may slightly increase postpartum hemorrhage
8. Work

• Harmful jobs are rare; most jobs are fine
  • Minimise the risk with human resources / occupational health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
9. Food

• Risk extremely low: raw eggs · deli meats · soft cheeses · sushi · most fish, eaten regularly
  • Avoid or limit
    • raw / rare / undercooked meat → toxoplasmosis, a much higher risk than from cats
    • top-predator fish, only rarely - they carry high mercury
  • Congenital toxoplasmosis, classic triad: chorioretinitis · hydrocephalus · intracranial calcifications
10. Supplements and caffeine

• Folic acid prevents neural tube defects and preterm birth
  • Caffeine ≤ 2 cups of coffee (300 mg) a day is safe

lectures.name: In-Class - Amenorrhea
lectures.title: Approach to Amenorrhea
lectures.framing: Amenorrhea is a compartment problem — the block sits in the outflow tract, the ovary, the pituitary or the hypothalamus — and two numbers sort it: the beta hCG first, always, then follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which says whether the pituitary is shouting at a dead ovary (high FSH) or not shouting at all (low FSH).
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ rule out pregnancy first, before any other test and whatever the story sounds like. High FSH means the ovary has failed; low FSH means the problem is above it — that one number splits the differential, and a normal FSH with normal prolactin and TSH points at anovulation, which is where PCOS lives. Pregnancy is the commonest cause of secondary amenorrhea; after it comes PCOS (28%). Turner is the commonest primary cause (27%). Pubarche and testosterone split MRKH (46,XX) from androgen insensitivity (46,XY).

blocks.html: 1. Primary and secondary amenorrhea

• Primary = no menses ever
    • no menses by 15, or more than 3 years after secondary sexual development began · no secondary sex characteristics at all by 13 is abnormal too
    • commonest: Turner syndrome (27%) · Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome (15%) · constitutional delay (14%)
  • Secondary = 3 months without menses after menarche (also used: ≤ 9 periods/year)
    • commonest cause: pregnancy · then polycystic ovarian syndrome (28%) · functional hypothalamic (15%) · prolactinoma or pituitary adenoma (10%)
  • ⚠ The workbook keys primary amenorrhea as "no periods by 16"; the lecture uses 13 and 15 — answer to the source in front of you
2. The compartments, side by side

blocks.alt: amenorrhea compartments - hypothalamus pituitary ovary uterus outflow tract - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The five compartments - hypothalamic, pituitary, ovarian, uterine, outflow tract - with the feedback questions for the top three and the anatomic questions for the bottom three

blocks.html: • Sort by FSH and estrogen; each column is one place the block can sit:

rows: Blood is made but cannot get out
No follicles left to answer the gonadotropins
No ovulation → no progesterone → no withdrawal bleed
imperforate hymen — commonest outflow anomaly · Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome (MRKH) (15%) · transverse vaginal septum · androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS)
Turner syndrome (27%) · gonadal dysgenesis (XX or XY)
polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) — uncommon this early
Asherman syndrome — after instrumentation · cervical stenosis
PCOS (28%) · late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia · thyroid disease
Cyclical pain with no bleeding, a midline mass, a purplish bulge at the introitus (hematocolpos); trapped blood → soft enlarged uterus (hematometra)
Vasomotor symptoms; short stature, webbed neck, shield chest
Galactorrhoea, headache, bitemporal field loss; failure to lactate after postpartum hemorrhage
hirsutism, acne, obesity; cycles irregular rather than absent
Ultrasound and bimanual for a uterus; then pubarche and testosterone split MRKH (46,XX, female range, hair present) from AIS (46,XY, male range, hair absent)
MRI only once functional causes are excluded
Hymenotomy, septum resection, adhesiolysis; excise the gonads in AIS — malignancy risk
Hormone replacement therapy to protect bone; donor oocyte for fertility
Dopamine agonist first line for a prolactinoma, not surgery; levothyroxine if hypothyroid
Restore energy availability; hormone replacement therapy if it persists
Combined oral contraceptive or cyclic progestin — oppose the estrogen, protect the endometrium

blocks.html: 3. Why thyroid and prolactin share a branch

• ↓ thyroxine → ↑ thyrotropin-releasing hormone → ↑ thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and ↑ prolactin → prolactin suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulses → anovulation
  • hyperprolactinemia is present in 10% of amenorrhoeic women and 50% of those with galactorrhoea
    • as often a drug as a tumour
4. The approach

blocks.alt: Approach to Amenorrhea.png
blocks.cap: The full lab-based approach, from the beta human chorionic gonadotropin (beta hCG) down

blocks.html: • Rule out pregnancy first, then check for a uterus, then prolactin and TSH, then FSH:

• History
    • cycle history · weight change, exercise load, stressors, eating pattern · galactorrhoea, headache, visual change, anosmia · hirsutism
    • postpartum haemorrhage · instrumentation (dilation and curettage, ablation) · ⚠ antipsychotics and other dopamine antagonists, contraceptives
  • Physical exam
    • plot the growth chart: overweight and not growing → endocrinopathy (hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome) · underweight → a calorie deficit (eating disorder, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease)
    • height and BMI · Tanner staging, pubic hair · visual fields · breast and expressed galactorrhoea
    • speculum and bimanual pelvic exam for a cervix, a uterus, a septum or an imperforate hymen
  • Investigations
    • beta hCG before anything else · serum FSH / serum luteinizing hormone · serum prolactin · serum TSH and free thyroxine · androgens · pelvic ultrasound
    • karyotype when FSH is high · ⚠ MRI is not first line
  • Follow-up: estrogen deficiency costs bone whatever the compartment, so treat it in all four

lectures.name: Hysterectomy Approaches
lectures.title: Hysterectomy approaches
lectures.framing: Choose the least invasive route the anatomy allows. Every approach is a "short stay" with same-day discharge except abdominal, and the lecture walks the routes down a ladder, each rung being what to use when the one above is blocked.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Abdominal is the only approach not planned as same-day discharge - it needs a 2-3 day hospital stay. Vaginal is the only approach without abdominal entry, and the one where tubes and ovaries are not as accessible. Shared limitation of every minimally invasive route is a large uterus; the vaginal-route pair add narrow introitus/pelvis and poor uterine descent, and the laparoscopic pair add suturing skill and operative time. TLH and robotic replace abdominal, not vaginal/LAVH.

blocks.html: 1. Choosing the route

• ⚠ When the indication is bleeding control, medical options come first - hysterectomy is for failed medical management and special circumstances
  • The ladder: vaginal → laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (LAVH) → total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH) or robotic → abdominal
  • The first four are minimally invasive · shared limitation of every minimally invasive route: a large uterus

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Hysterectomy planned"] --> B{"Anatomy amenable to a vaginal route?
(uterine descent, introitus/pelvis, uterine size)"} B -->|"Yes, and no prior pelvic surgery / scarring, tubes and ovaries not needed"| C["VAGINAL - no abdominal incision"] B -->|"Yes, but the pelvis must be assessed or tubes/ovaries removed"| D["LAVH - abdomen entered, uterus out through the vagina"] B -->|No| E{"Very large uterus, complex cancer, or a failed minimally invasive attempt?"} E -->|No| F["TLH or ROBOTIC - replaces abdominal, never vaginal/LAVH
Robotic: morbidly obese patients"] E -->|Yes| G["ABDOMINAL - not minimally invasive
2-3 day hospital stay"]

blocks.html: 2. Vaginal hysterectomy

• Minimally invasive · no abdominal incisions - the fewest incisions of any approach
  • Short stay · same-day discharge
  • Limitations
    • prior pelvic surgery · extensive scarring · large uterus · narrow introitus/pelvis · poor uterine descent
    • tubes/ovaries not as accessible
3. Laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (LAVH)

• Minimally invasive · requires entry into the abdomen · uterus removed via the vagina
  • Short stay · same-day discharge
  • Used in place of vaginal, when the pelvis needs assessing or the tubes and ovaries need removing
  • What it adds
    • assess the pelvis/scarring · bladder flap · remove tubes/ovaries · "second look" for hemostasis
  • Limitations: large uterus · narrow introitus/pelvis · poor uterine descent
4. Total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH)

• Minimally invasive · requires entry into the abdomen · short stay, same-day discharge
  • Used in place of abdominal - should NOT replace vaginal/LAVH
  • Limitations: large uterus · laparoscopic suturing takes skill and more operative time
5. Robotic-assisted hysterectomy

• Minimally invasive · requires entry into the abdomen · short stay, same-day discharge
  • Used in place of abdominal - should NOT replace vaginal/LAVH
  • Excellent option for morbidly obese patients
  • Limitations
    • large uterus (articulating instruments make it more manageable)
    • laparoscopic suturing takes skill and more operative time
6. Abdominal hysterectomy

• NOT minimally invasive · 2-3 day hospital stay
  • Reserved for
    • more complex cancers · patient factors not amenable to a minimally invasive approach · very large uterus · complications during a minimally invasive attempt
7. Types of hysterectomy
• Named by what comes out:

rows: Uterus, with or without cervix, with or without tubes

lectures.name: Dilation and Curettage
lectures.title: Dilation and curettage
lectures.framing: One procedure, one objective: know what goes wrong and what you do about it. Every complication is a consequence of one step, so learn the complications by the step that causes them.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated for therapeutic abortion but NOT for a D&C done for missed abortion or pregnancy loss - the same procedure, two indications, one gets antibiotics. Repeat curettage is what drives Asherman's. Hematometra is re-evacuated immediately; retained products may wait for medical management - the two "something is still in the uterus" complications get opposite tempos.

blocks.html: 1. What a dilation and curettage is

• Dilation and curettage (D&C) = vacuum aspiration of a pregnancy under 14 weeks through a rigid cannula on electric suction
  • Indications (both under 14 weeks)
    • first-trimester pregnancy loss: incomplete, inevitable, missed abortion
    • therapeutic abortion
  • Not for: ectopic pregnancy (nothing in the cavity) · termination over 14 weeks · endometritis
  • Sequence: cervical preparation → bimanual exam confirms gestation → paracervical block → mechanical dilation only if preparation was inadequate → suction curettage of all products
2. Cervical preparation
• May be unnecessary if the cervix is already open (incomplete or inevitable abortion):

rows: may be unnecessary if the cervix is already open (incomplete / inevitable abortion)
24 hours before, placed in the internal os
swells as it takes up fluid

blocks.alt: osmotic cervical dilators - laminaria and dilapan swelling over 24 hours.png
blocks.cap: Osmotic dilators: laminaria (seaweed) and Dilapan swelling from 0 to 24 hours

blocks.html: 3. Bimanual exam and anesthesia

• Bimanual exam confirms gestation and gestational age
  • Paracervical block at this step
  • Anesthesia overall: local (cervical block with or without conscious sedation) or general
4. Mechanical dilation and curettage

• Mechanical dilation with Hegar dilators, only if preparation was inadequate
    • amount of dilatation = weeks of gestation
    • skipping it lowers discomfort and infection
  • Suction curettage of all products · sharp curettage is unnecessary in most cases
5. Complications
• The lecture's only objective - each belongs to a step:

rows: suspected during the procedure; visceral injury in rarer cases
finish under ultrasound or laparoscopic guidance
prophylaxis for therapeutic abortion, NOT for missed abortion / pregnancy loss
points to uterine atony, low implantation, or larger gestational age
adhesions in the endometrial cavity → secondary amenorrhea
prevention: avoid repeat and sharp curettage

blocks.html:
• Asherman's risk
    • ⚠ Asherman's follows curettage in 8%, and repeat curettage (for retained products or retained placenta post partum) raises it to 30% by a third consecutive procedure (within 24 hours) (as the slide prints it; the commonly cited figures are about 16% after one curettage and about 32% after three or more, with no 24-hour window - check with the lecturer)
    • so retained products are managed with misoprostol where possible, rather than a reflex second D&C

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Menopause
lectures.title: Clinical approach to menopause
lectures.framing: Every treatment decision splits on which symptom you are treating: vasomotor symptoms (VMS) are systemic and need systemic therapy; genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) is local and is treated locally. Estrogen is the gold standard for VMS and the second line for GSM, so the real question is whether she can have it systemically.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Estrogen is the gold standard for VMS, and a woman with a uterus must have progesterone with it; estrogen alone only after hysterectomy. Vaginal estrogen treats GSM but not VMS, and systemic MHT can under-treat GSM, so some women need both. Transdermal estrogen skips first-pass metabolism and has the better clotting profile. A history of venous thromboembolism or stroke is enough to contraindicate estrogen - it need not be active.

blocks.html: 1. Menopause and perimenopause
• The terms are set by age and by the last period:

rows: Amenorrhea x 12 months · average age 51-52 in Canada
The transition; symptoms begin, possibly years before the last menstrual period · cycles shorten, then lengthen, then cease

blocks.html: • After menopause estradiol and progesterone fall while follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone rise (loss of feedback)

blocks.alt: menopause.png
blocks.cap: The dynamics of perimenopause: the follicle reserve runs out by about 51, so estradiol and progesterone fall and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) climbs; the final menstrual period marks menopause

blocks.html: 2. Staging and premature ovarian insufficiency

blocks.alt: straw 10 staging system - stages of reproductive aging.png
blocks.cap: Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop (STRAW+10) staging - reproductive years, menopause transition and postmenopause, with menstrual and hormone criteria

blocks.html: • Premature ovarian insufficiency (under 40) = disordered menses ≥ 4 months + follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) > 25 IU/L
3. Why early menopause matters

• Under 45: coronary heart disease events ↑ 50% · stroke ↑ 23% · cardiovascular mortality ↑ 19% · all-cause mortality ↑ 12% · cognition, quality of life, bone
  • Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) started before 50 → ↓ all-cause mortality (Nurses' Health Study)
4. Symptoms

• Vasomotor symptoms: hot flashes and night sweats, in 80% of patients
  • Three theories of VMS
    • narrowed thermoregulatory zone
    • kisspeptin-neurokinin B-dynorphin (KNDy) neurons hyperactivated by lack of estrogen
    • ↓ serotonin up-regulating hypothalamic 5-HT2A receptors, shifting the set point

blocks.alt: kndy neurons and nk3r antagonists in vasomotor symptoms.png
blocks.cap: Low estradiol over-activates KNDy neurons, which drive the thermoregulatory neuron to hot flashes; neurokinin 3 receptor antagonists block this

blocks.html:
• Genitourinary syndrome of menopause = estrogen deficiency of the genitourinary tract
    • signs: pale vulva · ↓ labial volume · loss of pubic hair · introital stenosis · thin vestibule · vaginal pH > 5.0
5. Approach to the patient
• Can she have systemic estrogen? no contraindications, younger than 60, and < 10 years post menopause

• History
    • menses: last menstrual period, regular, heavy, intermenstrual spotting
    • symptoms: hot flashes, sleep, mood, GSM, libido
    • contraindications to MHT: blood clot, breast cancer history
  • Physical exam
    • examine the vulva if she has GSM symptoms, to rule out skin conditions
  • Investigations
    • menopause is a clinical diagnosis (amenorrhea x 12 months)
    • the deck asks whether she needs a Pap or an endometrial biopsy, and leaves it open
  • Follow-up: review the risk-benefit profile annually · evaluate the endometrium for bleeding on MHT
6. Lifestyle

• cognitive behavioural therapy · clinical hypnosis · weight loss may help · cooling, avoid triggers
  • sodium < 1300 mg · vitamin D 800 IU · calcium 1200 mg
  • natural health products: no benefit shown · exercise and yoga: healthy, but not recommended for VMS specifically
7. Drug treatment

• Start at the lowest effective dose, titrated up
  • Transdermal estrogen skips first-pass metabolism and has the better clotting profile

rows: Estrogen: pill, transdermal patch or gel · progesterone: pill, levonorgestrel intrauterine device (5 years) · combined pill or patch
Replaces estrogen; progestin protects the endometrium
75% reduction in VMS · uterus → must add progesterone
Treats GSM, not VMS - no systemic absorption
Converted to testosterone and estrogen in the vaginal mucosa
Selective estrogen receptor modulator, tissue-selective agonist on epithelium
Oral - the one GSM drug not inserted
Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors: venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine · selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram
Not listed in The Menopause Society guideline
Dry mouth, gastrointestinal upset, constipation, blurred vision
The only class aimed at the mechanism

blocks.html: • Contraindications to hormone therapy:

rows: Breast cancer - known, suspected or history
Estrogen-dependent cancer (endometrial, ovarian) · coronary heart disease · venous thromboembolism or stroke, active or history · thrombophilia · active liver disease · pregnancy

lectures.name: Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
lectures.title: Ovarian neoplasms
lectures.framing: Every ovarian tumour is named by its lineage (epithelial, germ cell, sex cord/stromal) plus its behaviour (benign, borderline, malignant), and the age of the patient predicts the lineage: epithelial in adults, germ cell in the young.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Beware the bilateral atypical mucinous tumour: it is a metastasis until the appendix has been checked. Serous carcinoma is the #1 ovarian cancer and presents late, which is why mortality is high. Borderline vs carcinoma = invasion, not architecture. Mucinous carcinoma is the one carcinoma that is usually unilateral. Granulosa cell tumour recurs late (> 10 years) and ruptures; its estrogen shows up in the endometrium first.

blocks.html: 1. Approach to an ovarian mass

blocks.alt: ovarian tumour classification by cell of origin - germinal epithelium germ cell gonadal stroma - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Ovarian tumours by cell of origin - germinal epithelium, germ cell and gonadal stroma - each split into benign, borderline and malignant, with the layers of the follicle

blocks.html:
• Most ovarian neoplasms are not malignant; cancer is more likely post-menopausal
  • Presents as
    • pain (rupture, torsion) · distension (ascites, mass effect) · compression (change in bladder / bowel habits)
    • systemic (weight loss, fever, anorexia) · endocrine (estrogenic or androgenic)
    • often asymptomatic until late
  • Investigations
    • imaging finds the mass · in a young woman add germ cell serum markers (diagnosis and post-op monitoring)
    • the diagnosis is histologic
2. Epithelial tumours

• Naming: cell subtype (serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, transitional) + architecture (cyst-, -fibroma) + behaviour
    • serous cystadenoma (benign) · serous cystadenofibroma (cystic and fibrous, benign) · serous borderline tumour (pre-cancerous) · serous adenocarcinoma (malignant)
  • What separates borderline from carcinoma is stromal invasion

rows: Unilocular cyst, clear fluid, single bland layer
Serous = the most common epithelial subtype
Multilocular, jelly-like mucin, tall columnar mucin-filled cells; can be enormous
Papillary excrescences, complex architecture, atypical cells, no frank invasion
Pre-cancerous; excision, very good prognosis; can seed implants (serous only), adhere, recur, progress to low-grade carcinoma
Stromal invasion; solid and cystic, haemorrhage and necrosis
#1 ovarian cancer; often advanced at presentation; bilateral common
Bilateral + atypical mucinous = look for an appendix primary

blocks.html: 3. Ovarian carcinoma: origin, spread, treatment

• Origins
    • the ovary's own surface epithelium, dragged into the stroma at ovulation, forms epithelial inclusions that give rise to the epithelial tumours
    • a second pathway runs from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) in the fimbria, which exfoliates onto the ovary and peritoneum
  • Where it goes
    • pelvic peritoneum · omentum · bowel serosa · liver serosa · diaphragm · stomach · pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes · lungs
    • the uterus, tubes and broad ligament by direct extension

blocks.alt: ovarian carcinoma spread sites.png
blocks.cap: Where ovarian carcinoma spreads - peritoneum, omentum, serosal surfaces, diaphragm, lymph nodes and lungs

blocks.html:
• Treatment
    • surgery first: uterus, ovaries, tubes, omentum, peritoneal biopsies, with or without lymph nodes
    • chemotherapy for advanced stage
  • Prognosis: confined = good; higher stage = poor
4. Germ cell tumours
• The young patient's tumours · serum markers: alpha-fetoprotein (α-FP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG)

rows: "Dermoid cyst": hair, sebum, teeth; mix of mature tissues (skin, cartilage)
Benign; the most common benign germ cell tumour
Unilateral mass in a young patient

blocks.alt: ovarian germ cell tumor differentiation pathways.png
blocks.cap: Germ cell tumours by differentiation - dysgerminoma, embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, teratoma

blocks.html: • Which marker, which tumour:
5. Sex cord/stromal tumours
• Arise from the ovarian stroma and the cells around the follicle:

rows: Firm, white, nodular solid mass; whorled spindle cells
Found during a hysterectomy for other reasons
Yellow, solid and cystic with haemorrhage; cells form microfollicles
Uncommon; malignant but slow growing; late recurrence (> 10 years); prone to rupture (haemoperitoneum)
Estrogenic: endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma may be the first sign

blocks.html: 6. Metastases to the ovary

• Classic pattern: bilateral and multi-nodular
  • ⚠ Before calling a bilateral mucinous tumour a primary, check the appendix

rows: Abundant gelatinous mucin filling the abdomen ("jelly belly")
Appendiceal origin; also mucinous ovarian tumours

lectures.name: Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding
lectures.title: Post-menopausal bleeding
lectures.framing: The lecture walks the approach in the order you do it: define the bleed → work it up → list the causes → read the biopsy report → manage atrophy, hyperplasia or carcinoma. One rule runs through all of it: endometrial carcinoma must be excluded in every woman with post-menopausal bleeding, however benign the story.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Without atypia the management is medical; with atypia it is surgical - the atypia line is the whole biopsy-report question. Risk factors for hyperplasia and type 1 carcinoma are the same: unopposed estrogen. ⚠ Atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion - it must fit the other investigations. Endometrial cancer is the #1 gynecologic malignancy and the 4th most common cancer in women; endometrial names the site, endometrioid names the (most common) type.

blocks.html: 1. Definition

• Any bleeding after 12 months without menses is post-menopausal bleeding (PMB)
  • How common: 11% over one year in a diary study (Astrup 2004); the in-class deck (Rawlins 2025) says it occurs in 5-25% of post-menopausal women
  • The most common cause is atrophy; the most serious is carcinoma or hyperplasia.
  • The investigation is the same for both: speculum exam, transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS), and endometrial biopsy
2. Diagnostic pathway
