blocks.html:
• History
    • bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea · hormone replacement therapy (HRT) (63% bleed in the first six cycles) · tamoxifen
    • risk factors for unopposed estrogen (obesity, polycystic ovarian syndrome, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause) · family history of colorectal or endometrial cancer (Lynch)
    • in-class deck adds diabetes and age to the hyperplasia risk factors
  • Physical exam
    • general + abdominal + pelvic · uterus normal or enlarged
    • speculum exam every time - an endometrial mass at the os or an ulcerated cervical mass is a different diagnosis
    • in-class deck: inspect the vulva (lesions, atrophy, scratching) · human papillomavirus (HPV) test / cytology if not up to date · cervical biopsy if a lesion is seen · endometrial biopsy (Pipelle)
  • Investigations
    • TVUS (normal < 5 mm off HRT; the in-class hyperplasia slide says "typically normal < 4 mm" while its own ultrasound slide says < 5 mm - check with the lecturer) → endometrial biopsy for > 5 mm, any PMB, or recurrent bleeding at < 5 mm (skipping the last group misses 4% of cancers)
    • saline infusion sonohysterography for a thickened stripe (finds focal lesions, cannot tell benign from malignant) · hysteroscopy for focal lesions and when office biopsy is impossible · dilation and curettage (D&C) when nothing else is available
    • ⚠ a negative Pap does NOT end the workup

rows: < 5 mm = normal off HRT; on HRT the same cutoff applies but > 50% exceed it
Indicated for > 5 mm; sensitivity for focal lesions 93-100%, false positives 6-15%; cannot discriminate benign from malignant
99.6% sensitivity for cancer but blind, so poor for polyps and focal lesions
Direct visualization and biopsy of focal lesions; standard surgical risks
When office sampling or hysteroscopy is unavailable or contraindicated; in 50% of cases < 60% of the endometrium is sampled

blocks.alt: endometrial biopsy - sampling the endometrium through the cervix.png
blocks.cap: Endometrial biopsy: a thin catheter passed through the cervix samples the endometrium blind, which is why it is sensitive for cancer but misses polyps and focal lesions

blocks.html:
• Incidental thickening without bleeding
    • no routine sampling; decide case by case on risk factors · no routine ultrasound on tamoxifen · asymptomatic polyps triaged by size, age and risk factors
  • Refer to gynecology
    • PMB + risk factors for endometrial cancer · symptomatic or recurrent bleeding with a focal lesion on biopsy · stripe > 5 mm or a "vascular pedicle"
3. Causes

• Most common in PMB: atrophy · exogenous hormones (HRT, tamoxifen) · endometrial hyperplasia · endometrial polyp · endometrial adenocarcinoma, which must be ruled out
  • In-class differential: atrophic vaginitis · endometrial hyperplasia / adenocarcinoma · cervical cancer · cervical polyp · vulvar lesion · non-gynecologic bleeding; structural lesions shown: endometrial polyp, submucosal fibroid, endocervical polyp
  • Treatment follows the pathology report (sections 4-6)
4. Atrophy (genitourinary syndrome of menopause)

• Causes: hypoestrogenism → microerosion, inflammation, spotting; from the endometrium, vagina or vulva
  • Pathology: scant fragments of atrophic endometrium; a diagnosis of exclusion that must fit the other investigations
  • How common (in-class): vulvovaginal atrophy (VVA) affects 50-80% of post-menopausal women
  • Presents as
    • dryness · itching · burning · dyspareunia · postcoital bleeding
    • loss of labial fullness · pallor of urethral and vaginal epithelium · narrow introitus · minimal moisture · loss of urethral meatal turgor · (in-class) loss of rugae and elasticity · yellow thin discharge · petechiae
    • exclude lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, atopic or contact dermatitis, vulvar lesions
  • Treatment
    • atrophy → local estrogen (cream, pill / suppository, ring) or nothing if not troublesome · HRT · usually the family physician
    • in-class adds: water-based lubricants, vaginal moisturizers (Replens), vaginal hyaluronic acid suppositories · vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) suppositories
  • Prognosis: benign
5. Exogenous hormones and endometrial hyperplasia

• Exogenous hormones
    • HRT (63% bleed in first six cycles, 37% later) · tamoxifen
    • bleeding reflects regimen and hormone type · investigate if bleeding persists (> 50% on HRT have a stripe > 5 mm, < 4% have pathology)
    • unopposed systemic estrogen with a uterus → hyperplasia in 10% at 12 months, up to 50% at 24 months · adjust the regimen; never unopposed estrogen with a uterus · benign
  • Hyperplasia = ↑ gland:stroma ratio, crowded glands
  • Causes: Unopposed estrogen
    • endogenous: obesity, polycystic ovarian syndrome, granulosa cell tumor, infertility, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause
    • exogenous: HRT, topical, tamoxifen
  • Both present as PMB and are diagnosed on biopsy

rows: Crowded glands with atypia; 30-40% have concurrent adenocarcinoma at hysterectomy (in-class deck: up to 60% have an undiagnosed cancer missed on sampling - check with the lecturer)
Progestin (Megace, levonorgestrel intrauterine device; the in-class deck makes the levonorgestrel intrauterine system first-line) · repeat biopsy at 3 months · remove exogenous estrogen · weight loss
hysterectomy + BSO (abdominal, laparoscopic or vaginal) · high-dose progestin only if surgery contraindicated

blocks.html: 6. Endometrial carcinoma

• Presents as: 90% present with bleeding; 72% Stage 1; cramping, pressure; uterus normal or enlarged
  • In-class numbers: lifetime risk 2.6% · 10-15% occur before menopause · worse survival if elderly or diabetic · hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC, Lynch) carriers have 10x the risk · staging is surgical
  • Lynch syndrome: 40-70% lifetime risk; often the sentinel cancer · mismatch repair testing on every endometrial carcinoma (Ontario)

rows: Estrogen dependent; same risk factors as hyperplasia · Lynch syndrome
Estrogen independent; no unopposed-estrogen history; older, atrophic endometrium
Endometrioid adenocarcinoma, 90% of endometrial cancer; precursor is hyperplasia
Hysterectomy + BSO; with or without lymphadenectomy, staging, radiation/chemotherapy if higher grade or stage
As type 1, more often needing adjuvant therapy

blocks.html:
• Spread
    • direct invasion of myometrium (common) and cervix (fairly common) → lymphovascular to nodes and distant organs (rare) · transtubal to peritoneum (rare)
  • Staging
    • by the pathologist after resection with tumour, node, metastasis staging, translated to International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics staging; the stage decides adjuvant treatment

blocks.cap: Hysterectomy specimen showing endometrial carcinoma spreading into the myometrium, toward the cervix and transtubally

lectures.name: Pathology of the Breast
lectures.title: Pathology of the breast
lectures.framing: Place the lesion by the tissue it arises from, then tell the lesions of that tissue apart by presentation. The lecture goes anatomy → benign lesions → their cancer risk → malignant lesions → prognosis.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ inflammatory carcinoma is defined by the clinical appearance of diffuse acute mastitis; peau d'orange is neither necessary nor sufficient, and a skin punch biopsy confirms the cancer. ⚠ Breast cancer is the #1 cancer in Canadian women but the #2 cancer death, behind lung. ⚠ Two benign lesions mimic cancer clinically: fat necrosis (irregular mass, skin retraction) and a healed abscess (fixation by fibrosis). ⚠ Not every non-sporadic cancer is BRCA: 20% are non-sporadic but only 5-7% carry a high-penetrance mutation.

blocks.html: 1. Breast anatomy: disorders by tissue

blocks.alt: breast anatomy and disorders.png
blocks.cap: The breast by tissue of origin

blocks.html:
• Terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU): fibrocystic change and carcinoma (in situ and invasive)
  • Large ducts and nipple: papillomas, duct ectasia, mastitis and Paget's
  • Intralobular stroma: fibroadenoma and phyllodes
  • Interlobular stroma and fat: fat necrosis, pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia and mesenchymal tumours
  • Presentation (only five)
    • palpable mass · lumpiness without a discrete mass · pain · nipple discharge · mammographic abnormality
  • Sampling
    • nipple discharge (low-yield) · fine needle aspiration · core biopsy · punch biopsy (skin and nipple, and the fast route to a tissue diagnosis of inflammatory carcinoma)
    • breast duct excision · lumpectomy / partial mastectomy · mastectomy
2. Benign breast disorders

rows: May be a history of trauma; often superficial
Lactation: fissures and engorgement let Staphylococcus or Streptococcus in
Females in their 20s-30s; one of the most common benign lesions
Firm, irregular mass with or without erythema, skin retraction and dimpling (the benign lesion that mimics cancer)
Tense, hot, painful breast with or without enlarged tender axillary nodes
Bloody nipple discharge; more rarely a palpable areolar mass
Discrete, mobile, usually non-tender, rounded / lobulated, rubbery-to-firm; no skin dimpling or retraction
Lumpy masses that fluctuate with the menstrual cycle with or without pain / tenderness
May progress to abscess; heals by fibrosis, so fixation can mimic cancer
Tan-pink friable lesion inside a dilated duct
Biphasic: stromal + epithelial elements; no atypia, few stromal mitoses; may calcify
Cysts, fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia, mild usual epithelial hyperplasia

blocks.html: 3. Epithelial lesions and the risk of invasive carcinoma

• Non-proliferative, RR x1
    • fibrocystic change · duct ectasia · cysts · apocrine change · fibroadenoma
  • Proliferative without atypia, RR x1.5-2
    • moderate / florid epithelial hyperplasia · papillomas · sclerosing adenosis · radial scar · complex fibroadenoma
  • Atypical hyperplasia x4-5
    • atypical ductal hyperplasia · atypical lobular hyperplasia · x9-10 with a family history
4. Risk factors for breast cancer

• females > males · 75% at age 50+
  • 80% sporadic, 20% non-sporadic
    • high-penetrance hereditary 5-7%: BRCA1/2, p53, PTEN, STK11 · moderate < 3%: CHEK2, ATM · the rest familial / polygenic
  • Americas / Europe > Asia / Africa · European descent highest incidence (more estrogen receptor-positive) · Hispanic / African ancestry lower incidence but aggressive cancers at a younger age
  • early menarche, nulliparity, no breastfeeding, older first pregnancy
  • ionizing radiation to the developing breast · obesity, hormone replacement therapy, mammographic density, alcohol
5. Carcinoma in situ

rows: Linear / casting / pleomorphic calcifications on mammography; sometimes nipple discharge
Incidental on a biopsy done for another reason; no clinical, anatomical or mammographic correlate

blocks.html: 6. Invasive carcinoma

• 80% no special type (ductal)
    • poorly defined, stellate / "crab-like", gritty mass
    • graded on tubule formation, nuclear atypia, mitotic rate
  • 20% special type
    • tubular, cribriform, mucinous, medullary, papillary, lobular, metaplastic · recognised by morphology
    • in pure form better prognosis than no special type, except metaplastic and lobular
7. Two unique presentations: Paget's and inflammatory carcinoma

rows: Eczema of the nipple-areola: reddening, scaling, erosion, ulceration
Diffuse acute mastitis, often but not always with peau d'orange
Always an underlying carcinoma (ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive; a palpable mass means invasive) that has reached the nipple via the ducts
Carcinoma cells in the nipple epithelium
The clinical picture: peau d'orange alone, or dermal lymphatic obstruction alone, is NOT inflammatory carcinoma

blocks.alt: paget disease of the nipple - spread along the duct and histology.png
blocks.cap: Paget disease of the nipple - carcinoma tracking along a duct to the nipple skin, and Paget cells in the nipple epidermis

blocks.html: 8. Prognosis

• Major factors
    • invasive vs in situ · distant metastases (lung, pleura, liver, bone; adrenal, brain)
    • axillary node status, the most important factor once distant metastases are excluded
    • tumour size · local extension (deep = fixed to pectoralis; superficial = skin fixation, nipple retraction, ulceration, peau d'orange) · inflammatory carcinoma
  • Minor factors
    • subtype, grade, lymphovascular invasion (hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain)
    • estrogen receptor (ER) / progesterone receptor (PR): favourable, predict response to tamoxifen / aromatase inhibitors
    • Her2/neu: unfavourable, predicts response to trastuzumab
    • (special tests) with or without gene expression profiling, proliferative rate, PD-L1

blocks.alt: breast cancer er pr her2 immunostains.png
blocks.cap: Hematoxylin and eosin stain beside ER, PR and HER2 immunostains - the special tests that predict response to hormonal therapy and trastuzumab

lectures.name: Approach to Common Breast Problems
lectures.title: Approach to common breast problems
lectures.framing: Three presentations reach the family physician - a lump, a sore breast, nipple discharge - and every one is sorted the same way: the older the woman, the more likely the complaint is serious. The lecture takes them in turn (lumps in men first), then ends on risk factors and screening.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ pre-menopausal with a benign history and exam: re-examine after the next menstrual cycle; post-menopausal or high risk: investigate immediately. Imaging splits at 35 - ultrasound below, mammogram above. Galactorrhea is bilateral, multiple ducts; worrisome discharge is unilateral, single duct, spontaneous, bloody. Mammography misses 12-15%, and number needed to screen 721 per death prevented.

blocks.html: 1. Breast lumps in males

• Pubertal swelling: 85-90% resolve within 2 years
  • A mass reported as gynecomastia is benign - ask about meds
2. Breast lumps in females
• Most lumps are not cancer: cancer is ~10% of masses

• History
    • age · location · how and when found · skin changes · change in size · change with menstrual cycle · other lumps in axilla · family history
  • Physical exam
    • offer a chaperone · inspect with hands pushing on hips
    • nodes: central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral, infra- and supraclavicular
    • supine, vertical strips (better than pie or spiral), clavicle to inframammary fold, midsternal to posterior axillary line, pads of fingers 2-4, light/medium/deep · tail of Spence

blocks.alt: clinical breast exam - vertical strip palpation pattern.png
blocks.cap: Clinical breast exam: patient supine, palpating in vertical strips over the lateral (top) and medial (bottom) breast

blocks.html:
• Worrisome
    • single · hard · immovable · irregular borders · > 2 cm
    • ⚠ skin changes, peau d'orange and nipple retraction are late findings and rarely seen - their absence reassures nothing
  • Benign: smooth · normal/fibroglandular tissue, cyst, fibroadenoma
  • Follow-up: pre-menopausal, benign: re-examine after next cycle
  • Investigations
    • < 35 ultrasound (tissue too dense, risk too low for mammography) · MRI if < 35 and high risk
    • > 35 mammogram first +/- US
3. Breast pain

• History: uni vs bilateral · phasic with periods · hormone replacement therapy (HRT) / birth control pill · pregnancy, birth, loss · vigorous exercise
  • Cyclical - cyclical (2/3)
    • luteal phase (day 14) to menses · ducts (estrogen), stroma (progesterone)
  • Non-cyclic causes: mastitis · HRT/oral contraceptive pill (OCP) · Cooper's ligament stretch · extramammary
  • Worrisome: older woman · mass · only 8% of breast cancers present with pain
  • Investigations: < 35 + normal exam: no testing · suspicious finding: the lump approach
  • Treatment
    • low-fat high-complex-carb diet · bra · compresses · nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs · stop OCP/HRT · tamoxifen · treat if severe > 7 days

rows: antibiotics · continue breastfeeding, fully empty the breast
only if antibiotics fail: US, US-guided aspiration, incision and drainage (I&D)
rule out malignancy, especially if persistent · if imaging OK, repeat in 3 months

blocks.html: 4. Nipple discharge

• History: spontaneous vs expressed · single vs multiple ducts · bloody or serous · mass
  • Benign - galactorrhea: usually bilateral, multiple ducts, expressed on compression
    • not related to pregnancy/lactation
    • causes: stimulation · hyperprolactinemia · dopamine suppressors · chest wall injury · chronic kidney disease, hypothyroid, cirrhosis
  • Worrisome - unilateral, single duct, spontaneous
    • bloody or serous · mass · > 50
    • pathologic causes: papilloma (most common) · ectasia · fibrocystic · malignancy 5-10%
  • Investigations: identify duct/quadrant · rule out Paget's · periareolar US, mammogram · galactogram · cytology
  • Treatment: galactogram not diagnostic · must excise to be sure · surgical consult
5. Risk factors and screening

rows: 1st-degree relative < 50 · two 1st-degree relatives any age · ovarian cancer (self or 1st-degree) · male breast cancer in family · atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia, radial scar, phyllodes, lobular carcinoma in situ · density > 75%
biennial (Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care: every 2-3 years)
age 40-49 (conditional) · MRI, tomosynthesis, US (strong) · clinical breast exam · breast self-exam

blocks.html:
• Family history (relative risk, RR)
    • two 1st-degree 4-5 · one 1st-degree 2-3 · one 2nd-degree 1.2-1.5
  • Minor factors (RR 1.1-1.3)
    • inactivity · BMI > 30 · > 2 drinks/day · early menarche, late menopause · nulliparity, no breastfeeding · birth control pill > 5 years · combined HRT
  • BRCA carriers
    • lifetime 55-85% breast, 15-65% ovarian
    • prophylactic mastectomy 90% reduction, oophorectomy 50%, tamoxifen ?50%

lectures.name: OB Care Providers
lectures.title: Obstetrical care providers
lectures.framing: Three providers, one team, taken one at a time. For each, ask who can do what, and at which point a pregnancy leaves their scope: family medicine and midwives each carry a low-risk pregnancy from antenatal care to 6 weeks post partum, while the obstetrician is the consultant for anything complicated and the only one who operates.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Midwives provide informed choice rather than informed consent, which is why a client can choose outside the regular recommendations. ⚠ The obstetrician provides no care for the infant and has no lactation training; the family physician follows the baby from birth onward and the midwife for 6 weeks. Fetal anomalies at any stage go to MFM, not a general OB. Preeclampsia is a consult trigger in all three phases, and the post partum list is short: postpartum hemorrhage, a 3rd or 4th degree tear, preeclampsia. Asking for help is not a failure.

blocks.html: 1. Family medicine obstetrics

• Training: family medicine + 6-12 months of extra obstetrical training
  • Cares for: low-risk pregnancies - their own patients plus referrals from other physicians; all routine antenatal, intrapartum and post partum care
  • Delivery
    • vaginal · many perform vacuum-assisted deliveries
    • cesarean is a referral (rural exceptions)
  • Oxytocin in labour: all manage it (induction / augmentation)
  • Post partum
    • the patient: many see her until 6 weeks, then ongoing if in their practice; primary-care knowledge throughout
    • the infant: from birth onward, for years if their patient · some return the baby to the referring physician immediately
  • Distinct advantage: continuity of care and the "whole patient" - recognises and treats depression, upper respiratory tract infection etc. during antenatal and post partum care
2. Midwifery

• Training: direct entry, 4 years · 7 programs in Canada · regulated by province (unregulated only in Prince Edward Island and Yukon)
  • Cares for: low-risk pregnancy and birth, client-centred
  • Delivery
    • vaginal, low-risk · delivery at home, in a birthing centre or clinic, or in hospital
  • Oxytocin in labour: variable - use without an obstetrician consult depends on location and training · some sites also need nursing support for an epidural (changing in London)
  • Post partum
    • the patient: 6 weeks post partum, including breastfeeding · home visits are commonplace
    • the infant: cares for the infant for 6 weeks
  • Distinct advantage
    • informed choice, not informed consent (the client may choose outside the recommendations)
    • 30-90 min appointments · prenatal and post partum home visits
3. Obstetrics

• Training: generalist obstetrician (OB) = 5-year obstetrics and gynecology residency · maternal fetal medicine (MFM) = the same + a 2-year fellowship
  • Cares for: consultant to family medicine and midwives for complicated antenatal, intrapartum or post partum care · preconception counselling (MFM optimises the medically complex patient before conception)
  • Delivery: all forms - operative vaginal and cesarean section · manages the complicated case and every operative delivery
  • Oxytocin in labour: yes
  • Post partum
    • the patient: low-risk - often only a 6-week visit · not involved in most of the post partum transition · no lactation training (encourages breastfeeding from personal experience only)
    • the infant: no care for the infant after delivery
  • When to consult OB

rows: Medically complicated patient (diabetic, essential hypertension, prior preeclampsia, elevated BMI, systemic lupus erythematosus) · fetal anomalies (MFM) · atypical or abnormal antepartum fetal surveillance · need for a planned cesarean

Fetal anomalies (MFM) · atypical or abnormal fetal surveillance · labour dystocia, failure to descend, assessment and rotation of fetal position · considering operative vaginal delivery or cesarean · preeclampsia / eclampsia
Significant postpartum hemorrhage · 3rd or 4th degree tear · preeclampsia

4. The maternal health team

• Work together and communicate: each provider has their own strengths and skill sets
  • Asking for help is not a failure

lectures.name: Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding
lectures.title: Pathology of first trimester bleeding
lectures.framing: Three "baby" causes of first trimester bleeding, told apart by where the products of conception are and what the trophoblast is doing. The lecture lists the causes of bleeding, then takes spontaneous abortion → ectopic pregnancy → gestational trophoblastic disease in turn. Every one is worked up the same way, and the tissue goes to pathology, because only the microscope proves where the gestation was.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ complete = paternal only, diploid, no fetus, high hCG, big uterus; partial = triploid, fetus possible, low-normal hCG, small uterus. Choriocarcinoma has no villi; a mole has too many swollen ones. hCG can be negative in an ectopic. Choriocarcinoma goes to the lung first (> 90%) but kills through liver or brain.

blocks.html: 1. Causes of bleeding and the workup

• Causes of bleeding in a reproductive-age woman, ABCDEHIN
    • Anatomic (PALE: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, endometritis)
    • Baby (spontaneous abortion, ectopic, gestational trophoblastic disease)
    • Coagulopathy · Dysfunctional uterine bleeding · Endocrine · Hormones (exogenous) · Infectious · Neoplasia
  • History
    • amenorrhea or a light last period, bleeding, cramping, passage of clot or tissue
  • Physical exam
    • vitals (shock = rupture) · uterus large for dates = complete mole, small for dates = partial · adnexal mass · cervix open or closed
  • Investigations
    • serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) + pelvic ultrasound are the two investigations that matter
    • then every piece of tissue passed or sampled goes to pathology
    • ⚠ an endometrial sample cannot diagnose an ectopic, it can only fail to find products of conception

flowchart TD A["Reproductive-age woman: bleeding ± pain, positive β-hCG"] --> B["Serum β-hCG + pelvic ultrasound"] B --> C{"Gestational sac in the uterus?"} C -->|"No sac, adnexal mass"| D["ECTOPIC

malignant trophoblast, no villi"]

blocks.html: 2. Spontaneous abortion

• Definition: loss of a gestation before fetal extrauterine viability (< 20 weeks)
  • 15% of known pregnancies (underestimated)
  • Causes
    • mostly unknown · fetal chromosomal / congenital abnormality is #1
    • TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, other, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) · maternal: implantation, chronic disease, endocrine, infection
  • Presents as: bleeding, cramping, clot or tissue
  • Pathology
    • Products of conception (villi, trophoblast, ± fetal parts) + gestational endometrium (glands, decidualized stroma)
  • Diagnosis
    • clinical, or microscopy of curettage or passed tissue · must see products of conception to prove intrauterine gestation
  • Prognosis: incomplete may need dilation and curettage

rows: May need dilation and curettage for the remainder

blocks.alt: spontaneous abortion types.png
blocks.cap: Types of spontaneous abortion: the cervical os is closed in threatened, complete and missed, and open in inevitable and incomplete; only threatened keeps fetal cardiac activity for sure

blocks.html: • Follow-up: ≥ 3 spontaneous abortions = recurrent: work-up + medical genetics
3. Ectopic pregnancy

• Definition: implantation of products of conception at a site other than the endometrium
  • 1-2% of gestations · #1 site: fallopian tube (90%) · others: ovary, abdominal cavity, cervix
  • Causes
    • pelvic inflammatory disease (commonest) · intrapelvic adhesions (surgery, appendicitis) · endometriosis · intrauterine device · previous ectopic
  • Presents as
    • triad: amenorrhea, pain, adnexal mass · shock if ruptured
    • hCG normal, declining or negative
  • Pathology
    • Hematosalpinx, wall thinned or ruptured · villi, trophoblast, fetal parts in the tube
    • endometrium decidualized but NO products of conception
  • Diagnosis
    • no sac in the uterus + adnexal mass on ultrasound · products of conception absent from endometrium, present at the ectopic site
  • Prognosis: rupture and hemorrhage
4. Gestational trophoblastic disease
• Definition: abnormal trophoblast proliferation · three types: complete mole (commonest), partial mole, choriocarcinoma

rows: Empty ovum + 1 sperm that duplicates (90%) or 2 sperm (10%) · diploid 46 XX or XY, paternal only
Ovum + 2 sperm (diandric), or 1 that duplicates · triploid 69 XXX or XXY: 2 paternal + 1 maternal

Abundant swollen hydropic villi, no fetal tissue · diffuse hydropic change + trophoblastic proliferation
Lower volume · two villous sizes (hydropic + small normal or fibrotic) · less trophoblastic proliferation · irregular-shaped villi with stromal inclusions · fetal tissue may be present
Red hemorrhagic uterine mass, any size · no villi, malignant trophoblast, hemorrhage + necrosis
1/1000 USA, 1/500 Asia · bleeding · uterus large for dates · hyperemesis 25%, hypertension / pre-eclampsia 25%, hyperthyroidism · hCG markedly elevated
Bleeding · uterus small for dates · the complete-mole symptoms are rare · hCG low to normal
"Snow storm" without fetus · caught early (8-12 wk) on routine ultrasound
Focal cystic change with fetus formation · often under-recognized clinically
Often presumptive on clinical findings · malignant trophoblast in the sample
80% cured by curettage · 15% invade or persist · 2-3% become choriocarcinoma · serial hCG
Most cured by curettage · 5-10% invade or persist · rarely choriocarcinoma · serial hCG
> 90% lung metastases at diagnosis · 80% 5-year survival with chemotherapy · death from liver or brain metastases

lectures.name: Teratogenesis
lectures.title: Teratogenesis
lectures.framing: A teratogen is judged by what it hits and when: the same exposure does nothing in weeks 1-2, produces a major structural anomaly during organogenesis (weeks 3-8), and a functional or minor defect in the fetal period. The lecture then walks the four kinds of teratogen: physical → infectious → maternal condition → chemical.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Weeks 3-8 (organogenesis) is the window of greatest sensitivity; weeks 1-2 are usually not susceptible, and the fetal period is less sensitive - CNS, eyes and external genitalia stay sensitive to term. ⚠ FDA category C means no data, not safety; the D/X split is benefit may outweigh risk vs. risk outweighs any benefit. Hyperthermia and maternal diabetes both cause neural tube defects and cardiovascular defects - hyperthermia adds abdominal wall defects and spontaneous abortion, diabetes adds CNS, spine and limb defects.

blocks.html: 1. What a teratogen is, and when it matters

• 9 in 10 pregnant women take at least one medication, so the question is rarely whether she is exposed but how to counsel her
  • Anomaly size
    • major = affects life expectancy, health status, physical or social functioning
    • minor = little or no impact on health or short- or long-term function

blocks.alt: tereatogenesis timeline.png
blocks.cap: The susceptibility timeline: embryonic period (organogenesis) vs. fetal period

blocks.html:
• History
    • every drug, supplement, herbal, recreational drug and occupational exposure
    • timing against the last menstrual period (organogenesis or not)
    • infections, fever ≥ 39°C, radiation · maternal diabetes and its control · rubella immunity
2. Physical teratogens

• radiation · hyperthermia (core ≥ 39°C, extreme or prolonged)
  • Defects: spontaneous abortion, neural tube defects, cardiovascular defects, abdominal wall defects
  • Radiation: fetal dose not to exceed 50 rads
  • Heat: the hazard is extreme heat, not exercise
    • ⚠ do NOT tell her to stop exercising or to fear a short sauna - core temperature does NOT exceed 39°C with exercise in pregnancy
3. Infectious teratogens

• TORCH: toxoplasmosis · other (syphilis, zika, parvovirus, varicella zoster virus, Listeria) · rubella · cytomegalovirus · herpes simplex virus
  • vertical transmission: in utero, at delivery, or after birth via breast milk
  • Cytomegalovirus: #1 infectious cause of birth defects in North America · 40% transmission with a 1st maternal infection
  • Herpes simplex virus: caught in the last 3 months: 30-50% transmission → cesarean section
  • Rubella: vaccinate · check titres
  • Toxoplasmosis: cat feces, uncooked meat · not routinely screened in Canada
4. Maternal conditions

• diabetes
    • Defects: neural tube, central nervous system (CNS), spine, cardiovascular, and limb defects
    • Prevention: glycemic control before conception and through pregnancy · folic acid before conception
5. Chemical teratogens

• medications · vitamins/minerals/herbal products · recreational drugs · toxins
  • doxylamine-pyridoxine (Diclectin) is the only anti-nausea drug approved in pregnancy
  • The deck's case: mycophenolate ~25% malformation, ~50% spontaneous abortion
  • Risk graded by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) categories:

cols: The discriminator: which studies, and what they show
rows: controlled human studies show no risk
no human studies; animal studies show no risk
no controlled studies in animals OR humans
evidence of human risk exists; benefits may outweigh risks in certain situations
paroxetine · diazepam · lisinopril · phenytoin · lithium
both animal and human studies show fetal abnormalities; risk outweighs any possible benefit

blocks.html:
• Counselling by phase
    • Pre-conception (the moment to counsel): optimize disease management · 1 mg folic acid daily for antiepileptics · minimize dose and number of therapeutics · consider switching to an alternative medication · counsel on potential teratogenesis
    • Antenatal: potential dose increases
    • Post-partum: dose adjustments · breastfeeding considerations · restarting medications · switching back to previous therapeutics
  • Resources and referral
    • FRAME Clinic (Fetal Risk After Maternal Exposure, Western / Children's Hospital London Health Sciences Centre) · Reprotox · LactMed · MotherToBaby

lectures.name: Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound
lectures.title: First trimester ultrasound and hCG
lectures.framing: Two questions, one for each half of the lecture. For dating: which landmark is visible decides which measurement dates the pregnancy, and each landmark is retired the moment the next one appears. For a positive test with an empty uterus: a single human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) value never settles a pregnancy of unknown location; only the rate of change does, so the answer is almost always to repeat it.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Once an embryo is seen, MSD is never used again: CRL dates the pregnancy, best when > 10 mm (7 weeks), accurate to 3-8 days. A gestational sac is visible from 32 days, a yolk sac from 5 to 5+5 weeks, a heartbeat by 6+0. hCG level does not predict ectopic rupture, and a falling hCG does not exclude an ectopic: 8% of untreated ectopics fall at the same rate as a miscarriage (Silva 2006). MSD is also retired once it passes 14 mm, and CRL hands over to the BPD after 84 mm (14 weeks), where the two are equally good at 12-14 weeks.

blocks.html: 1. First trimester ultrasound: when and how

• All women should be offered a dating scan at 7-12 weeks; it beats the last menstrual period and cuts inductions for post-dates
  • Quality standard: transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) of uterus and adnexa · transabdominal only for a high mass or free fluid
2. Dating a pregnancy: why the last period is not enough

• Last menstrual period (LMP) dating assumes regular 28-day cycles, mid-cycle ovulation and fertilization, correct recall, off the oral contraceptive pill for months
  • Even a correct LMP cannot fix implantation without assisted reproductive technology
    • follicular waves · sperm survive 5-7 days · ovulation-to-implantation varies by up to 11 days
3. The ultrasound landmarks, in the order they appear

rows: 2-3 mm at ~32-33 days on high-frequency TVUS · present weeks 3-5 · grows ~1 mm/day
Chorionic cavity; echogenic rim = implanting villi + decidua · mean of 3 orthogonal inner-to-inner diameters, cursors on the sac not the rim · gestational age (days) ≈ MSD (mm) + 30
MSD > 14 mm, or as soon as an embryo is identified
Can be seen at MSD 5-6 mm (~5 wk) · should be seen at MSD 8 mm (5+5 wk)
First structure inside the sac; confirms an intrauterine pregnancy · max 6 mm by 10 wk, then disappears
5+5 wk at ~1-2 mm · fetal heart by 6+0 wk at ~3 mm
Longest straight line, outer cephalic margin to rump, neck neutral · transabdominal is not inferior to transvaginal if a CRL is used and measured after 6 wk
3-8 days · smallest error at 7-60 mm · most reliable > 10 mm (7 wk); with several scans, use the earliest with CRL > 10 mm
More reliable than CRL after 84 mm / 14 wk

blocks.html: 4. hCG in pregnancy

• Source: placental syncytiotrophoblast
  • Turns positive as implantation begins: 21-22 days post LMP = 8 days post ovulation
  • Shape of the curve
    • Exponential rise → plateau late 1st trimester → decline → steady state through the second and third trimesters
    • peaks 9-12 wk LMP (25,700-288,000 mIU/mL)
  • Shifted by maternal age, BMI (↓ with BMI), smoking (↓ if continued), fetal sex (girls higher)
    • all four also raise adverse-outcome risk · total hCG ∝ placental weight at birth
  • Does
    • maintains the corpus luteum and drives progesterone → implantation · placenta + cord development · suppresses myometrial contractions · fetal organ growth and angiogenesis

blocks.alt: beta hCG high and low.png
blocks.cap: Range of hCG values in early pregnancy: high and low curves both peak around 10 weeks, then fall to a plateau

blocks.html: 5. The rise of hCG: how the teaching changed

cols: Rate of rise in a viable intrauterine pregnancy (IUP)
rows: Any deviation read as failing fetus, threatened miscarriage or ectopic
Lower limit of an 85% confidence interval (CI), so 8% of viable IUPs rose slower
99% CI: < 1% of viable pregnancies rise slower

blocks.html:
• The deck's normal range: rise ≥ 53% over 2 days (99% CI), or a doubling time of 1.4-2.1 days
  • ⚠ A "normal" rise does not exclude an ectopic: a non-viable IUP or an ectopic can rise like a viable IUP
    • Horne 2004: 340 women with pain/bleeding < 12 weeks and an inconclusive scan; of the 63 with a ≥ 66% rise, 10 (16%) had an ectopic
    • Silva 2006: of 200 diagnosed ectopics, 60% had a rising hCG at diagnosis and 21% rose ≥ 53% over 2 days
6. The discriminatory zone

• the hCG above which TVUS should show a gestational sac in a normal IUP
  • The old 1000-2000 cut-off ignored slow-rising and low-normal viable pregnancies and mislabelled them as failed or ectopic
  • 2000-3000 keeps them in the pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) differential (the conclusion slide words it as raising the range from 1500 IU to 2000-3000 for stable patients)
  • By the numbers in PUL
    • ≥ 2000: most likely a non-viable IUP (NVIUP), 2x as likely as an ectopic
    • 2000-3000: ectopic 19x more likely than a viable IUP (38 NVIUP : 19 ectopic : 1 viable IUP, 2% chance)
    • ≥ 3000: ectopic 70x more likely than a viable IUP (140 : 70 : 1, 0.5% chance)
7. Pregnancy of unknown location and falling hCG

• Investigations
    • serial hCG rather than one absolute value
    • ⚠ a single hCG in the overlap zone does not distinguish viable IUP, non-viable IUP and ectopic
  • Treatment
    • stable + hCG 2000-3000 + no ectopic seen → repeat, do not act
    • this spares inappropriate misoprostol, dilation and curettage and laparoscopy
  • Rate of decline in a failing pregnancy (Barnhart 2004, 710 NVIUP managed expectantly): quadratic, and depends on the level
    • ≥ 5000 mIU/mL: at least 35% over 48 h · 500: at least 24% · 50: 12%
    • the conclusion slide says 12-32% over 2 days in spontaneous abortion - its top figure does not match the 35% on the data slide; check with the lecturer
    • a declining hCG without ultrasound evidence of an IUP is a non-viable pregnancy
  • Follow-up
    • a pregnancy is resolved only below 5 mIU/mL
    • ⚠ a resolving ectopic can still rupture while its hCG falls · rupture under close surveillance: 0.03% of all PUL, 1.7% of diagnosed ectopics

lectures.name: Hypertension in Pregnancy
lectures.title: Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy
lectures.framing: Every decision turns on two questions: when did the blood pressure (BP) rise relative to 20 weeks, and is the high BP the disease itself (chronic / gestational) or a symptom of it (pre-eclampsia / eclampsia)? The first sets the diagnosis; the second sets whether you treat the number or deliver the patient. The lecture goes normal BP → the disorders → their complications → management.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ 20 weeks is the line: HTN diagnosed before it is chronic, after it (with normal BPs documented) is gestational; pre-eclampsia adds proteinuria. Mild is >140 / >90, severe is >160 / >110, always 2 readings >15 min apart. ⚠ HELLP can present with a completely normal BP. The primary maternal danger of severe HTN is stroke, so any neurological symptom means investigate for an intracranial event. Treat the number in chronic / gestational HTN; in pre-eclampsia the number is a symptom and complications drive delivery planning.

blocks.html: 1. Normal blood pressure in pregnancy

• ↓ systemic vascular resistance outpaces ↑ blood volume, so BP falls from weeks 8-12 and returns to pre-pregnancy norms at 20-24 weeks
  • In pre-eclampsia this normal 8-24 week dip fails (↑ systemic vascular resistance)
2. The hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

• Measuring it
    • 2 readings >15 min apart, seated, calm, correct cuff size · exclude white-coat and pain-driven elevation
    • mild is >140 / >90, severe is >160 / >110

rows: HTN >20 weeks, normal BPs documented to that point · isolated BP elevation, no adverse conditions
HTN + proteinuria · with or without adverse conditions / severe complications
Earlier onset ⇒ more placental dysfunction, more progression to pre-eclampsia
Earlier onset ⇒ more severe, more progression to pre-eclampsia
Late gestation, primiparous · de novo, or secondary to chronic / gestational HTN
Typically from poorly controlled pre-eclampsia · rarely de novo (more so with chronic HTN or kidney disease)
From any hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, or de novo
Abnormal response to vasoactive substances ⇒ hyperactive vasoconstriction in end organs · normal 8-24 week BP dip fails (↑ systemic vascular resistance)
New / worsening proteinuria, headache, neurological irritability (clonus, photosensitivity)
Hemolysis, ↑ liver function tests, platelets ↓ with a normal BP
BP is the primary problem ⇒ treat the BP
BP is the primary problem ⇒ treat the BP
BP is a symptom ⇒ secondary; goal is maternal / fetal morbidity and mortality

blocks.html: 3. Complications

• History
    • onset vs 20 weeks · headache, visual disturbance, clonus / photosensitivity (eclampsia precursors) · right upper quadrant pain, nausea / vomiting · chest pain, dyspnea
    • co-morbid diabetes / kidney disease · parity (pre-eclampsia favours primiparous)
  • Investigations
    • urine protein · platelets, white blood cell count, international normalized ratio (INR), partial thromboplastin time
    • creatinine, uric acid · liver function tests (LFTs), albumin · oxygen saturation
    • fetal: growth, amniotic fluid, umbilical artery end-diastolic flow
  • The primary maternal danger of severe HTN is stroke: neuro symptoms ⇒ rule out an intracranial event

rows: Eclampsia, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, transient ischemic attack / stroke, Glasgow Coma Scale <13, retinal detachment / cortical blindness
Severe HTN, myocardial infarction, oxygen saturation <90%, pulmonary edema, inotrope support
↑ white blood cell count, INR, partial thromboplastin time · ↓ platelets
Nausea / vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, ↑ LFTs, ↓ albumin
intrauterine growth restriction, oligohydramnios, reversed / absent end-diastolic flow
Abruption with compromise, reversed ductus venosus flow, intrauterine fetal death

blocks.html:
• Early severe HTN with no hypertensive disorder of pregnancy ⇒ think
    • thyroid storm (high human chorionic gonadotropin) · molar pregnancy (extremely high human chorionic gonadotropin) · theca lutein cysts (ovarian hyperstimulation)
4. Management

• Treatment
    • chronic / gestational ⇒ treat the BP
    • pre-eclampsia ⇒ BP is secondary; minimise maternal / fetal morbidity · magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) once delivery is decided
    • complications decide delivery planning
  • Contraindicated
    • diuretics - ↓ intravascular volume in a state built for fluid retention
    • angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors / angiotensin receptor blockers - toxic to fetal kidneys (2nd-3rd trimester) ⇒ oligohydramnios, renal failure; increasing evidence of 1st-trimester teratogenicity

rows: 100-400 mg by mouth twice to three times daily, max 1200 mg/day
20 mg IV, repeat 20-80 mg every 30 min to max 300 mg; or 1-2 mg/min infusion, then oral
Extended-release 20-60 mg by mouth once to twice daily, max 60 mg/day (as the slide prints it; guideline teaching allows up to 120 mg/day of nifedipine XL - check with the lecturer)
250-500 mg by mouth twice to four times daily, max 2 g/day
5 mg IV, repeat 5-10 mg every 30 min; or 0.5-10 mg/h to max 20 mg
Load 4 g in 100 mL normal saline over 20 min, then 1-2 g/h until delivery + 12-48 h post-partum
Raises the seizure threshold; started when delivery is decided in severe pre-eclampsia

lectures.name: Second Trimester Ultrasound
lectures.title: Second trimester ultrasound
lectures.framing: One screening scan with five jobs, walked in the order the lecture takes them: dating and growth → number of fetuses → placental location → anatomy screen → soft markers. The scan is a screen, so what it finds leads to more testing, not to a diagnosis.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Every pregnant person in Canada should have the screening anatomy scan between 18 and 22 weeks; no risk factor is required to earn it, so age, prior losses, a prior affected baby and a normal amniocentesis all get the same scan. ⚠ Fetal well-being (biophysical profile) is a 3rd trimester assessment and is not part of the 2nd trimester scan. ⚠ A soft marker is not a birth defect; it changes a risk, not a diagnosis. Dating, fetal number and chorionicity are all done in the 2nd trimester only if the 1st trimester did not settle them.

blocks.html: 1. Which trimester's scan does what

rows: Pregnancy dating (the most accurate time to do it) · genetic screening (nuchal translucency)
The screening anatomical scan at 18-22 weeks, with the five purposes below
Fetal growth and well-being (the biophysical profile lives here, NOT in the 2nd trimester scan)

blocks.html:
• The five purposes of the 2nd trimester scan
    • 1. Dating and growth · 2. Number of fetuses · 3. Placental location · 4. Screen of fetal anatomy · 5. Soft markers for aneuploidy
2. Dating and fetal growth

• Fetal biometry = standardized measurements and formulas
    • biparietal diameter (BPD) and occipital-frontal diameter (OFD) across the skull · head circumference (HC) around it · femur length (FL) end to end
  • What it settles
    • sonographic dating only if not already done in the 1st trimester · growth against gestational age

blocks.alt: fetal biometry on ultrasound - head measurements and femur length.png
blocks.cap: Fetal biometry - BPD, OFD and HC across and around the skull, FL along the femur

blocks.html: 3. Number of fetuses

• Count, then a full anatomical assessment of each fetus
  • Confirm chorionicity (the type of multiple pregnancy)
  • Confirms the multiple pregnancy; easier and more accurate in the 1st trimester
4. Placental location

• Wall: anterior or posterior
  • Relationship to the cervix
    • a placenta reaching the internal os is placenta previa
  • Cord insertion: into the placenta and into the fetus

blocks.alt: placenta, cervix and internal os on second trimester ultrasound.png
blocks.cap: Placental location - placenta, fetal head, cervix and internal os on ultrasound

blocks.html: 5. Screen of fetal anatomy

• The main job: rule out major congenital anomalies
    • birth defects affect 2-3% of all pregnancies, and many are diagnosed antenatally
  • What is looked at, each reported normal or abnormal
    • head (posterior fossa: cerebellum, vermis; thalami, fornices, choroid plexus) · facial profile · spine · 4-chamber heart with its axis · outflow tracts · abdomen · cord vessels · limbs
  • What follows a birth defect: further genetic testing or more detailed imaging for prenatal diagnosis, especially when several combine
  • Why look for anomalies at all (the module's own three reasons)
    • counsel the parents on what to expect · direct further investigations antenatally or postnatally · decide the place of delivery and level of care the finding needs

blocks.alt: fetal anatomy screen on ultrasound - cerebellar view, facial profile, spine.png
blocks.cap: Anatomy screen views - cerebellar view of the head, facial profile, spine

blocks.html: 6. Soft markers for aneuploidy

• Soft marker = an ultrasound finding tied to ↑ risk of trisomy 21 or 18
    • choroid plexus cysts · short femurs · intracardiac echogenic focus · echogenic bowel
  • They are NOT birth defects; if seen, further genetic screening/testing may be offered

rows: A normal-variant finding that raises the odds of aneuploidy
Further genetic testing or more detailed imaging for prenatal diagnosis, especially when several combine
An offer of further genetic screening or testing, not a diagnosis

lectures.name: Topics of Antenatal Care
lectures.title: Topics in antenatal care
lectures.framing: Three routine pieces of antenatal care, in lecture order, each with a when and a why: feed the pregnancy (folate + iron), vaccinate it (inactivated only), and screen the mother's blood. The antibody question turns on one thing: does she already have an antibody?
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The only vaccine category not considered safe is live attenuated (measles-mumps-rubella, varicella, bacille Calmette-Guérin), and the reason is a theoretical one, not an observed one. Tdap is timed (27-32 weeks) because the point is the baby's passive immunity; influenza is not timed because the point is the mother. RhIG is prophylaxis for the unsensitized: it clears fetal cells before the maternal immune system responds, so it does nothing once an antibody exists. ⚠ A titre of 1/8 or greater is the line for severe-anemia risk; below it, keep testing monthly. Sensitization needs a source: previous pregnancy, transfusion, or drug abuse (module Q94), and the fetus is only at risk if it carries the antigen, hence the partner screen.

blocks.html: 1. Diet and nutritional requirements

• Energy: +350-450 kcal/day on average, but healthy eating matters more than specific foods or weight gain
    • less if high body mass index (BMI), more if low
    • the extra goes to uterine muscle, breast tissue, and ↑ blood volume / hemoglobin
  • Supplements: daily prenatal multivitamin (not an adult one)
    • folate and iron are the most commonly required supplements
    • iodine where locally deficient · vitamin C, vitamin D, calcium and zinc after gastric bypass

rows: Most commonly required supplement; fetal + maternal red blood cells

blocks.html: 2. Vaccination

• Most vaccines are safe; the ones with a potential risk are delayed until post-partum
  • History: vaccines received or needed

rows: Hepatitis A and B · Haemophilus influenzae type b · meningococcus · rabies
Theoretical risk of improper preparation → active infection (realistically very low)
Safety established by decades of observational data; clear benefit to mother and/or fetus
Indicated by exposure or risk, not routine
Delay until post-partum; may consider if risk/benefit favours vaccinating
Tdap 27-32 weeks → maternal antibodies cross the placenta = passive immunity to the baby · Influenza any gestational age or post-partum, in flu season → ↓ maternal risk/severity

blocks.html: 3. Antibody screening and Rh immunoglobulin

• Group & screen in the 1st trimester for all
    • blood type + Rh status + any maternal antibodies
  • Sources of sensitization (ask in the history): previous pregnancy, blood transfusion, drug abuse
  • No antibody and Rh negative → Rh immunoglobulin (RhIG) to every Rh negative mother
    • after 8-10 weeks with bleeding, an invasive procedure or trauma · routinely 28-30 weeks · post-partum if the baby is Rh positive
    • it clears fetal cells before the maternal immune system responds, so RhIG prevents an antibody; it does nothing once one exists

lectures.name: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
lectures.title: Care for pregnancy in the first trimester
lectures.framing: Three jobs in the first 12 weeks, in the lecture's order: confirm the pregnancy, date it, and screen it - then count the obstetric history (GTPAL) and follow the uterus as it grows. Every question turns on a threshold or a counting rule.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ EDB is fixed once set by the most reliable method - later discrepancies are growth, not dating. A gestational sac alone does not confirm a pregnancy; the yolk sac is required, and location excludes ectopic. CRL after 14 weeks is not a dating tool. Herpes simplex virus and hepatitis C are not routine bloods. Symphysis-fundal height matches weeks only from 20 weeks.

blocks.html: 1. Diagnosing and confirming pregnancy

• Presents as: missed menses with or without nausea / vomiting, urinary frequency, breast tenderness, bloating
    • irregular cycles: symptoms matter more, amenorrhea is not apparent
    • ⚠ Early symptoms should never be relied on exclusively; some have none, some are misattributed (the flu)
    • ⚠ bleeding in early pregnancy is mistaken for menses and delays diagnosis, especially at the extremes of age and on the oral contraceptive pill
  • History: last normal menstrual period (LNMP) and cycle regularity · prior ectopic / recurrent miscarriage (the reason to bother confirming with human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG))
  • Serum hCG thresholds

rows: Very early pregnancy or assay error

blocks.html: 2. Dating the pregnancy

• The rule above the rest: once the estimated date of birth (EDB) is set by the most reliable method (in vitro fertilization (IVF) transfer date, or 1st-trimester ultrasound) it is FIXED
    • a later scan that disagrees is reporting growth, not a new due date

rows: LNMP + 7 days - 3 months + 1 year (gestation ~280 days = 40 completed weeks)
Depends on a known, normal LNMP
Most accurate: little biological variability; use the first scan with CRL ≥ 10 mm (~7 weeks) if several exist

head circumference, biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference, femur length combined
Any ultrasound < 23 weeks still beats LNMP (Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada #303)

blocks.html: 3. Early pregnancy investigations

• Routine for ALL pregnancies
    • complete blood count (hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, platelets) · group and screen (type, Rh, antibodies) · rubella immunity · hepatitis B, HIV, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test · gonorrhea/chlamydia · urine culture (asymptomatic bacteriuria)
  • Enhanced first trimester screen (eFTS), 11-14 weeks
    • nuchal translucency ultrasound + 4 serum analytes · offered to all regardless of age or risk
  • Selected populations only
    • ⚠ herpes simplex virus, hepatitis C are NOT routine - high risk or exposure only
    • thyroid-stimulating hormone (known thyroid disease, dose adjustment) · hemoglobinopathy screen (Mediterranean, Southeast Asian, African for sickle cell, or low mean corpuscular volume/hemoglobin) · non-invasive prenatal testing / chorionic villus sampling (known carrier: balanced translocation, muscular dystrophy)
4. GTPAL
• GTPAL (gravida, term, preterm, abortions, living) = the counting rule for the obstetric history

rows: A neonatal death after a term delivery still counts as T
Twins = two L; stillbirth and neonatal death = not L

• Physical exam in the 1st trimester: uterus closed fist → small grapefruit by 12 weeks, fundus reaching the pelvic brim / symphysis; not a dating tool in the first trimester

lectures.name: Approach to Sexual Health
lectures.title: Approach to sexual health
lectures.framing: Two halves to this lecture: the physiology you contrast between cis-men and cis-women, and the interview you run so the patient can raise the problem they came in with. The whole conversation turns on one move: know your own biases, then ask permission, so the patient never has to raise it first.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The refractory period is the sex difference: males are physiologically incapable of another orgasm after the first; females have none and can have multiple orgasms. NO is the neurotransmitter of clitoral engorgement, and photoplethysmography is how VBV is measured. Orgasm is cerebral, not spinal. The interview separates on repetition as the tool that unpacks a euphemism, and on asking permission first. ⚠ Never assume orientation or monogamy in the wording: "How many partners in the past year?", not "Are you monogamous?"; say "partner".

blocks.html: 1. Step one: your own biases, and who has concerns

• Acknowledge your own implicit biases before you walk into the room, so they are not carried into the encounter
  • Who has concerns
    • 50-98% of women: interest · orgasm · lubrication · dyspareunia · body image · unmet needs · need for information · abuse/coercion
    • 40% of men, mainly erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation · men are the ones most likely to feel ashamed asking for help
2. Models of the sexual response cycle

rows: direct laboratory observation (>10,000 episodes; 382 women, 312 men) · criteria precise but arbitrary, vary dramatically between individuals
most widely used · intimacy / motivations → variable desire → attention to stimuli → subjective arousal + autonomic nervous system response → arousal triggers desire → satisfaction feeds back

blocks.cap: The Masters & Johnson sexual response cycle, male vs female

blocks.cap: Basson circular model (2001): multiple motivations lead to attention to stimuli, then subjective arousal with an autonomic response that triggers desire; desire can arise at any point, and the rewards feed the next cycle

blocks.html: 3. The four phases, female vs male

clitoral + labial engorgement · inner ⅔ of vagina expands · ↑ vaginal blood flow · vaginal walls thicken · uterus elevates + engorges · breast enlargement
penile erection · ↑ testicular volume · testes elevate · scrotum contracts

physiology unclear · primarily a cerebral event (occurs after complete spinal cord injury) · contractions at 0.8-second intervals
rhythmic contractions of vaginal walls, anal sphincter, uterus · pleasure located subjectively in different genital areas

internal bladder sphincter spasm → vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate contract → emission into bulbous urethra → propulsion via external sphincter relaxation + bulbocavernosus contraction · pleasure ∝ contraction strength
myotonia dissipates · BP, HR, respiration return to baseline
nipples, clitoris, vaginal walls, uterus, labia shrink back · NO refractory period → multiple orgasms possible
loss of erection · testes + scrotum return to size · refractory period: physiologically incapable of another orgasm or ejaculation

• Modulators of desire and subjective arousal
    • pro-sexual: noradrenalin · dopamine · melanocortin · oxytocin · serotonin at some receptors
    • inhibitory: prolactin · serotonin at 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 · glutamate · vasopressin · gamma-aminobutyric acid
  • Female arousal is measured, not assumed
    • vaginal blood volume (VBV) by photoplethysmography (refractive index of light entering the vagina as vasocongestion varies)
    • in women genital and subjective responses are not necessarily concordant, and visual/tactile awareness of genital arousal matters less

blocks.html:
• Making the patient comfortable
    • assure complete confidentiality very early · nonjudgmental whatever the patient admits to
  • Body language: hands/arms · pectoral flush · position in chair · postural echo (mirror-image sitting = harmony)
  • Determining the problem
    • terminology the patient knows ("sex", not "intercourse") · open questions, silence, repetition
    • repetition unpacks a euphemism: "Checkup?" → "Performing?" → "Ashamed?"
5. Creating a safe space

• staff trained in culturally sensitive terminology · gender-inclusive forms · diverse waiting-room images
  • two-step method (gender identity + sex assigned at birth) · ask pronouns
  • Trauma-informed: adverse childhood experiences limit what a patient can discuss
6. A productive conversation and the 5 P's

• Ask permission to talk about sexual health, proactively, so the patient never has to raise it first
  • ⚠ There is NO standard validated comprehensive sexual health assessment tool
  • ⚠ Never assume orientation or monogamy in the wording: "How many partners in the past year?", not "Are you monogamous?"; say "partner"
  • The 5 P's: Partners · Practices · Protection / Past sexually transmitted infection · Pregnancy plans · (optional) Pleasure
7. Terminology, sexual preferences and illness

• Terminology
    • sex = biologic category assigned at birth (chromosomes, anatomy, hormones) · gender identity = self-determined sense of being along or outside the spectrum
    • cisgender = gender consistent with sex assigned · transgender = gender does not match, or is inconsistent over time
    • gender expression = external signals · gender perception = how others read it · sexual orientation = self-determined identity in relation to the gender(s) attracted to
  • When illness may affect sex: give permission to be curious ("Many people are concerned about how this condition might affect their sex life. What is your experience?"); the patient's response decides what information you offer

lectures.name: Physiologic Changes in Pregnancy
lectures.title: Physiologic changes in pregnancy
lectures.framing: Pregnancy rewrites the "normal" for almost every organ system, and the whole lecture is one question asked seven times: is this number physiologic (expected in pregnancy) or pathologic (disease)? Part 1 walks the systems in the order the slides take them; Part 2 applies the question to the two findings that are almost universal, anemia and a low platelet count.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Platelets below 100,000 are not gestational thrombocytopenia until proven otherwise - gestational is 75% of cases, starts mid-to-late second trimester, rarely drops below 100,000 and needs nothing; ITP starts before or early in pregnancy, goes below 100,000, and does not normalize post partum. Anemia cut-offs are 110 in the first trimester and 105 after, dilution is the commonest cause and iron deficiency (ferritin under 30) the commonest disease. Creatinine in the 80s is abnormal in pregnancy even when the lab says normal. Resting heart rate above 110 is not "just pregnancy." Total T4 rises with TBG; free T4 holds; TSH dips with the hCG peak and is observed, not treated. D-dimer is up in every pregnancy, so a high one does not diagnose a pulmonary embolism - but the threshold to look for a clot is lower, not higher.

blocks.html: 1. The hormones that drive it

• Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) climbs steeply in the first trimester, peaks at about 8-12 weeks, then falls to a low plateau for the rest of pregnancy
  • Estrogens and progesterone start low and rise steadily to term, crossing above hCG at about 24 weeks
  • Why it matters for the rest of the chart: progesterone relaxes smooth muscle and drives breathing · estrogen raises binding proteins (thyroid) · the hCG spike is what unsettles thyroid tests in the first trimester

blocks.alt: hormone levels across pregnancy - hCG estrogen progesterone - lecture slide.jpg
blocks.cap: Relative hormone levels across the 40 weeks: hCG spikes in the first trimester and falls; estrogens and progesterone rise steadily to term

blocks.html: 2. Cardiac

• One of the most clinically important and most visible systems affected
  • What changes
    • progressive rise in red cell volume, plasma volume and heart rate
    • cardiac output rises 40%, mostly from stroke volume (a little from heart rate) · maximal at 20-28 weeks (apart from delivery itself), peaking in the 3rd trimester
    • the heart dilates physiologically and contractility increases (holds more, pumps better)
    • vascular resistance falls from the first trimester, so blood pressure falls, lowest at about 22-24 weeks · pulmonary vascular resistance falls too
    • low oncotic pressure → higher risk of pulmonary edema
  • The numbers
    • blood pressure: systolic drops ~1 mmHg from 12-18 weeks then rises ~7 mmHg to 40 weeks · diastolic drops ~1 mmHg from 12-19 weeks then rises ~9 mmHg to 40 weeks
    • heart rate (median): lowest 82 beats/min at 12 weeks, highest 91 at 34 weeks (a 9-point rise), 89 at 40 weeks
  • Clinically
    • lower blood pressure in the first half → physiologic vs pathologic hypotension is hard to separate, and symptoms do not separate them either (both can be symptomatic)
    • higher heart rate → physiologic vs pathologic tachycardia is hard to separate · upper limit at rest is still about 110 beats/min · be careful about "writing off" tachycardia as normal
    • palpitations are common (more plasma volume → more awareness of the heartbeat), but pregnancy is also linked to a first presentation of supraventricular tachycardia, so do not write them off either
    • more risk of pulmonary edema → more judicious, monitored IV fluid
3. Respiratory

• What changes
    • respiratory rate is unchanged
    • progesterone stimulates ventilation → tidal volume ↑ → minute ventilation ↑ → breathes off more CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis with a compensatory metabolic acidosis; overall pH stays normal
    • total lung capacity, residual volume and functional residual capacity all ↓
    • oxygen consumption ↑ 15-20%
    • anatomy: chest wall diameter ↑ up to 2 cm · diaphragm rises up to 4 cm · more blood flow in the upper airways → nasal congestion and nosebleeds (epistaxis)
    • shortness of breath (dyspnea) affects 60-75%, often from the first trimester, levelling off in the third · cause unclear, perhaps the progesterone-driven ventilation
  • Clinically
    • the lung-volume changes and the very small fall in diffusing capacity (DLCO) are not clinically apparent
    • oxygen saturation stays normal despite the extra demand
    • slightly low serum bicarbonate is expected (metabolic compensation for the alkalosis)
    • dyspnea of pregnancy is very common and hard to tell from the sinister causes (pulmonary embolism, pneumonia)
4. Renal

• What changes
    • renal blood flow ↑ 60-80% by the second trimester (the same widespread vasodilation) → glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ↑, so creatinine falls
    • physiologic proteinuria: up to 30 mg/mmol on a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (uPCR) or 300 mg/day on a 24-hour collection (normal non-pregnant loss ~100 mg/day; pregnancy 150-200 mg/day)
    • physiologic hydronephrosis, more on the right, from the enlarging uterus plus progesterone relaxing smooth muscle
    • glucosuria on dipstick reflects the higher filtration and is not useful for screening for diabetes
  • Clinically
    • a creatinine in the 80s or above is suspicious - renal impairment in pregnancy can sit inside the lab's "normal" range and never be flagged
    • a uPCR over 30 is one of the clues to preeclampsia (see 12 - Hypertension in Pregnancy)
    • urinary frequency and nocturia are very common and physiologic
5. Endocrine: blood sugar

• Diabetes in pregnancy = pre-existing (type 1 or type 2) or gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), which accounts for most of it
  • Insulin resistance starts and increases through pregnancy: it worsens control in type 1 and type 2, and tips others into GDM
  • Clinically: tighter sugar targets than usual because hyperglycemia is a teratogen and harms both fetus and mother
6. Endocrine: thyroid

• Two separate effects, so the lab picture is confusing
    • estrogen ↑ thyroid binding globulin (TBG) → the body makes more T3/T4 to keep up → total T3/T4 ↑ but free T3/T4 stays roughly steady
    • hCG shares a subunit with thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), so the first-trimester hCG peak stimulates the TSH receptor → T3/T4 nudge up (usually within normal) and TSH looks slightly suppressed
    • with very high hCG (also linked to hyperemesis) TSH can be quite suppressed = a possible transient subclinical hyperthyroidism → observe, do not treat; it resolves as hCG falls after the first trimester
  • Clinically
    • already hypothyroid → needs more replacement in pregnancy: usual trick is to double the pre-pregnancy levothyroxine dose on Saturday and Sunday only
    • the hard calls: gestational transient thyrotoxicosis vs Graves disease · treating by TSH depending on thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody status

blocks.alt: maternal thyroid function across pregnancy - TBG total T4 free T4 hCG TSH - lecture slide.jpg
blocks.cap: Maternal thyroid function across pregnancy: TBG and total T4 rise and plateau; free T4 bumps up and TSH (thyrotropin) dips exactly where hCG peaks

blocks.html: 7. Hematologic

• What changes
    • plasma volume ↑ 30-50% but red cell mass ↑ only 20-30% → hemoglobin falls (dilution) · red cell lifespan slightly shorter · erythropoietin ↑ · mean cell volume slightly ↑
    • trimester-specific hemoglobin cut-offs for anemia: under 110 in the 1st trimester, under 105 in the 2nd and 3rd (some references use 110 throughout)
    • platelets: no change to slightly ↓ · white cells ↑ (neutrophilia) = mild leukocytosis; lymphocytes and monocytes unchanged
    • clotting: pro-coagulant factors ↑ (fibrinogen, factors II, VII, VIII, X, XII, XIII up 20-200%, von Willebrand factor, PAI-1/PAI-2) · anti-coagulant protein S ↓ and resistance to activated protein C ↑ · D-dimer ↑ · prothrombin time slightly shorter, bleeding time unchanged
    • all of this is an adaptation to prevent hemorrhage at delivery → pregnancy is a pro-thrombotic state with a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE)
  • Clinically
    • anemia, thrombocytopenia and leukocytosis are common findings - each one needs the physiologic-or-pathologic question asked (is the high white count really infection or inflammation?)
    • lower threshold to consider VTE in a pregnant patient with symptoms of a clot in the lung (pulmonary embolism) or leg (deep vein thrombosis) - and a raised D-dimer does not by itself mean a pulmonary embolism
8. Immunologic

• Less cell-mediated immunity, more humoral (antibody) immunity - protects the fetus from the mother's immune system · also changes the course of autoimmune disease (inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatologic conditions, multiple sclerosis)
  • Clinically
    • less lymphocyte proliferation (2nd and 3rd trimester) and less natural killer (NK) cell activity → more severe flu: more preterm delivery, pneumonia, hospitalization, intensive care, and maternal and fetal death
    • the flu shot and oseltamivir are safe in pregnancy · the nasal flu vaccine is live, so it is not (no live vaccines in pregnancy)
9. Gastrointestinal

• What changes
    • progesterone ↓ motility through the whole gut · secretion and absorption are unchanged
    • nausea and vomiting affect the majority of pregnancies
    • reflux (GERD) in over half: lower esophageal sphincter tone ↓ (progesterone or estrogen)
    • the placenta makes alkaline phosphatase (ALP) → a "liver marker" that is raised in normal pregnancy
    • lipids rise (triglycerides and LDL) → do not measure them in pregnancy; isolated rises need no treatment
    • more gallstones (cholelithiasis)
  • Clinically: constipation and bloating (slow gut) · GERD and gallstones more common · nausea and vomiting in many pregnancies
10. Part 2: Anemia - dilution or disease?

• Causes, in order of frequency
    • physiologic (dilutional) anemia from the plasma-volume rise = most common cause overall
    • iron deficiency = most common pathologic cause · then B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, thalassemia
    • telling dilution from the rest usually needs further tests
  • Symptoms: fatigue or weakness · dyspnea · lightheadedness or presyncope · pica and restless legs point to iron deficiency · or none - and all of these are common in normal pregnancy, so keep a degree of suspicion
  • Screening: routine bloodwork for anemia in the 1st trimester and again at 24-28 weeks

rows: ferritin under 30 · or Tsat under 20% when ferritin may be falsely normal (it is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation or infection raises it) · microcytic
very low MCV · often first found in pregnancy · can coexist with iron deficiency and dilution
everyone should already be on folic acid for neural tube defect prevention
much less likely in pregnancy; consider only with a predisposing condition (malignancy, rheumatologic disease)

blocks.html: 11. Iron deficiency: how much, and how to replace it

• How common and why: 30%+ of pregnancies · stores already low from periods and prior pregnancies · requirements higher (maternal red cell expansion and fetal red cell production)
  • Why treat: linked to low birth weight, preterm delivery, postpartum hemorrhage and the child's later neurologic development
  • Three routes
    • diet: food aversions (red meat is a common one) and usually not enough to meet the need
    • oral iron: a prenatal vitamin has only ~30 mg (preventative rather than treatment) → add an oral iron supplement for proven deficiency · daily, or every other day if side effects (nausea, constipation are common) · take with ~250 mg vitamin C or orange juice · away from prenatal vitamins, calcium, dairy, coffee and tea · all formulations acceptable; only ~28% of the elemental dose is absorbed at best
    • IV iron: not in the first trimester · iron sucrose, 300 mg IV, 3 doses one week apart (Monoferric is the non-pregnant choice) · needs a monitored infusion setting, so hard to arrange · preferred when oral iron is not tolerated, hemoglobin under 100, or delivery is close
  • Assessing response (American Society of Hematology): first trimester → oral iron for 2 weeks, a hemoglobin rise of 1 g/dL or more means keep going; a smaller rise past 13 weeks → IV iron · second trimester → oral if hemoglobin ≥ 10.5 g/dL, IV if lower · third trimester → IV iron · recheck counts 6 weeks post partum

blocks.alt: iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy treatment algorithm by trimester - lecture slide.jpg
blocks.cap: How to treat and assess iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy by trimester: oral iron with a 2-week recheck early on; IV iron when the response is poor, the hemoglobin is low, or delivery is near

blocks.html: 12. B12, folate and thalassemia

• B12 or folate deficiency can be isolated or travel with iron deficiency through poor intake
    • treat B12 deficiency when found: 1000-2000 mcg oral vitamin B12 daily
    • folic acid for every pregnancy, pre-conception and throughout, to prevent neural tube defects: 400-800 mcg, ideally from 1 month pre-conception · higher doses for pre-existing diabetes, a prior neural tube defect, or anti-epileptic use
  • Thalassemia: order a hemoglobinopathy screen on suspicion · specialist (hematology) care for iron needs (some are iron-overloaded from past transfusions, some have different hemoglobin targets) · test the partner for fetal risk - if all 4 alpha globin genes in the fetus are non-functioning, alpha thalassemia major is usually fatal
13. Part 2: Thrombocytopenia - pooling or pathology?

• Physiologic: platelets fall in every pregnancy from splenic and placental pooling plus hemodilution · 4-11% go under 150,000 · under 1% go below 100,000 → 100,000 is the mental cut-off for further investigation
  • There is no test that separates gestational thrombocytopenia from the sinister causes → clinical acumen and a high degree of suspicion; the others need intervention and can harm mother and baby

rows: 1 in 1,000-10,000 pregnancies (~5,000-6,000 deliveries a year in a major hospital)
more often in severe preeclampsia · platelets are part of HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets)
before pregnancy or early in pregnancy
can present for the first time in pregnancy
bleeding with past procedures or dental work · platelets fail to normalize post partum
blood pressure over 140/90 · proteinuria · HELLP has no hypertension in 15%
altered mental status, renal insufficiency, fever, anemia (rarely all) - can't-miss diagnoses
"secondary causes" screen: hepatitis C, H. pylori, TSH, INR/PTT, ANA
urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, urinalysis or dipstick · liver enzymes · look for anemia and hemolysis
beware the triad of anemia + renal impairment + thrombocytopenia

blocks.html:
• ITP: why one drug over the other: IVIg works in days, prednisone in 1-2 weeks → IVIg when late in the third trimester with no time to trial prednisone · IVIg is expensive, hard to organize, a blood product with blood-product risks, and rarely causes aseptic meningitis
  • ITP and the baby: 5-10% chance of fetal thrombocytopenia → check the baby's platelets at birth and avoid a difficult instrumental delivery (lowers the risk of intracranial hemorrhage)
  • Every thrombocytopenic patient is assessed for preeclampsia and HELLP (preeclampsia = hypertension + proteinuria or other organ involvement; HELLP has hypertension 85% of the time, but its absence does not rule it out)
