lectures.name: Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation
lectures.title: Antepartum hemorrhage
lectures.framing: Bleeding in the 2nd/3rd trimester turns on two questions: is it painful, and whose blood is it? The lecture walks the sources, then each placental cause in turn, then the management that applies to all of them: assess mother and fetus together, continuously.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Painful bleeding + tender uterus = abruption; painless bleeding = previa; small bleed + fetal distress = vasa previa, and the blood is fetal. ⚠ Never examine the cervix of a bleeder until ultrasound has cleared the placenta. Kleihaur-Betke finds fetal blood in the mother; Apt finds it in the vaginal blood - only Apt diagnoses vasa previa. Abruption is a diagnosis of exclusion; previa is an ultrasound diagnosis. A previous C/S raises the risk of previa and accreta, not vasa previa; vasa previa comes from a velamentous cord (type 1) or a succenturiate lobe (type 2).

blocks.html: 1. Where the bleeding comes from

• Non-obstetrical: hemorrhoids/varices · bladder infection/renal stones · rarely masses, lacerations → treat the cause, as in a non-pregnant patient
  • Obstetrical: placental/uterine, cervical or fetal
    • always assess for labour: cervical dilatation frequently causes bleeding ("show")
    • a painful bleed with a tender uterus is an abruption · a painless bleed is a previa until the ultrasound says otherwise · a small bleed with a distressed fetus is fetal blood - a vasa previa
2. The four placental causes side by side

rows: Premature separation of the placental/maternal interface (1st trimester = subchorionic hemorrhage)
Implantation over, or just adjacent to, the internal cervical os · marginal/partial = within 2 cm · complete = covering the os
Unprotected umbilical vessels traverse the cervix / within 2 cm · Type 1 = velamentous cord insertion · Type 2 = succenturiate lobe / multilobed placenta
Abnormal placental invasion into the uterus over a previous uterine incision lacking complete endometrial cover
~1/300 at term · seen at the 18-20 week morphology scan, often resolves by 3rd trimester · sentinel bleed 26-28 weeks, then 30-40% rebleed
Risk rises with previous C/S / uterine surgery with or without previa

Painful active bleeding, mild to profuse · "unrelenting contractions" · tender, sometimes rigid uterus · mother and fetus usually stable unless severe · concealed (central) form: no bleeding, pain out of keeping, fetal distress
Painless bleeding, mild or severe · fetus stable unless mother hemodynamically unstable
Volume may be very small but fetal distress is frequent
Often silent until delivery: bleeding the myometrium cannot contract to control
Diagnosis of exclusion once other sources are ruled out (edge bleeds drain out, so ultrasound is often unrevealing)
Apt test on vaginal blood; heightened suspicion with known velamentous cord
Blood irritates the myometrium, so it may progress to labour; risk of rupture of membranes as membranes stretch over clot · deliver by maternal/fetal status
Complete previa: cesarean section · marginal >1 cm from the os may allow vaginal birth in select cases · aggressive transfusion + clotting-factor replacement pre and post delivery
Deck gives no specific management beyond the shared pathway (fetal distress drives delivery decisions)
Almost always hysterectomy unless the invasion is very focal
Larger area affected in concealed abruption

Any cervical change (dilatation, even thinning) disrupts the implantation · the cervix is not designed to shed and has no myometrium to clamp the vessels · hypovolemia/shock, consumptive coagulopathy, ↑ hysterectomy
A tiny volume is a large share of the fetal blood volume
Myometrium cannot contract over the invaded site

blocks.html: 3. Placental abruption

• Two forms
    • at the placental edge (most): active vaginal bleeding with cramping
    • concealed (central): blood trapped behind the placenta - no bleeding, pain out of proportion, more fetal distress
  • Risk factors
    • hypertension · trauma · previous abruption · autoimmune condition · preterm prelabour rupture of membranes · smoking/cocaine · intrauterine infection

blocks.alt: types of placental abruption.png
blocks.cap: Placental abruption: an edge separation drains as vaginal bleeding with cramping, while a central (concealed) separation traps the blood behind the placenta, giving no bleeding and pain out of proportion

blocks.html: 4. Placenta previa

• Types: marginal or partial = within 2 cm of the cervix · complete = covering the cervical os
  • Complications
    • maternal hemorrhagic shock · disseminated intravascular coagulation · preterm birth · cesarean delivery · maternal transfusion
    • not fetal hemorrhage (the blood is maternal) and not pre-eclampsia

blocks.alt: placenta previa types - marginal partial vs complete - lecture slide.png
blocks.cap: Placenta previa: marginal or partial within 2 cm of the cervix vs complete covering the cervical os

blocks.html: 5. Vasa previa

• The only cause where the blood is fetal, so a small bleed matters
  • Type 1: a velamentous cord insertion · Type 2: vessels running between the lobes of a succenturiate (multi-lobed) placenta
    • either way, exposed fetal vessels lie over the cervix

blocks.alt: types of vasa previa.png
blocks.cap: Vasa previa: type 1 from a velamentous cord insertion, type 2 from vessels running between the lobes of a succenturiate (multi-lobed) placenta; either way, exposed fetal vessels lie over the cervix

blocks.html: 6. Placenta accreta spectrum

• Accreta attaches to the myometrium · increta invades into it · percreta goes through it to the serosa and beyond
  • Previous C/S or uterine surgery raises the risk; the myometrium cannot contract over the invaded site → almost always hysterectomy
7. Managing obstetrical hemorrhage

• History: previous bleeding this pregnancy · previous abruption · trauma (motor vehicle collision, fall) · hypertension, autoimmune disease · smoking/cocaine · previous C/S or uterine surgery (accreta) · placental location on the anatomy scan
  • Physical exam: maternal vitals · abdominal exam for uterine tenderness/rigidity and fetal presentation · speculum for the source
    • ⚠ no cervical examination until ultrasound has shown the placenta is clear of the cervix - examining a previa can precipitate massive hemorrhage
  • Investigations
    • stat complete blood count (baseline hemoglobin, platelets) · international normalized ratio / partial thromboplastin time / fibrinogen (coagulopathy) · creatinine · with or without liver function tests (rule out pre-eclampsia, acute liver injury) · group and screen
    • Kleihaur-Betke test = fetal blood in the maternal circulation (trauma, abruption) · Apt test = fetal blood in the vaginal bleed (vasa previa) · ultrasound for placental location
  • Treatment
    • active bleed + preterm: birthing unit, continuous fetal monitoring, steroids for lungs, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, neonatal intensive care unit / tertiary consult if <28-32 weeks, serial bloods every 4-6 hours
    • term or late preterm (>35-36 weeks): deliver - induction if reassuring, C/S if not
  • Follow-up: preterm, stable and bleeding settled → antenatal ward, non-stress test + growth/placental-function ultrasound, periodic bloods by initial values and rebleeding
  • How hemorrhage becomes coagulopathy
    • the high-volume flow to the placental-uterine interface and the inability to acutely clot over large exposed vessels means platelets and clotting factors are quickly consumed - a consumptive coagulopathy, which is why fibrinogen is on the stat bloodwork
    • ongoing bleeding depletes clotting factors at the placental interface

lectures.name: Approach to the Small Fetus
lectures.title: Approach to the small fetus
lectures.framing: Three labels that sound alike and mean different things, then the hunt for the one that is pathological. Find the fetus with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) as early as possible, name the cause, then let the Doppler and the gestational age decide delivery.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ SGA is a percentile (<10th), LBW is a weight (<2500 g), IUGR is a process, and an IUGR fetus can be above the 10th percentile. SFH >2-3 cm less than weeks screens; ultrasound EFW confirms. A trisomy is the intrinsic cause; smoking, hypertension and multiples restrict nutrient delivery. Placental insufficiency below the 3rd percentile shows absent EDF and ↓ amniotic fluid, not polyhydramnios. Delivery, not time, is the only way to feed the fetus better.

Repeat growth scans"] C -->|Yes| E["Find the cause: enhanced first trimester screen / non-invasive prenatal testing / amniocentesis
Toxoplasmosis / cytomegalovirus screen"] E --> F["Fetal well-being: umbilical artery (UA) Doppler, amniotic fluid volume, non-stress test (NST)"] F --> G{"Gestational age?"} G -->|">37 weeks"| H["DELIVER - limited benefit to staying in utero"] G -->|"32-37 weeks"| I["Deliver if oligohydramnios or persistently abnormal Dopplers
(even resistive index >95th percentile alone)"] G -->|"<32 weeks"| J["MONITOR unless fetal distress:
abnormal NST, absent or reversed end-diastolic flow (EDF)"]

blocks.html: 2. Small for gestational age, low birth weight and IUGR

• Small for gestational age (SGA) is a percentile, low birth weight (LBW) is a weight, IUGR is a pathological process, and the first two say nothing about the third
  • Estimated fetal weight (EFW) by the Hadlock formulas: head circumference · abdominal circumference · biparietal diameter · femur length

cols: LBW / very low birth weight / extremely low birth weight
rows: A pathological process impairing growth potential (↓ growth rate)
Absolute birth weight: <2500 g / <1500 g / <1000 g
Yes: the actual weight for the label varies with gestational age
No cut-off at all: can still sit above the 10th percentile and be IUGR
Something is wrong: maternal, fetal or placental
Risk of neonatal complications (a paediatric / neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) cut-off)
May be normal for parental size

blocks.alt: estimated fetal weight vs. birth weight.png
blocks.cap: Birth weight against gestational age: low, very low and extremely low birth weight are fixed lines at 2500, 1500 and 1000 g, while small and large for gestational age follow the curving 10th and 90th percentiles

blocks.html: 3. Identifying IUGR

• Physical exam: SFH from 20 weeks, cm = weeks
    • >2-3 cm behind = suspect
    • ⚠ SFH only suggests; ultrasound is the only confirmation
  • Ultrasound EFW percentile: <10th = SGA · <3rd = adverse-outcome risk
  • History: maternal medical (hypertension, chronic kidney disease, lupus / autoimmune, smoking / substance use) · obstetrical (a previous IUGR baby)
    • a risk factor buys extra growth scans at 26-28 weeks and 34-36 weeks
4. Causes of IUGR

rows: Hypertension, chronic kidney disease, lupus / autoimmune, smoking / substance use, previous IUGR baby
Trisomy 21 / 18 / 13, single-gene disorders, translocations, intrauterine infection, multiple gestation
Often known at conception; damages the placental microvasculature
Abnormal genetic material impairs cell replication; infection damages fetal tissue
Microvascular (small clots: lupus, smoking) or disrupted implantation (abruption); overlaps with maternal and fetal

blocks.html: 5. Investigations

• Find the cause: enhanced first trimester screen / non-invasive prenatal testing / amniocentesis; toxoplasmosis / cytomegalovirus
  • Fetal well-being: UA Doppler, amniotic fluid volume, NST
  • Follow-up: frequency set by severity and by NST / Doppler findings

rows: Continuous forward flow through the whole cycle
Baseline EDF drops toward the zero line

blocks.alt: placental insufficiency doppler ultrasound.png
blocks.cap: Umbilical artery Doppler waveforms in placental insufficiency

blocks.html: 6. Management and delivery

• Treatment
    • reverse the reversible (smoking, hypertension) to limit worsening
    • ⚠ no catch-up growth in utero; delivery is the only true way to improve nutrient delivery
    • if premature: steroids for lung maturation, transfer to NICU-level care
  • Delivery by gestational age
    • >37 weeks: deliver, even with no other risks
    • 32-37 weeks: deliver if oligohydramnios or persistently abnormal Dopplers, even just resistive index >95th percentile
    • <32 weeks: monitor unless fetal distress (abnormal NST, absent or reversed EDF)
  • Mode of delivery follows the usual obstetric indicators, but oligohydramnios or abnormal Dopplers raise the cesarean section risk

lectures.name: Approach to Preterm Labour
lectures.title: Approach to preterm labour
lectures.framing: Everything turns on where she sits on one line: threatened preterm labour → preterm labour → preterm birth, with membranes intact or ruptured. Each step adds the intervention that buys the next one time, and the lecture walks them in that order.
lectures.keypoints: ⚠ Antibiotics in PPROM INCREASE latency (the inherited note had it backwards). ⭐ Steroids are the one intervention given at every stage; tocolysis needs contractions, magnesium needs an imminent birth, penicillin needs a delivery. Cerclage is for cervical insufficiency before 24 weeks, never for ruptured membranes. Dehydration and UTI mimic TPTL: hydrate and dip the urine before reaching for a tocolytic.

blocks.html: 1. The preterm line: definitions

rows: Signs or symptoms of labour, cervical change not required
May resolve without delivery or progress
Regular contractions leading to cervical dilatation
May still resolve, or lead to preterm birth
Membrane rupture before 37 weeks, before labour

blocks.alt: threatened preterm labour to preterm birth continuum - lecture slide.png
blocks.cap: Threatened preterm labour to preterm labour to preterm birth, where either early stage can resolve without delivery

blocks.html: 2. Causes of preterm labour

• premature maternal or fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation · inflammation and infection · decidual hemorrhage · pathologic uterine distension · idiopathic (common)
  • PPROM adds mechanical stress and bleeding weakening the membranes
3. Consequences of prematurity

• respiratory distress syndrome, apnea, bronchopulmonary dysplasia · intraventricular hemorrhage · glucose abnormalities · necrotizing enterocolitis · retinopathy · sepsis · prolonged neonatal intensive care unit stay
4. Risk factors

• previous spontaneous preterm birth · multifetal gestation · cervical surgery (cone > loop electrosurgical excision procedure) · short cervix · cervicitis (gonorrhea, chlamydia, bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas, ureaplasma, mycoplasma)
  • non-Hispanic black race (?socioeconomic confounders) · age extremes · assisted reproductive technology · Mullerian anomalies, fibroids · chronic disease · Ehlers-Danlos · smoking/substances · no prenatal care
5. Assessment

• History
    • gestational age · previous spontaneous preterm birth · cervical surgery (cone > loop electrosurgical excision procedure) · smoking/substances · prenatal care · progesterone prophylaxis
    • contraction onset, frequency, duration · bleeding, leaking fluid, infectious symptoms
  • Physical exam: Leopold's for presentation · cervical exam (dilatation, consistency) · fetal heart rate · speculum for pooling if fluid suspected
  • Investigations
    • nitrazine + ferning, ultrasound for low amniotic fluid
    • urinalysis (urinary tract infection (UTI) mimics TPTL) · group B streptococcus (GBS) swab if not done
    • ⚠ amniocentesis for bacteria is NOT a validated test for rupture of membranes
6. Managing threatened preterm labour

• Hydrate, then tocolyse to buy 48 hours, spend them on steroids and transfer, and when birth is imminent switch to magnesium and penicillin
  • Follow-up: admit for monitoring

rows: Contracting, membranes intact; hydrate first (dehydration → uterine irritability); drugs if no response
Birth imminent and < 34 weeks (e.g., 6 cm dilated)
Delivering preterm with GBS positive or unknown status
Betamethasone 12 mg intramuscular x 2, 24 hours apart
Intravenous (IV) bolus then continuous infusion to the mother
Antibiotic course (Mercer protocol: 2 days IV, 5 days oral)
Penicillin IV, first line if no allergy
Delays birth by about 48 hours: enough for transfer to a tertiary centre and/or steroids; not a cure
Type-2 pneumocytes → surfactant → ↓ respiratory distress syndrome; also ↓ intraventricular hemorrhage, ↓ necrotizing enterocolitis, ↓ perinatal mortality
↓ neonatal cerebral palsy; mechanism of action unclear (stabilizes cerebral circulation, blocks excitatory injury, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory)
↑ latency from PPROM to delivery; prolongation improves neonatal outcomes
Not contracting (PPROM without labour); no benefit past the 48-hour window
Stable, no imminent birth: short acting, so wasted early

blocks.html: 7. Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

• Confirm it: a gush on history · speculum for pooling · nitrazine · ferning · low amniotic fluid on ultrasound
  • Without intervention, under 32 weeks: 50% deliver within 48 hours, 75% within 7 days
  • Treatment: antibiotics for latency (Mercer protocol) · complete the steroid course · watch for chorioamnionitis

blocks.alt: preterm prelabor rupture of membranes diagnosis.png
blocks.cap: Confirming ruptured membranes: a history of a gush, pooling of fluid in the vaginal fornix, nitrazine paper turning from orange to dark blue, and a fern pattern when amniotic fluid dries on a slide

blocks.html: 8. When preterm birth is imminent

• Magnesium sulfate: birth imminent and under 34 weeks → IV bolus + infusion for neuroprotection (↓ cerebral palsy)
  • Penicillin: IV if GBS positive or status unknown and the birth is preterm

lectures.name: Process of Labour and Birth
lectures.title: Process of labour and birth
lectures.framing: Each stage of labour asks the same two questions: what event ends it, and what am I measuring to know it is progressing. The 1st stage is measured on the cervix, the 2nd on the fetus, the 3rd on the placenta, the 4th on the mother - and the lecture walks them in that order.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ true labour = regular contractions causing progressive cervical dilation; Braxton Hicks change nothing at the cervix. Station is measured from the ischial spines, dilation is complete at 10 cm. ⚠ The earliest sign of placental separation is the firm, globular uterus, not the gush of blood. ⚠ In the 4th stage the danger is postpartum hemorrhage on top of a 500 mL autotransfusion, so a cardiac patient needs watching for the ↑ cardiac work.

blocks.html: 1. Labour and its four stages

• Labour = regular uterine contractions causing progressive cervical dilation
  • Contraindications to labour: placenta previa · vasa previa · cord presentation · abnormal lie · prior classical cesarean section or significant uterine surgery · active genital herpes
  • Friedman curve = a guideline, not a rule

rows: onset of labour → full dilatation · latent 0-4 cm, active 4-10 cm
full dilatation → delivery of the fetus ("pushing")
delivery of fetus → expulsion of placenta
primiparous 6-18 h, active phase 1.2 cm/h · multiparous 2-10 h, active 1.5 cm/h

blocks.alt: Friedman curve.png
blocks.cap: The stages of labour on the Friedman curve

blocks.html: 2. Before labour: preparation and initiation

• Pre-labour
    • Braxton Hicks from ~28 weeks, painless, no cervical change
    • effacement · engagement ~2 weeks before labour in a primiparous woman
  • Initiation
    • oxytocin receptors switch on at term · progesterone falls relative to estrogen · fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis · prostaglandin F
    • withdrawal of inhibitors: progesterone, relaxin, prostacyclin, parathyroid hormone, nitric oxide
3. First stage: fetal heart rate monitoring
• Fetal heart rate (FHR) intermittent every 15 min (low risk) or continuous (high risk)

rows: pre-eclampsia, bleeding, atypical or abnormal FHR, induction or augmentation with Syntocinon, vaginal birth after cesarean

normal / atypical / abnormal (Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada #197) · normal: continue · atypical: resuscitate and find the cause · abnormal: resuscitate and prepare for delivery

blocks.html:
• Decelerations (shape against the contraction)
    • early = mirror of the contraction, head compression
    • variable = sharp V, no fixed relation, cord compression
    • late = starts after the peak, recovers after the end, ↓ uteroplacental flow

blocks.alt: early variable and late decelerations on fetal heart rate tracing - lecture slide.png
blocks.cap: Early, variable and late decelerations, each drawn against its contraction

blocks.html:
• Intrauterine resuscitation (atypical or abnormal tracing)
    • scalp clip (is it fetal?) · vaginal exam (rule out cord prolapse; station, position, dilation, effacement) · left lateral (or right if already left) · oxytocin OFF · oxygen by mask · 500 mL bolus (normal saline or Ringer's lactate)
    • then decide the mode of delivery if it continues
4. First stage: contractions, the cervix and pain

• Contractions: palpation every 30 min early · tocometer if high risk or slow · intrauterine pressure catheter
  • Cervical change every 2-3 hours (sooner for symptoms or FHR changes)
    • dilation 0-10 cm, effacement 0-100%, station
    • more exams = ↑ chorioamnionitis
  • Pain control: 1st stage pain from T10-T12 → epidural (most common), spinal, Lamaze, nitrous oxide, patient-controlled analgesia
5. Fetal lie, presentation, position and station

rows: <mark class="lo">long axis of fetus vs mother</mark>
vertex 95%, breech 4% · frank (70%, knees extended, vaginal OK) vs complete vs footling (not vaginal)
occiput, sacrum or chin vs right/left and anterior/posterior of the canal
left occiput anterior most common · occiput anterior presents the biparietal diameter (9.5 cm), occiput posterior presents the widest part and pushing is long

blocks.html: • Lie and presentation are confirmed by vaginal exam, Leopold maneuvers (fundus → fetal back → part at the inlet → attitude) and/or ultrasound
6. Second stage

• Progress = station: 0 = ischial spines, then +1 to +5 cm (or thirds)
    • trial of labour is the only true test of pelvic adequacy
  • Cardinal movements (Every Darn Fetus Is Extremely Eager to Exit)
    • engagement → descent → flexion → internal rotation → extension → external rotation (restitution) → expulsion (anterior shoulder under the pubis first, then posterior)

blocks.alt: cardinal movements of labour - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The cardinal movements of labour, step by step: head floating before engagement, engagement with flexion and descent, further descent with internal rotation, complete rotation and beginning extension, complete extension, restitution (external rotation), delivery of the anterior shoulder, then of the posterior shoulder

blocks.html:
• Pelvis: best gynecoid and android · platypelloid and anthropoid (narrow or flat) inhibit the cardinal movements
  • Monitoring: FHR intermittent every 5 min or continuous
  • Pain from S2-S4 → pudendal block (local)
7. Third stage

• Signs of separation: uterus firm and globular (earliest) · gush of blood · uterus rises (placenta in the lower segment) · cord lengthens
  • Active management (WHO / Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada)
    • uterotonic (Syntocinon or ergot) + gentle cord traction + fundal massage
    • involution is oxytocin-mediated · inspect and repair lacerations

rows: anal sphincter complex: 3a <50% of external anal sphincter · 3b >50% of external anal sphincter · 3c internal anal sphincter torn

blocks.html: 8. Fourth stage

• Mother: maternal vitals · autotransfusion up to 500 mL → ↑ cardiac work · watch for postpartum hemorrhage
  • Baby: accommodation to air · breastfeeding

lectures.name: Abnormal Labour
lectures.title: Abnormal labour and birth
lectures.framing: The lecture walks the fixes in the order you reach for them when labour stalls: work out which of the 4 P's is the problem → induce or augment → help with an instrument → cesarean section. It ends on the two things that go wrong around birth: uterine rupture and postpartum hemorrhage.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Uterine atony is the #1 cause of PPH - so a firm uterus sends you looking for tears instead. Abnormal FHR is the #1 reason for forceps or vacuum, and the first sign of uterine rupture. Vacuum cannot rotate; forceps can. A previous C/S for dystocia lowers the odds of a VBAC; one for breech raises them. Bishop under 6 → ripen before you induce. Carboprost: not in asthma. Ergonovine: not in hypertension.

blocks.html: 1. Labour dystocia and the 4 P's

• Labour dystocia = abnormally slow progress through labour
    • slow cervical dilatation = failure to progress · slow descent = failure to descend
    • the most common reason cited for a cesarean section (C/S)
    • not the same as shoulder dystocia, which is an emergency (shoulder stuck behind the pubic bone)
  • When labour is slow, go through the 4 P's and fix the ones you can:

rows: Weak contractions: <mark class="lo">artificial rupture of membranes (ARM), then IV oxytocin</mark> · weak pushing: oxytocin, coaching, pain relief
Cannot be changed without breaking bone · symphysiotomy only in theory (last resort in severe shoulder dystocia)
Presentation and position yes, size no
Breech → external cephalic version (ECV), before labour · rotate (by hand or forceps) to occiput anterior · too big to fit → C/S for cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
Continuous support improves maternal and fetal outcomes · pain control as the patient wishes (not an epidural for everyone)

blocks.html: 2. Induction of labour

• Indications - any condition that raises the risk to mother or fetus
    • post dates · preeclampsia · diabetes · maternal disease (cardiac, renal, respiratory) · prelabour rupture of membranes · fetal growth restriction · placental abruption or insufficiency · twins · oligohydramnios · cholestasis of pregnancy · fetal anemia from alloimmunization · fetal demise
    • low risk at 39 weeks (ARRIVE trial): fewer cesareans, less preeclampsia, fewer stillbirths
  • Contraindications (anything that rules out labour): placenta previa, vasa previa, cord presentation · transverse lie · prior classical C/S or major uterine surgery · active genital herpes · invasive cervical cancer
  • Pre-induction assessment
    • confirm the due date · fetal position · estimated fetal weight · cervical exam · consent
    • cervix scored by the Bishop score: under 6 = unfavourable → ripen it first · over 6 = favourable (shorter induction, more vaginal births)
    • also raise success: multiparity · ruptured membranes · lower BMI · taller height · smaller baby · no preeclampsia
  • Method, in two steps
    • ① Cervical ripening to about 2 cm: chemical = prostaglandins (Cervidil, Prostin gel, misoprostol) · mechanical = Foley catheter balloon
    • ② ARM, which may start labour on its own · if not, IV oxytocin

blocks.alt: Bishop score.png
blocks.cap: Bishop score: dilation, effacement, consistency, position and station each scored; under 6 needs ripening

blocks.html: 3. Augmentation with oxytocin

• Indication: labour has started but is not progressing (dystocia)
  • ARM, then an oxytocin infusion titrated to a good contraction pattern and cervical change
    • oxytocin can start contractions, strengthen weak ones, and boost pushing
    • contractions hard to measure → intrauterine pressure catheter
    • on oxytocin → continuous fetal heart monitoring, with time between contractions for the fetus to recover
4. Operative vaginal delivery

• Forceps or vacuum to speed up the 2nd stage (pushing)
  • Indications
    • fetal: atypical or abnormal fetal heart rate (FHR) - the #1 reason · head turned the wrong way (occiput transverse or posterior)
    • maternal: must avoid straining (cerebrovascular or cardiac disease) · exhaustion or ineffective pushing
    • labour: prolonged 2nd stage
  • Contraindications
    • absolute: unengaged head · cervix not fully dilated · not head-first (or face, brow) · CPD · fetal bleeding or bone disorder · any reason not to deliver vaginally
    • relative: poor head flexion · rotation over 45° (vacuum only) · head still mid-pelvis · prematurity

rows: Cannot apply them properly · no descent with traction · 20 min
Mother: more tears · baby: facial nerve palsy, eye injury

blocks.html: • Newborn scalp collections: subgaleal hemorrhage spreads (dangerous) · cephalohematoma is cut off at the suture lines · caput succedaneum = swelling with a poorly defined edge

blocks.alt: newborn scalp layers - caput cephalohematoma subgaleal hemorrhage - lecture slide.png
blocks.cap: Newborn scalp layers: caput above the galea, cephalohematoma under the periosteum, subgaleal hemorrhage under the galea

blocks.html: 5. Cesarean section

• Indications
    • the big four, 70% of all C/S: dystocia · abnormal FHR · previous C/S · malpresentation (breech or transverse)
    • others: abnormal placenta (previa, vasa previa, accreta) · blockage (fibroid, mass) · maternal infection (herpes, HIV) · twins or more · cervical cancer · fetal anomalies
    • breech is more likely with: uterine anomalies · pelvic tumours · previa · hydrocephalus or anencephaly · oligohydramnios · a lax uterus (many births, polyhydramnios, multiples) · previous breech
    • cord prolapse: overt (cord seen or felt) · occult (beside the head) · cord presentation (below the head, before the waters break) · most likely in transverse lie, least in head-first
  • Incisions
    • skin: Pfannenstiel (low transverse) is standard · vertical midline for a crash section, obesity, an old scar, a bleeding disorder
    • uterus: low transverse is standard and allows a later trial of labour · a classical (vertical) or T-shaped scar does not
  • Complications
    • infection: endometritis 4-5% (35-40% without antibiotics) · wound infection
    • bleeding: average loss 800-1000 mL · 1-2% need a transfusion
    • blood clots (venous thromboembolism) 4× a vaginal birth · bladder injury ~1% · death 0.53 vs 0.04 per 1000
    • next pregnancy: placenta previa 2-3×, placenta accreta 5×
    • injury to bowel, ureters, nerves · more pain, longer recovery · anesthetic risks

blocks.alt: cesarean uterine incisions including T-extension and classical - lecture slide.png
blocks.cap: Uterine incisions: low transverse is standard; a T-extension or classical scar rules out a trial of labour

blocks.html: 6. Trial of labour after cesarean (TOLAC)

• A trial of labour that succeeds = a vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC), 60-80% of the time
  • Who can try: 1-2 prior low transverse C/S · over 18 months since · emergency laparotomy available within 30 min · no contraindication to labour · the patient agrees
  • Who cannot: classical or inverted-T scar · previous surgery entering the uterine cavity (hysterotomy, myomectomy) · previous uterine rupture · a contraindication to labour · the patient prefers a repeat C/S

rows: Previous vaginal birth or VBAC · favourable cervix · labour starts on its own · last C/S for a one-off reason (breech) · age under 40
Last C/S for dystocia · needs induction or augmentation · past 40 weeks · baby over 4000 g · BMI over 30 · hypertension

blocks.html:
• Benefits of a VBAC: shorter stay · fewer blood clots · less pain · less blood loss · fewer newborn breathing problems · lower risk of previa and accreta next time · fewer infections and hysterectomies
  • Risks of TOLAC: scar separation 0.5% · true uterine rupture 0.1%
7. Uterine rupture

• Mostly a scarred uterus in a TOLAC · rare without a scar (trauma, prolonged labour, oxytocin)
  • Risk factors: many previous births · uterine anomaly · older mother · dystocia · big baby · multiples · short gap between pregnancies
  • Presents as: abnormal FHR (the first sign) · contractions stop · the presenting part is lost on exam · abdominal pain · vaginal bleeding · blood in urine · mother unstable · fetal parts felt through the abdomen
  • Outcome: fetal death or brain injury · maternal transfusion, hysterectomy, organ injury, death
8. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)

• Definition: over 500 mL after a vaginal birth · over 1000 mL after a C/S · or any loss making the mother unstable
    • early = within 24 hours · late = 24 hours to 12 weeks
    • 5.6 per 100 deliveries in Canada · a top-5 cause of maternal death · 60% have a risk factor you can spot before delivery
    • severity: stage 2 = systolic 80-100, heart rate over 110 · stage 3 = systolic under 80, heart rate over 120

rows: Overstretched (polyhydramnios, multiples, big baby) · tired muscle (long labour, many births, long oxytocin use, general anesthetic) · infection · fibroids, previa
Extra placental lobe · placenta stuck to the wall · clots
Fast or instrumental delivery · previous uterine surgery · inversion from pulling too hard on the cord
von Willebrand disease, hemophilia A · disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) · HELLP syndrome · abruption · amniotic fluid embolism · blood thinners

blocks.html:
• Complications: maternal death · iron deficiency anemia · Sheehan's syndrome (pituitary infarction → poor milk supply) · transfusion · clotting failure · organ damage from shock
  • Prevention: treat anemia in pregnancy · spot risk factors before delivery · give a uterotonic in the 3rd stage (oxytocin or carbetocin) · act fast
  • Management ("ORDER": oxygenate, restore volume, drugs, evaluate, remedy the cause):

lectures.name: Hemorrhagic Shock
lectures.title: Hemorrhagic shock
lectures.framing: Shock is cellular hypoxia, and hemorrhagic shock is the hypovolemic kind: lost blood → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output. The lecture walks it in order: recognise shock → grade the loss from the vitals → remember why the obstetric patient fools you → resuscitate → prevent the lethal triad, because she is young, healthy and volume-expanded, so she compensates until she suddenly does not.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Blood pressure is normal through class II (up to 30% loss, ~1500 mL); it falls only in class III, so a normal BP does not exclude shock and tachycardia (> 100, class II) is the first vital to move. ⚠ Do not overlook the young healthy patient: she may surprise you with how much she has lost while still looking well. Bleeding is treated by stopping the bleeding; fluids and blood buy time, and each unit given feeds the coagulopathy arm of the triad.

blocks.html: 1. Shock and its features

• Shock = cellular and tissue hypoxia (↓ oxygen delivery, ↑ oxygen consumption, or poor oxygen use)
    • hypovolemic shock = ↓ intravascular volume → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output
    • two kinds: hemorrhagic (blood loss) · non-hemorrhagic (↓ circulating volume, e.g. extreme dehydration)
  • Presents as - the 8 features of shock
    • hypotension · tachycardia · oliguria · abnormal mental status · tachypnea · cool, clammy, cyanotic skin · metabolic acidosis · hyperlactatemia
2. Classes of hemorrhagic shock
• The pattern to learn: blood pressure holds through class II · the earliest signals are a ↑ pulse and a ↓ pulse pressure
3. Why obstetrics and gynecology is different

• The population is young and healthy
  • The post-partum woman has a pregnancy-expanded blood volume, built for the blood loss of delivery
    • so she compensates well despite a large loss

blocks.title: Do not overlook the young healthy patient
blocks.html: ⚠ She may surprise you with how much she has lost while still looking well.
4. Initial management

• First moves
    • airway, breathing, circulation and call for HELP
    • vitals: heart rate, blood pressure (BP), respiratory rate, O2 saturation · arterial blood gas / venous blood gas
    • Foley to urometer (urine output is a vital sign here)
  • Investigations
    • complete blood count · group and screen · partial thromboplastin time / international normalized ratio · fibrinogen · creatinine
  • Resuscitation
    • large-bore intravenous (IV) x 2, crystalloids / colloids · O2
    • blood products (packed red blood cells, platelets, cryoprecipitate, fresh frozen plasma) → consider massive transfusion protocol
  • Treat the cause
    • identify and address the cause, stop the bleeding
  • Transfer of care
    • consider the intensive care unit (ICU): inotropes, central lines
  • Throughout: prevent the lethal triad (section 5)
5. The lethal triad

rows: Impairs the clotting complexes that involve Ca2+; at pH 7.0 recombinant activated factor VII activity falls 90%
Maintain tissue perfusion: O2, IV fluids, red blood cell transfusion
A significant drop, below 35°C, also impairs clotting
Warmed IV fluids · Bair Hugger · Level I warmer
Dilutional: IV fluid plus transfused packed red blood cells dilute her own clotting factors; worsens progressively at 10, 20, 30 units
Limit blood loss: every unit avoided is coagulopathy avoided

lectures.name: Lactation
lectures.title: Lactation
lectures.framing: Lactation needs three things: prolactin to make milk, oxytocin to eject it, and removal of milk by infant or pump, which must begin by day 3. Nearly every breastfeeding problem is a failure of one of the three, so ask which one broke.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ By day 3 control switches from endocrine to autocrine: milk removal, not hormone, now drives supply, which is why removal must start by day 3 and why poor extraction lowers production. Low supply is the most common reason to stop breastfeeding. Mastitis is treated by continuing to nurse, not by stopping; an abscess needs drainage. Breast size doesn't matter. Alcohol is not a contraindication; smoking and street drugs are to be avoided.

blocks.html: 1. The four stages

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • 4 stages: mammogenesis (breast preparation) → lactogenesis (synthesis from alveoli; stage 1 mid-pregnancy, stage 2 copious after delivery) → galactokinesis (ejection) → galactopoiesis (maintenance)
2. Breast anatomy

• Lobes: 15-20 per breast, split by fibrous septae · each drained by a lactiferous duct
  • Lobules inside each lobe hold the terminal duct lobular units - the milk-making alveoli, wrapped in myoepithelial cells that contract to squeeze milk out
  • Milk's path: terminal ducts → lactiferous ducts → lactiferous sinus → opening on the nipple

blocks.alt: breast anatomy - lobules alveoli lactiferous ducts.png
blocks.cap: Breast anatomy: lobules and alveoli drain through lactiferous ducts and sinuses to the nipple

blocks.html: 3. Physiology: prolactin and oxytocin

rows: Suckling, nipple stimulation · even the sound of the cry

blocks.alt: milk production and let-down reflex - prolactin and oxytocin.png
blocks.cap: Suckling reflex: prolactin from the anterior pituitary makes milk, oxytocin from the posterior pituitary ejects it

blocks.html:
• Endocrine → autocrine
    • early on, hormones drive milk-making · by day 3, milk removal does
    • so removal must start by day 3, and poor extraction lowers production

blocks.alt: lactogenesis timeline - endocrine to autocrine control.png
blocks.cap: Lactogenesis timeline: hormonal control in pregnancy switches to local milk-removal control after birth

blocks.html: 4. Breast milk over time

rows: Antibodies, cells, vitamins A, D, E, K · passive immunity
Exclusive to 6 months, then complementary foods, breastfeeding to 2 years+
Content varies by woman, stage and time of day

blocks.html: • Breast size doesn't matter for the ability to breastfeed
5. Feeding in the first week

• Start within 1 hour of birth, skin to skin, feed on infant cues
  • Storage - laws of 6: room 6 hours · fridge 6 days · freezer 6 months
6. Troubleshooting: low supply, mastitis, abscess
• Low supply is the most common reason to stop breastfeeding · it is either inadequate production or poor extraction

• Insulin resistance, ↑ androgens, polycystic ovarian syndrome, prolactinoma

• Preterm · neonatal intensive care unit · separation of mother and infant

Breast infection · Staphylococcus aureus most common organism

Incise and drain / needle aspirate + analgesia, bra, emptying, antibiotics

blocks.html: 7. Medications, alcohol and drugs

• Medications: milk concentration < 10% of maternal weight-adjusted dose
  • Alcohol is not a contraindication · smoking and street drugs are to be avoided
8. Contraindications to breastfeeding

• HIV in developed countries (World Health Organization: OK if both on antiretroviral therapy)
  • active psychosis · active tuberculosis · herpetic breast lesions · antineoplastic drugs
  • infant galactosemia · phenylketonuria with high infant phenylalanine
  • patient refuses
9. Stopping breastfeeding

• Urgent: cabergoline 1 mg once
  • ⚠ Abrupt weaning not recommended - rapid ↓ prolactin may ↑ depressive symptoms
  • Gradual, child-led after 6 months is easiest
  • Comfort: supportive bra, ice, analgesics, cabbage leaves
10. Supplementing with formula
• Reasons: patient choice · inadequate supply with poor growth / failure to thrive · infant dehydration, hypoglycemia, weight loss or poor gain
11. Contraception while breastfeeding

• ⚠ Avoid estrogen-containing products - ↓ quality and quantity of milk.
  • Safe: hormonal or copper intrauterine device · progesterone-only pill · barrier · Depo-Provera

lectures.name: Postpartum Care
lectures.title: Postpartum care
lectures.framing: The puerperium is a return to baseline on a fixed timetable, so the complication is whatever breaks the timetable: blues past 2 weeks, bright red bleeding returning after 24 h, fever on 2 of the first 10 days.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Blues that last more than 2 weeks, or are severe within the first 2 weeks, are postpartum depression. ⚠ EPDS item 10 scored 1-3 at any total is a self-harm risk needing immediate assessment. The puerperal-infection clock excludes the first 24 h, and delayed PPH starts after 24 h. Refer ALL antepartum and postpartum patients to pelvic floor physiotherapy.

blocks.html: 1. Discharge from hospital

• Discharge < 48 h: assess the 4 B's - bleeding · bowel · bladder · baby care
  • Contraindications: preeclampsia · postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) · fever · unstable medical condition
2. Perineal and bowel care

• Perineum: clean, dry, sitz baths, pericare bottle
  • Bowel: fibre, fluids, laxatives · no rectal (per rectum) medications after a 3rd or 4th degree tear
3. Sex, ovulation and fertility

• Sexual activity: most wait a minimum of 6 weeks · contraception starts at 6 weeks
  • ⚠ Lactational amenorrhea is NOT contraception: ovulation can occur without menstruation
4. Back to baseline: the timetable

rows: cardiac output (↑ stroke volume from venous return) · leukocytosis within the first days
blood volume · cervical canal reforms (50% of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions regress)
placental site involuted · contraception starts · pelvic floor physiotherapy can start
<mark class="lo">lochia may last this long (rubra → serosa → alba)</mark>

blocks.alt: pregnancy and lactation hormone and milk changes over time.png
blocks.cap: Hormones across pregnancy and lactation: progesterone and estrogen fall at birth, prolactin stays up, colostrum gives way to mature milk

blocks.html: 5. Postpartum mood changes

rows: major depression within 6 months · suspect if blues > 2 weeks, or severe in the first 2
weepiness · insomnia · poor concentration · anxiety · irritability · lability
M-SIGECAPS · severe = disrupted attachment, poor bonding, suicidal or homicidal ideation
cannot discern real from unreal · often with other mood disorders

previous depression (30% recurrence) · postnatal stress (neonatal intensive care unit, stillbirth) · poor support · age < 25 · single · family history · intimate partner violence · unintended pregnancy
younger age · primiparity · family history of psychiatric illness · previous bipolar or schizoaffective

blocks.html: • Screening for depression: the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) on the antenatal record, then the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) or Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)
6. Delayed bleeding, infection and clots

rows: temperature > 38.0°C on any 2 of the first 10 days, excluding the first 24 h (oral, at least four times daily)
return of bright red bleeding with or without fever, chills, tender uterus
most common postpartum complication · endometritis: cesarean section (CS) 30% non-elective, 7% elective, 3% vaginal
deep vein thrombosis · pulmonary embolism · septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
antibiotics · ultrasound to rule out retained products of conception · uterotonic if tissue vs dilation and curettage
amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 875 mg by mouth twice daily for 7-10 days · septic: clindamycin + gentamicin intravenous

blocks.html: 7. The postnatal visit

• History
    • review of birth (obstetric anal sphincter injury, cesarean section) · bladder · bowel · sexual function · lochia / menses · perineum / incision
    • emotional wellbeing + EPDS · feeding · smoking, alcohol, substances
  • Physical exam
    • weight vs pre-pregnancy · blood pressure · affect · thyroid · breasts · abdomen · perineum · pelvic
  • Investigations
    • rubella immune? tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis vaccine up to date? · influenza · last Pap
  • Counsel
    • contraception · pelvic floor exercises · future pregnancies, and if CS, mode of birth + spacing
8. Contraception

• No estrogen-containing method before 21 days (venous thromboembolism) · debated effect on breastmilk
  • Usable: barriers, combined hormonal contraceptives, progesterone-only pill, depot Provera, hormonal and copper intrauterine devices
9. Pelvic floor physiotherapy

• Refer every antepartum and postpartum patient · can start from 6 weeks postpartum
  • Benefits: ↓ severe tears · ↓ length of pushing · better recovery · ↓ urinary incontinence after birth

lectures.name: Approach to Neonatal Care
lectures.title: Approach to Neonatal Care
lectures.framing: Every newborn is examined within 24 h and kept pink, warm and sweet; the extra care turns on which reserve this baby lacks: heat (no shivering), glucose (glycogen lasts 8-10 h, gluconeogenesis not normal until 2-4 days), or bilirubin clearance.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Symptomatic hypoglycemia is a medical emergency: IV dextrose, not a feed (a jittery IDM who cannot latch, glucose 2.3). The GA curves run higher the more mature the baby, so the same TSB can need treatment at 35 weeks and not at 40. ⚠ Sepsis runs through all three: hypoglycemia can be a sign of it, it causes hyperbilirubinemia, and temperature instability is a jaundice risk factor, so consider it in any sick baby.

blocks.html: 1. The Apgar score
• Scored at 1 and 5 minutes · maximum 10 · 7+ normal · 4-6 low · under 3 critically low → resuscitate
2. The full newborn exam

• Examine every newborn within 24 h - about 3% have a major congenital malformation
  • Look for: dysmorphic features · a blocked gut · congenital heart disease · tone and feeding · urine and meconium passed before discharge
  • Growth: head circumference, length and weight plotted on a growth curve
3. Hypothermia - keep them warm

• Why newborns: warm womb → naked, wet, large surface area · variable fat · cannot shiver
  • At risk: preterm · < 1500 g
  • Presents as: cold stress
  • Treatment: dry · wrap · hats · ↑ room temperature · incubator (< 1500 g) · radiant warmer · humidity
  • Harm: feeds hypoglycemia (excess use)

blocks.alt: newborn heat loss - conduction convection evaporation radiation.png
blocks.cap: The four ways a newborn loses heat: conduction, convection, evaporation and radiation

blocks.html: 4. Hypoglycemia - keep them sweet

• Why newborns: fetus wholly on maternal glucose · glycogen for 8-10 h · gluconeogenesis normal only at 2-4 days
  • At risk
    • Inadequate substrate: intrauterine growth restriction, maternal hypertension, multiples, prematurity
    • Excess use: large for gestational age (LGA), infant of a diabetic mother (IDM), hypothermia, sepsis, asphyxia
  • Presents as: jittery, irritable, lethargic, poor feeding
  • Screen: at-risk babies only, 2 h after first feed · "2.6, no more sticks"
  • Treatment: early frequent feeds · intravenous (IV) dextrose if symptomatic · glucagon
  • Harm: neuronal injury

blocks.html: 5. Jaundice: physiology and who is at risk

• All babies' bilirubin rises in the first days · most common cause = exaggerated physiologic / breastfeeding jaundice
  • At risk: isoimmune hemolysis · glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency · asphyxia · respiratory distress · bruising / cephalohematoma · sepsis · acidosis · preterm · sibling needed phototherapy · East Asian
  • Presents as: yellow, spreading head → toe

blocks.alt: neonatal bilirubin metabolism pathway.png
blocks.cap: Bilirubin metabolism: production from heme, albumin transport, liver uptake and conjugation, excretion and enterohepatic circulation

blocks.html: 6. Jaundice: screening and investigation

• Screen: universal at 24-48 h, transcutaneous or blood · plot on normative curve
  • Red flags
    • jaundice in the first 24 h is pathologic · cord bilirubin > 68 μmol/L · rise > 85 μmol/L/day · total > 340 μmol/L
    • direct > 30 μmol/L or > 20% of total · jaundice > 2 weeks in a term infant · unwell child
  • History: feeding and activity · septic risk factors · birth trauma / hypoxia · family history (G6PD deficiency)
  • Physical exam: blanch the nose · progresses head to toe · ⚠ colour is not predictive of the bilirubin level · weight change
  • Investigations: total and direct bilirubin · direct antiglobulin test · hemoglobin · maternal and baby blood groups and antibodies
7. Jaundice: treatment and complications

• Plot total serum bilirubin (TSB) on the gestational age (GA)-specific curve
  • Neurotoxicity risk factors (act at a lower TSB): < 38 weeks · albumin < 30 · suspected hemolysis · suspected sepsis · hemodynamic or respiratory instability
  • Rules of 30 (≥ 35 weeks): phototherapy when within 30 μmol/L of the threshold in a baby with these risk factors · stop when > 30 below (≥ 38 weeks) or > 60 below (35-37 weeks)
  • Treatment: phototherapy (blue, 460-490 nm) · treat the cause · intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) · exchange transfusion
  • Phototherapy works three ways: Z → E isomerization (to bile) · cyclization to lumirubin (bile, urine) · oxidation (urine)

blocks.alt: phototherapy mechanism - blue light and bilirubin isomers.png
blocks.cap: Phototherapy: blue light around 460-490 nm turns bilirubin into isomers excreted in bile and urine

blocks.html:
• Harm: acute bilirubin encephalopathy → kernicterus (basal ganglia, brainstem nuclei)
    • lethargy, hypotonia, poor suck → hypertonia with opisthotonos and retrocollis, high-pitched cry, fever → seizures, coma
8. Global perspectives

• 5.4 million under-5 deaths a year, 44% neonatal (2,532,000)
  • Biggest neonatal slices: preterm complications 15%, intrapartum events 11%, sepsis 7%
  • Helping Babies Survive (American Academy of Pediatrics, World Health Organization, United States Agency for International Development)
